items.stem: A 34-year-old man admitted last night for opioid use disorder asks to start buprenorphine right away — 'I don't want to get sick.' His last heroin use was about 6 hours ago. He is anxious but has no yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, or piloerection; his COWS score is 4. Best next step?

options.t: Start buprenorphine now, before the withdrawal becomes severe

trap.name: Comfort-first induction
trap.note: Starting early to spare the patient discomfort is what causes the discomfort — induction waits for objective withdrawal, not for the request.

options.t: Continue serial COWS scoring and start buprenorphine once objective withdrawal is present (COWS roughly 8 to 12)
Give a benzodiazepine to control the withdrawal symptoms

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines treat alcohol and sedative withdrawal — opioid withdrawal is tracked with the COWS and treated with agonist therapy.

options.t: Reassure him that opioid withdrawal is not dangerous and defer any medication

trap.name: Not lethal = not treatable
trap.note: Opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal but intensely miserable — and untreated it drives discharge against advice into the highest-overdose-risk window.

items.why: Comfort-first induction is the trap the request invites — buprenorphine started before objective withdrawal precipitates the withdrawal it was meant to prevent. Serial COWS scores make the timing objective: induction begins at roughly 8 to 12, not at the patient's anxiety. The benzodiazepine belongs to alcohol and sedative withdrawal, and 'not dangerous' is not a plan when MOUD linkage is the discharge intervention.
items.pearl: Do not start buprenorphine until objective withdrawal is on board (COWS roughly ≥ 8 to 12) or you may precipitate withdrawal.
items.evidence: t_sud.md 'Acute inpatient management' — begin buprenorphine induction only once objective withdrawal is present (roughly COWS ≥ 8 to 12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal from displacing residual full agonist too early.

tier2.q: Why must buprenorphine wait for objective withdrawal?

options.t: Buprenorphine is ineffective until the urine drug screen has cleared
Early dosing risks oversedation and respiratory arrest from stacking agonists
As a high-affinity partial agonist, buprenorphine displaces residual full agonist from the receptor — started too early, it precipitates withdrawal
Waiting builds the patient's motivation to engage with treatment

tier2.why: It is a receptor-displacement problem, not a clearance, sedation, or motivation problem — the partial agonist evicts the remaining full agonist and the net signal drops abruptly. Making the patient 'earn' the dose has no place in a non-judgmental, brain-disease framing of addiction.

items.stem: A family meeting is held the day before planned discharge for a 52-year-old man admitted after a suicide attempt by overdose. When the agenda reaches safety and warning signs, his wife says: 'We'll keep a close eye on him. And you don't need to worry about the guns — he would never use them, and they're put away.' The attending invites your input. Which response is best?

options.t: 'It makes sense that everyone is exhausted and scared. Before discharge, who can confirm that the firearms — and any stockpiled medications — are actually secured, and how will we know it's done?'
'Firearms are involved in about half of US suicides and are lethal in 85 to 90 percent of attempts — "put away" isn't good enough.'

trap.name: Quoting statistics at families
trap.note: The numbers explain the why to you — recited at a frightened family they become an argument, and arguing invites defense of the status quo.

options.t: 'That's reassuring — we'll document that the family will keep him safe and that the guns are secured.'

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Family support is data, not a substitute for risk reasoning — a safety plan with unconfirmed means safety is a known failure mode, not a completed task.

options.t: 'Discharge can't move forward unless you agree to remove every firearm from the home today.'

trap.name: Making the family responsible
trap.note: The goal is to understand what support is realistic, not to hand the family the treatment — and disposition ultimatums are not the student's call.

items.why: The best response validates first, stays inside the student role, and converts 'put away' into a concrete, verifiable step — who secures the items and how the team will know. Quoting lethality statistics at the family is the righting reflex in evidence clothing; accepting reassurance leaves means safety unconfirmed at the exact moment risk peaks; and an ultimatum makes the family responsible for treatment while overstepping the student's role.
items.pearl: Means safety is a lethality intervention, not a formality — 'who can confirm items are secured before discharge?' is a clinical act.
items.evidence: exp_family.md 'Why It Matters' — structured lethal-means counseling (CALM) cut attempts/deaths from 3.3% to 0.83% at 180 days; suicide risk peaks in the first week post-discharge (Chung et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017).

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman on hospital day 3 after hip-fracture repair is referred to psychiatry for 'depression.' She is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeps much of the day; her nurse notes she was conversational yesterday evening but is 'flat' this morning. She cannot recite the months of the year backward. Most likely explanation?

options.t: Major depressive episode — recommend starting an antidepressant

trap.name: Hypoactive delirium labeled depression
trap.note: The withdrawn, flat, quiet patient is the delirium presentation that gets missed — depression does not fluctuate across a single shift.

options.t: Early dementia unmasked by hospitalization

trap.name: Confused elder = dementia
trap.note: Dementia is chronic and progressive over months — a change that arrived in hours to days and waxes and wanes is delirium until proven otherwise.

options.t: Hypoactive delirium — screen for precipitating causes and deliriogenic medications
Expected postoperative fatigue — reassure the team and sign off

trap.name: Quiet patient = stable patient
trap.note: No one is alarmed by a quiet patient — which is exactly why hypoactive delirium is missed and carries worse outcomes.

items.why: Acute onset, a course that fluctuates across one shift, and failed months-backward — inattention, the cardinal deficit — assemble the CAM picture; low arousal makes it hypoactive delirium, the form most often mislabeled as depression or overlooked because the patient is quiet. Dementia declines over months, not shifts, and 'postoperative fatigue' does not take attention with it. The work now is finding the drivers — infection, metabolic derangement, deliriogenic medications, retention, constipation, pain.
items.pearl: Hypoactive delirium is the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, and easily mislabeled as depression.
items.evidence: delirium.md 'Recognize and screen' — Confusion Assessment Method (CAM, Inouye et al.): acute onset and fluctuating course, plus inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman is admitted for a severe depressive episode with passive suicidal ideation. The intern plans to start sertraline today. Before initiating an antidepressant, the most important step is which of the following?

options.t: Start sertraline now — the diagnosis of major depressive disorder is established by her current presentation

trap.name: Antidepressant before bipolar screen
trap.note: Starting an antidepressant without screening for bipolarity can destabilize an unrecognized bipolar patient into mania or rapid cycling.

options.t: Obtain a collateral history and formally screen for any prior manic or hypomanic episode before prescribing an antidepressant
Start sertraline and add lithium prophylactically to cover any occult bipolar risk

trap.name: Polypharmacy first
trap.note: Layering a mood stabilizer on an unconfirmed diagnosis substitutes complexity for the needed diagnostic step.

options.t: Start sertraline and a PRN benzodiazepine, since anxiety commonly accompanies depression

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Adding a benzodiazepine before the mood diagnosis is established compounds diagnostic uncertainty and adds dependence risk without benefit.

items.why: Antidepressant before bipolar screen is the key trap: an SSRI started in unrecognized bipolar disorder can trigger mania or rapid cycling. Obtaining collateral and screening for past mania or hypomania is the gatekeeping step before any antidepressant is written. Prophylactic lithium without a diagnosis is premature polypharmacy, and the reflexive benzodiazepine adds risk without resolving the diagnostic question.
items.pearl: Screen every depressed patient for past mania before writing for an antidepressant.
items.evidence: t_mood.md 'High-yield pearls' — Screen every depressed patient for past mania before writing for an antidepressant.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium maintenance for two years, presents with a 2-day course of worsening tremor, confusion, and vomiting. Five days ago he began ibuprofen for back pain. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

options.t: A breakthrough manic episode — agitation and confusion signal mood destabilization

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Mania does not cause vomiting and an acute 2-day toxic picture — this is a medication interaction problem, not a mood relapse.

options.t: Viral encephalitis — the confusion warrants urgent neuroimaging and lumbar puncture

trap.name: Missing the interaction
trap.note: Attributing a toxic picture to an infectious cause before checking the medication list in a patient on a narrow-therapeutic-window drug is a systematic miss.

options.t: Serotonin syndrome — lithium combined with ibuprofen triggers excess serotonin activity

trap.name: Wrong toxidrome
trap.note: Serotonin syndrome requires serotonergic agents and presents with clonus and hyperreflexia — neither fits; the clinical picture and the drug interaction both point to lithium toxicity.

options.t: Lithium toxicity precipitated by ibuprofen reducing renal lithium clearance

items.why: Treat the number not the patient, Missing the interaction, and Wrong toxidrome are the traps. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window; NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal clearance and push lithium levels into the toxic range — a textbook drug interaction. The 2-day picture of tremor, confusion, and vomiting in a lithium-maintained patient who just started an NSAID is lithium toxicity until proven otherwise.
items.pearl: NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push lithium levels toward toxicity — check the list when lithium patients deteriorate.
items.evidence: t_mood.md 'Lithium' — lithium runs a narrow therapeutic window (~0.6–1.2 mEq/L); NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push levels toward toxicity.

tier2.q: Why does ibuprofen raise lithium levels?

options.t: Ibuprofen displaces lithium from plasma protein binding, increasing free drug levels
Ibuprofen inhibits hepatic metabolism of lithium, slowing its clearance
Ibuprofen blocks gut absorption of lithium, causing erratic bioavailability and rebound toxicity
Lithium is cleared almost entirely by the kidney; NSAIDs impair prostaglandin-dependent renal handling, reducing lithium clearance and raising serum levels

tier2.why: Lithium is not protein-bound and not hepatically metabolized — it is excreted almost entirely by the kidney. NSAIDs impair prostaglandin-mediated renal perfusion and tubular handling, reducing lithium clearance. This is why the page flags them alongside dehydration and other drugs that reduce glomerular filtration or tubular function as conditions that push levels toward toxicity.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is admitted for new-onset paranoid ideation, disorganized behavior, and auditory hallucinations. Her chart notes she was started on high-dose prednisone three weeks ago for an autoimmune flare. Before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis, the most important step is which of the following?

options.t: Take a thorough medication and medical history and consider a substance- or medication-induced cause before labeling this a primary psychotic disorder
Start a second-generation antipsychotic immediately — symptom control should not await diagnostic clarity

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Treating before excluding a secondary cause may mask a reversible etiology and commit the patient to a diagnosis that is not hers.

options.t: Diagnose schizophreniform disorder based on symptom type and the absence of a prior psychiatric history

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Schizophreniform disorder requires exclusion of medical and substance causes — the diagnosis cannot be established while a high-dose corticosteroid is on board.

options.t: Reassure the family that first-episode psychosis in young adults is almost always primary and will respond to antipsychotics

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: First-episode psychosis has a broad differential — medication-induced, autoimmune, and substance-related causes must be excluded before prognosis can be offered.

items.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia is the trap in two forms: treating immediately or diagnosing before excluding secondary causes. Psychosis is a syndrome with a broad differential — corticosteroids are a recognized cause of secondary psychosis, and the clinical picture (new-onset, no prior history, active steroid course) demands a medical workup first. Face-value reassurance skips that step and commits to a prognosis without a diagnosis.
items.pearl: Psychosis is a syndrome — exclude delirium, substances, medications, and autoimmune causes before settling on a primary disorder.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md 'Differential and can't-miss mimics' — Always exclude secondary/medical psychosis before settling on a primary disorder. Screen for substance-induced causes (stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, withdrawal) and any medical or medication cause; corticosteroids are a recognized secondary cause (general clinical principle, not individually named on this source page). Do not miss autoimmune/limbic encephalitis.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on haloperidol 5 mg/day and sertraline 100 mg/day for a comorbid depressive episode. His sertraline was increased to 150 mg two days ago. He now presents with fever (38.9°C), agitation, diaphoresis, and muscle rigidity. CK is mildly elevated at 680 U/L. The differential includes serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Which finding, if present on examination, would most strongly support serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.t: Uniform lead-pipe resistance throughout the passive range of motion of the upper and lower extremities, with normal deep tendon reflexes.

trap.name: Lead-pipe rigidity = NMS, not SS
trap.note: Lead-pipe rigidity — uniform resistance throughout the passive range of motion — is the hallmark of NMS, produced by dopaminergic pathway dysfunction. Serotonin syndrome produces clonus and hyperreflexia, not lead-pipe rigidity; choosing this option confuses the two syndromes' defining physical features.

options.t: Creatine kinase (CK) above 5,000 U/L with rising creatinine suggesting early rhabdomyolysis.

trap.name: Markedly elevated CK = NMS signature
trap.note: Dramatically elevated CK (often tens of thousands) is a hallmark of NMS, driven by sustained muscular rigidity and potential rhabdomyolysis. CK in serotonin syndrome may be mildly elevated but rarely reaches NMS levels; a markedly elevated CK increases suspicion for NMS, not SS.

options.t: Gradual onset of rigidity and fever developing over 48–72 hours after the haloperidol was started three months ago, with no change in the serotonergic regimen.

trap.name: Subacute onset + dopamine blocker = NMS pattern
trap.note: A gradual onset timed to a dopamine-blocking agent rather than to a serotonergic change is the NMS pattern. Serotonin syndrome typically occurs within hours of a serotonergic dose increase or drug addition — the history in this option (no serotonergic change, onset tied to the antipsychotic) would favor NMS.

options.t: Ankle clonus with brisk, brisker-than-baseline deep tendon reflexes throughout the lower extremities.

items.why: Lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia → SS. The three distractors all describe NMS features: lead-pipe rigidity (A), dramatically elevated CK (B), and subacute onset tied to the dopamine blocker rather than the serotonergic change (C). Ankle clonus with lower-extremity hyperreflexia (D) is the hallmark physical finding of serotonin syndrome — it reflects serotonin-mediated hyperactivation of spinal reflex arcs and is absent in NMS, where rigidity comes from central dopaminergic dysfunction. The added clinical clues — onset after the sertraline increase, mild rather than dramatic CK — also favor SS over NMS. In practice, both syndromes require stopping the offending agent; the physical exam reflex pattern is the fastest bedside discriminator.
items.pearl: NMS vs. SS at the bedside: lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS (dopamine blocker, subacute onset); clonus + hyperreflexia → SS (serotonergic agent, rapid onset hours).
items.evidence: psychotic_disorders_inpatient_teaching.md 'Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs. serotonin syndrome' — The key discriminator: lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia = NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia (especially ankle clonus) = SS. Onset timeline and offending agent class support the differentiation (Boyer and Shannon, N Engl J Med 2005; Strawn et al., Am J Psychiatry 2007).

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman admitted for a manic episode is started on risperidone. Two days later she is restless, pacing the hallway, unable to sit through meals, and says she 'can't stop moving.' She denies worsening mood symptoms. Which of the following best explains her presentation?

options.t: Worsening mixed mania with motor agitation — increase the risperidone

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Adding more dopamine blockade to akathisia worsens the very symptom it is meant to treat — the restlessness is medication-induced, not mood-driven.

options.t: New-onset generalized anxiety disorder unmasked by hospitalization stress

trap.name: Missing the iatrogenic cause
trap.note: A new anxiety disorder diagnosis requires ruling out medication-induced causes — akathisia began 48 hours after a dopamine blocker was started.

options.t: Restless legs syndrome — the urge to move is confined to the lower extremities at rest

trap.name: RLS vs akathisia
trap.note: RLS is a distal, rest-provoked urge that improves with movement — akathisia is a global inner restlessness that does not resolve with movement and is not limb-specific.

options.t: Akathisia — medication-induced inner restlessness from dopamine blockade that worsens with more antipsychotic

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic is the dangerous error: escalating the dopamine blocker intensifies akathisia. Missing the iatrogenic cause leads to a wrong new diagnosis. RLS vs akathisia distinguishes them by distribution and provocation — RLS is limb-specific and rest-provoked; akathisia is global, medication-timed, and worsens with increased dosing.
items.pearl: Akathisia is the classic inpatient miss — inner restlessness from antipsychotics that worsens with more dopamine blockade, not less.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md 'Differential on the unit' — akathisia is the classic miss: restless, driven motor anxiety from antipsychotics that worsens if you reflexively treat it as 'agitation' with more dopamine blockade.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman admitted for a severe depressive episode is also found to have untreated PTSD — she endorses daily nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance behaviors that have persisted for two years since an assault. She has no history of substance use disorder. After addressing the acute safety concern, which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for her PTSD?

options.t: Start scheduled lorazepam — benzodiazepines reduce hyperarousal and improve sleep, targeting PTSD's core neurobiological substrate

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines drive dependence, falls, and delirium and are not a treatment for PTSD — standing benzodiazepines for anxiety disorders are explicitly to be avoided on the inpatient unit.

options.t: Start an SSRI or SNRI, counsel her about delayed onset, and plan trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) as a discharge goal
Start propranolol — beta blockade prevents autonomic consolidation of traumatic memories and is first-line for established PTSD

trap.name: Wrong mechanism for PTSD
trap.note: Propranolol is studied as an acute peritraumatic adjunct — it is not first-line pharmacotherapy for established PTSD; SSRIs and SNRIs are.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic for the intrusive re-experiencing — flashback-like episodes indicate psychotic features requiring dopamine blockade

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Intrusive re-experiencing in PTSD is not psychosis — antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD and conflating the two is the inpatient trap that delays correct treatment.

items.why: The reflexive benzodiazepine is the most common trap — standing benzos for PTSD create dependence without treating the disorder and are explicitly avoided on the inpatient unit. SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across all anxiety disorders and PTSD; definitive treatment pairs medication with trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) planned at discharge. Propranolol is studied in acute peritraumatic settings, not as first-line pharmacotherapy for established PTSD. Antipsychotics conflate re-experiencing with psychosis.
items.pearl: SSRIs/SNRIs are first-line for PTSD — benzodiazepines are a liability on the unit; pair medication with trauma-focused therapy (PE or CPT) at discharge.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md 'Acute inpatient management' — SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD; avoid standing benzodiazepines on the unit; pair pharmacology with disorder-specific behavioral work — prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) for PTSD.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of heavy daily alcohol use is admitted in early withdrawal — tremulous and tachycardic. A nurse is about to start an IV dextrose infusion for a fingerstick glucose in the low-normal range. The most important step before administering the glucose is which of the following?

options.t: Obtain a CIWA-Ar score to guide benzodiazepine dosing before starting any IV fluids

trap.name: Sequence error
trap.note: CIWA-Ar scoring is essential for withdrawal management but does not address the thiamine-before-glucose imperative — both are needed, but thiamine is the safety gate specifically for glucose administration.

options.t: Confirm his blood alcohol level has cleared to zero before giving glucose-containing fluids

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Waiting for alcohol clearance before glucose misses the danger — the risk is Wernicke encephalopathy from carbohydrate loading in a thiamine-depleted brain, not from residual alcohol.

options.t: Administer thiamine before or with the glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Reassure the team that Wernicke encephalopathy risk applies only to patients with a documented prior episode

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Wernicke risk exists in any patient with heavy alcohol use and thiamine depletion — a prior documented episode is not a prerequisite.

items.why: Sequence error and It's just withdrawal are the traps. Administering carbohydrate to a thiamine-depleted patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy — a preventable neurologic emergency. The rule is simple and categorical: thiamine before glucose, every time, without requiring a prior history of encephalopathy.
items.pearl: Thiamine before glucose, every time — carbohydrate loading in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
items.evidence: t_sud.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Give thiamine before glucose — administering carbohydrate to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. High-yield pearl: 'Thiamine before glucose, every time.'

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disorder is found mute and immobile in her room, staring past the examiner. When the examiner positions her arm in an awkward posture, it remains in place for over a minute. A colleague suggests starting haloperidol for presumed psychosis. Best next step?

options.t: Evaluate for catatonia using a structured rating instrument before initiating any antipsychotic
Start haloperidol immediately — mutism and posturing indicate untreated psychosis

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Giving an antipsychotic before catatonia is excluded can precipitate or worsen neuroleptic malignant syndrome — mutism and waxy flexibility are catatonic signs, not automatically psychotic symptoms.

options.t: Apply a physical hold for safety while awaiting psychiatric evaluation

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Restraint is the least-restrictive principle's last resort — an immobile, mute patient is not threatening anyone; the priority is diagnostic evaluation.

options.t: Order a urine drug screen and defer further evaluation to the morning team

trap.name: Quiet patient = stable patient
trap.note: An immobile, mute patient in a sustained abnormal posture requires urgent evaluation — deferring because she appears calm is the hypoactive-delirium error applied to catatonia.

items.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia drives the dangerous action: haloperidol in an unexcluded catatonia can precipitate NMS. Waxy flexibility (sustained posturing) is a catatonic sign — catatonia must be rated before any dopamine blocker is started. Restraint first violates least-restrictive principle; Quiet patient = stable patient defers an urgent evaluation.
items.pearl: Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is excluded — they can precipitate or worsen NMS and malignant catatonia; the lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
items.evidence: catatonia.md 'Management principles' — avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is excluded — they can precipitate or worsen NMS and malignant catatonia. A positive lorazepam challenge both supports the diagnosis and begins treatment.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man with a history of depression on high-dose sertraline is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after a second serotonergic medication was added to his regimen. Examination shows agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and clonus; reflexes are brisk and symmetrically hyperactive throughout. Temperature is 38.3°C. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

options.t: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — high-dose SSRIs can block dopamine receptors

trap.name: Wrong toxidrome
trap.note: NMS requires a dopamine blocker and presents with lead-pipe rigidity — clonus and hyperreflexia are the serotonin syndrome fingerprint.

options.t: Anticholinergic toxidrome — sertraline has strong anticholinergic activity

trap.name: Wrong toxidrome
trap.note: SSRIs have minimal anticholinergic activity; anticholinergic toxidrome presents with dry/flushed skin, urinary retention, and confusion — not clonus or diarrhea.

options.t: Alcohol withdrawal — autonomic instability and agitation are hallmarks

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Alcohol withdrawal produces tremor, diaphoresis, and tachycardia but not clonus or hyperreflexia — and there is no alcohol use context in this stem.

options.t: Serotonin syndrome — rapid onset after a second serotonergic agent was added, with hyperreflexia, clonus, and autonomic instability

items.why: Wrong toxidrome is the common trap in two directions: NMS (requires a dopamine blocker, slower, lead-pipe rigid) and anticholinergic (dry skin, urinary retention, no clonus). It's just withdrawal misreads autonomic instability without the serotonin-specific signs. Serotonin syndrome is the answer: rapid onset after serotonergic augmentation, clonus, hyperreflexia, and autonomic instability are its distinguishing features.
items.pearl: Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset, clonus, hyperreflexia after a serotonergic agent was added. NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, elevated CK, on a dopamine blocker — slower and stiffer.
items.evidence: psychopharm_primer.md — Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, and autonomic instability with rapid onset, usually after a serotonergic agent was started or increased. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: 'lead-pipe' rigidity, hyperthermia, and elevated CK in someone on a dopamine blocker — slower and stiffer than serotonin syndrome.

tier2.q: Why does this presentation fit serotonin syndrome rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.t: Both syndromes are clinically indistinguishable — only CK level reliably separates them
NMS occurs only with first-generation antipsychotics; sertraline is an antidepressant
Serotonin syndrome requires two agents simultaneously; this patient is only on one medication
The reflexes distinguish them: serotonin syndrome produces clonus and hyperreflexia; NMS produces lead-pipe rigidity — and this patient has no dopamine blocker on board

tier2.why: Clonus is the serotonin syndrome fingerprint at the spinal cord — it distinguishes it from NMS (lead-pipe rigidity) and from anticholinergic toxidrome (no clonus). NMS can occur with second-generation antipsychotics, so drug class alone does not settle it. The absence of a dopamine blocker on this patient's list and the presence of clonus together confirm serotonin syndrome.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has just been started on clozapine. He reports feeling better than he has in years. The treatment team asks the student to identify the most critical ongoing monitoring parameter for this medication. Which of the following is correct?

options.t: Monthly liver function tests — clozapine is heavily metabolized by the liver and hepatotoxicity is the primary dose-limiting toxicity

trap.name: Wrong monitoring target
trap.note: Hepatotoxicity is not the primary safety concern for clozapine — agranulocytosis is the life-threatening adverse effect that drives mandatory blood monitoring.

options.t: Absolute neutrophil count monitoring per prescribing requirements — clozapine carries a risk of agranulocytosis
Serum clozapine levels at every visit — toxicity is reliably predicted by drug concentration

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Serum levels inform clinical decisions but do not replace the ANC monitoring that is the mandatory safety requirement for this medication.

options.t: Monthly QTc interval on ECG — clozapine's primary dose-limiting toxicity is cardiac arrhythmia

trap.name: Wrong monitoring target
trap.note: QTc prolongation is the primary concern for other antipsychotics (thioridazine, ziprasidone); clozapine's specific mandatory monitoring is the ANC for agranulocytosis.

items.why: Wrong monitoring target in two forms — LFTs and QTc — and Treat the number not the patient (serum levels without ANC) are the traps. Clozapine's mandated monitoring is the absolute neutrophil count due to the risk of potentially fatal agranulocytosis. Serum levels and LFTs may be checked but do not constitute the primary safety obligation.
items.pearl: Clozapine requires mandatory ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis; also watch for myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, and seizures.
items.evidence: psychopharm_primer.md — Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia: ANC monitoring per prescribing information; also watch for myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, and seizures.
