items.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted after a near-lethal suicide attempt. He has expressed persistent hopelessness and a stated wish to die for three days. On hospital day 4, nurses report he seems 'much better' — calm, well-rested, and telling the team he is ready to go home. His affect is bright and he is chatty with staff. No clinical change or social development explains the shift. Best next step?

options.t: Begin discharge planning — improvement is the goal of admission and this patient has achieved it

trap.name: Sudden improvement = recovery
trap.note: Unexplained brightening after severe suicidality is an established escalation trigger — it is not the same as clinical improvement with a clear cause.

options.t: Reduce his observation level and move him to a lower-acuity room to reinforce the progress

trap.name: Quiet patient = stable patient
trap.note: The calm, engaged patient after a lethal attempt is precisely the scenario the escalation list exists for — reducing vigilance based on surface behavior is the error.

options.t: Escalate to the attending immediately — unexplained sudden improvement after severe suicidality is a warning sign requiring reassessment
Update the safety plan and schedule discharge within 24 hours while the patient is engaged

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: A safety plan is one component of the risk formulation — it does not substitute for the clinical escalation this presentation demands.

items.why: Sudden improvement = recovery is the most dangerous trap: the pocket card explicitly lists unexplained sudden improvement as an immediate escalation trigger. Quiet patient = stable patient reduces vigilance at exactly the wrong moment. Safety plan = discharge permission slip conflates a tool with a risk decision.
items.pearl: Sudden unexplained improvement after severe suicidality is an escalation trigger, not evidence of recovery.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'What to escalate immediately' — Sudden improvement after severe suicidality without clear explanation.

items.stem: A patient is pacing the hallway, speaking loudly, and waving his hands. He has not threatened anyone and is not in immediate danger of harming himself or others. You are the student. Which response is best?

options.t: Approach calmly, introduce yourself, acknowledge that he looks upset, and offer him a choice — 'Would it help to step somewhere quieter, or is there something I can get you?'
Return to the nursing station and request a PRN intramuscular medication order before approaching

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Medication is not the default first step when verbal de-escalation has not been attempted — the framework starts with presence and listening, not a syringe.

options.t: Call for additional staff and prepare for restraint in case the patient escalates

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Restraint is the last resort of the least-restrictive principle — preemptive preparation for restraint before de-escalation has been tried violates that principle.

options.t: Instruct him firmly to return to his room or staff will have to intervene

trap.name: Commands over choices
trap.note: Issuing a command rather than offering a choice removes the patient's sense of control — the opposite of what the de-escalation framework centers.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Restraint first, and Commands over choices are the three forms of the same error: defaulting to force or medication before de-escalation. The Project BETA framework begins with calm presence, acknowledgment of distress, and genuine choices — not commands or preemptive escalation.
items.pearl: Verbal de-escalation — calm presence, acknowledgment, and genuine choices — is the default first response to agitation, not a courtesy step before medication.
items.evidence: agitation.md 'Verbal de-escalation, first' — This is the default response, not a courtesy step. The Project BETA de-escalation framework (Richmond et al. 2012) centers respect, simple boundaries, listening, and offering choices rather than issuing commands.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder tells her student doctor that she trusts only her and that the other staff 'just don't care.' Night nurses describe her as cooperative and warm; day nurses report she screams at them. How is this pattern best understood?

options.t: The patient has genuine rapport with the student and a legitimate complaint about day staff behavior

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Taking the patient's report at face value misses the clinical process — the same person being warm to nights and hostile to days is the diagnostic picture, not a staff quality problem.

options.t: Splitting — a feature of BPD in which people are experienced as entirely good or bad, requiring team consistency as the antidote
Deliberate manipulation — the patient is consciously exploiting the split to get preferential treatment

trap.name: Manipulation framing
trap.note: Labeling splitting as manipulation invites punitive responses and misses the clinical process — it is a symptom of affect dysregulation, not a conscious strategy.

options.t: A delusional belief about staff intentions that warrants diagnostic reassessment for a psychotic disorder

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Splitting is not a fixed false belief — the patient's experience of staff shifts with context and person, which is characteristic of BPD, not psychosis.

items.why: Face-value reassurance takes the report at face value and misses the clinical process. Manipulation framing leads to punitive responses that worsen therapeutic alliance. Psychosis = schizophrenia misapplies a diagnostic frame to a personality-disorder phenomenon. Splitting — all-good or all-bad experiencing of staff — is a feature of BPD; the intervention is team communication and consistency, not confrontation.
items.pearl: Splitting is a feature of BPD, not a character flaw — team consistency and shared notes are the antidote, not confrontation.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Splitting — experiencing staff as all-good or all-bad — is common and is a feature of the illness, not a character flaw or manipulation.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted in crisis with severe anxiety and sleep disturbance. She has been engaged in DBT for six months with good skill use documented. She is asking for 'something for her nerves.' The pharmacologic approach most consistent with evidence-based practice for BPD is which of the following?

options.t: Prescribe lorazepam PRN — addressing the anxiety will help her engage with skills

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines in BPD carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied and worsen disinhibition — they are contraindicated in this context.

options.t: Add a nightly benzodiazepine for sleep — insomnia is fueling the crisis cycle

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Scheduled benzodiazepines compound the dependence and suicide risk seen with this class in BPD — sleep disturbance in crisis is treated with the crisis, not with hypnotics.

options.t: Add an SSRI — anxiety in a BPD patient with good DBT engagement suggests an undertreated mood component requiring pharmacological augmentation.

trap.name: Polypharmacy first
trap.note: Adding a second antidepressant without evidence of benefit in BPD, when DBT skill use is documented, substitutes medication for the more effective behavioral approach.

options.t: Minimize pharmacotherapy — if needed, a single low-risk agent for ≤1 week, preferring a sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine over a benzodiazepine.

items.why: The reflexive benzodiazepine in two forms (PRN and scheduled) and Polypharmacy first are the traps. No medication treats BPD itself; the evidence base supports skills over pills, and benzodiazepines in BPD carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied (HR 1.61, Lieslehto 2023). The NICE-aligned approach is a single, low-risk agent at the minimum dose for ≤1 week — sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine preferred over benzodiazepines.
items.pearl: Benzodiazepines in BPD carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any class studied — reach for skills, not pills.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — do not start or escalate benzodiazepines — they carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied in BPD (HR 1.61, Lieslehto 2023) and worsen disinhibition. If a crisis genuinely needs pharmacology, follow the NICE rule: a single agent at the minimum effective dose for ≤1 week (prefer a sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine over benzodiazepines and TCAs).

items.stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the inpatient unit by his parents after three weeks of dramatically decreased need for sleep (sleeping two to three hours and feeling rested), expansive and grandiose mood, pressured speech, and impulsive spending. His parents note he has always been 'a little hyper' in school but never like this. He takes no medications and denies substance use. Most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Bipolar disorder, manic episode — the episodic 3-week course with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity distinguishes this from ADHD
ADHD, first recognized in adulthood — the impulsivity and hyperactivity confirm childhood-onset ADHD now decompensated

trap.name: ADHD vs mania
trap.note: ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood — an episodic, 3-week onset with grandiosity and dramatically decreased need for sleep is not ADHD, even with a baseline 'hyper' history.

options.t: Brief psychotic disorder — the grandiosity indicates loss of reality testing

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Grandiosity in the setting of a manic episode is a mood symptom — it does not automatically indicate a primary psychotic disorder.

options.t: Adjustment disorder — the academic stress of college explains the sleep changes and mood elevation

trap.name: Adjustment by default
trap.note: Attributing a full manic symptom cluster to situational stress avoids the diagnosis and delays treatment — adjustment disorder cannot account for decreased need for sleep and grandiosity sustained over three weeks.

items.why: ADHD vs mania is the key discrimination: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood, not episodic with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity. Psychosis = schizophrenia misreads a mood symptom as a primary psychotic feature. Adjustment by default collapses a manic episode into a stress reaction.
items.pearl: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic — episodic ADHD-like symptoms are a mood or substance flag.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — ADHD vs bipolar mania: ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic with mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity. Episodic 'ADHD-like' symptoms are a mood or substance flag.

items.stem: An autistic adult admitted after aggression at his group home is increasingly distressed on the inpatient unit — covering his ears, rocking, and repeatedly asking when it will be quiet. He is not in imminent danger. No PRN medication has been given. The most appropriate first step is which of the following?

options.t: Administer a PRN antipsychotic — irritability and agitation in autism respond to targeted medication

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Medication before environment in ASD skips the intervention with the best evidence: reducing sensory load and providing predictability.

options.t: Engage him in a group activity to normalize the milieu and reduce his isolation

trap.name: Group = stimulation
trap.note: Group environments increase sensory load and unpredictability for autistic patients — the opposite of what is needed when sensory overwhelm is the problem.

options.t: Move him to a quieter space and establish a predictable routine to reduce sensory load
Assign a staff member to redirect him verbally and prompt use of calming strategies

trap.name: Verbal prompting first
trap.note: Verbal redirection adds auditory stimulation and demand to a patient already overwhelmed by sensory input — environment comes before coaching in ASD.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic skips the evidence-based first step. Group = stimulation adds sensory load when reduction is the goal. Verbal prompting first increases auditory demand on an already overloaded sensory system. The environment-first approach — quiet space, predictable routine, reduced sensory input — is the foundational intervention in ASD on the inpatient unit.
items.pearl: In ASD, lead with the environment — predictability, reduced sensory load, and concrete communication — before reaching for medication.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Lead with the environment and communication, not medication. Provide predictability (routine, visual schedules, consistent staff), reduce sensory load, allow extra processing time, use concrete language.

items.stem: A 16-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa has been restrictive for 4 months and is medically admitted with critically low weight. Before nutritional rehabilitation begins, which approach most directly reduces the risk of refeeding syndrome?

options.t: Start full nutritional rehabilitation immediately at a standard adult caloric target to restore weight as rapidly as possible.

trap.name: Faster is safer
trap.note: Rapid nutritional restoration in the severely malnourished is the trigger for refeeding syndrome — the metabolic shift to anabolism precipitates life-threatening electrolyte shifts; starting at a conservative rate is essential.

options.t: Give prophylactic anxiolytics and monitor for 24 hours before introducing nutrition — anxiety increases metabolic demand in malnourished patients.

trap.name: Sedation before nutrition
trap.note: Refeeding syndrome risk is metabolic (phosphate, potassium, and magnesium shifts), not anxiety-driven — benzodiazepines are not part of the refeeding protocol; the intervention is conservative caloric refeeding with electrolyte monitoring.

options.t: Correct all electrolyte abnormalities to normal before introducing any nutrition — electrolyte imbalances worsen if nutrition begins before they are stable.

trap.name: Normalize first
trap.note: Waiting for perfect electrolytes before any nutrition is not standard — some electrolyte correction runs in parallel with conservative refeeding; withholding all nutrition delays recovery without preventing the syndrome.

options.t: Start caloric refeeding at a conservative initial target and advance slowly; administer thiamine before or with carbohydrate and check phosphate, potassium, and magnesium at least daily early in refeeding.

items.why: Faster is safer, Sedation before nutrition, and Normalize first all create delay or metabolic risk. The source's 'start low, go slow' principle is the safety framework: conservative start, daily electrolyte checks, and thiamine before carbohydrate to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
items.pearl: Refeeding syndrome prevention: start low, go slow, give thiamine before carbohydrate, check phosphate daily.
items.evidence: t_eating.md — Refeeding syndrome: the safe posture is 'start low, go slow': begin conservative caloric refeeding, check phosphate/potassium/magnesium at least daily early, supplement phosphate and give thiamine before or with carbohydrate, and advance calories per protocol as electrolytes stay stable.

items.stem: A 27-year-old mother, 9 days postpartum, arrives with acute confusion and delusions that her infant 'was sent to test her faith.' Her husband reports hours of apparent lucidity followed by rapid deterioration. The diagnosis of postpartum psychosis is made. Which management priority is most immediately critical?

options.t: Refer for outpatient psychiatry follow-up and prescribe a low-dose antipsychotic — postpartum psychosis in first-time mothers without prior mental illness typically resolves with minimal intervention.

trap.name: Outpatient sufficient
trap.note: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency — outpatient management is inadequate; the waxing-and-waning course and infant-focused delusions create immediate risk to mother and infant requiring inpatient admission.

options.t: Immediate psychiatric hospitalization — postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency; explicitly assess and restrict unsupervised access to the infant, start acute pharmacotherapy (lithium or antipsychotic), and protect sleep.
Prioritize medical workup to rule out thyroid dysfunction and eclampsia before any psychiatric treatment — pharmacotherapy is premature until medical causes are excluded.

trap.name: Medical workup before treatment
trap.note: Medical mimics (thyroid, eclampsia, infection) should be evaluated in parallel, but they do not delay the psychiatric hospitalization that a postpartum psychosis presentation requires — medical workup and urgent psychiatric treatment proceed simultaneously.

options.t: The lucid interval between episodes provides reassurance — waxing-and-waning symptoms are inconsistent with psychosis; this is most likely a severe postpartum adjustment reaction.

trap.name: Lucid interval = reassurance
trap.note: The waxing-and-waning course with lucid intervals is a feature of postpartum psychosis, not reassurance against it — the source explicitly states: 'a lucid interval does not rule out psychosis.'

items.why: Outpatient sufficient, Medical workup before treatment, and Lucid interval = reassurance all miss the emergency framing. The source states: 'POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS IS A PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently.' The safety assessment must explicitly include the infant.
items.pearl: Postpartum psychosis = immediate hospitalization, restrict unsupervised infant access, start lithium or antipsychotic urgently.
items.evidence: t_perinatal.md — POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS IS A PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently. The safety assessment must explicitly include the infant: assess risk to the baby, the parent's current access to the baby, and available supervision.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia is voluntarily admitted and refuses his prescribed antipsychotic. When asked, he explains what the medication is for, articulates specific concerns about its side effects, understands the risks of not taking it, and asks whether alternatives exist. Best next step?

options.t: Conduct a formal capacity assessment; if he has capacity, his refusal must be respected, documented, and an alternative offered
Override the refusal — voluntarily admitted patients accept the prescribed treatment plan as a condition of admission

trap.name: Refusal = no capacity
trap.note: Voluntary admission does not imply consent to every prescribed treatment — a patient with demonstrated decision-making abilities retains the right to refuse.

options.t: Seek an emergency court order — a schizophrenia diagnosis with medication refusal requires judicial review

trap.name: Refusal = no capacity
trap.note: A psychiatric diagnosis does not equal incapacity — capacity is four specific, assessable abilities; if he has them, a court order for medication requires a non-emergency legal process, not reflexive judicial referral.

options.t: Discharge him against medical advice — he is voluntary and refusing treatment

trap.name: Discharge for refusal
trap.note: Discharging a patient for refusing a medication without first assessing capacity bypasses the clinical and ethical obligation — the appropriate response is assessment, not expulsion.

items.why: Refusal = no capacity in two forms — assumed from admission type and assumed from diagnosis — is the central error. Capacity is decision-specific and clinical: the four abilities are assessed, not inferred from the admission voluntary/involuntary status or from a psychiatric diagnosis. Discharge for refusal conflates refusal with grounds for discharge. This patient's demonstrated abilities (communicating, understanding, appreciating, reasoning) point toward capacity — in which case his refusal must be honored.
items.pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and clinical — a psychiatric diagnosis and even a refusal do not equal incapacity; assess the four abilities.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Capacity is decision-specific and clinical (a physician assesses it). The four abilities: communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, and reason. Competent patients (including many involuntarily hospitalized ones) generally retain the right to refuse medication. Overriding that refusal requires either a true emergency or a separate legal/adjudicated process.

items.stem: An outpatient therapist is meeting with a 34-year-old patient who describes, in specific detail, a plan to assault a named family member. He states his intent to act before the end of the week and describes the location and means. The therapist's obligation is which of the following?

options.t: Maintain confidentiality — disclosing the patient's statements would violate the therapeutic relationship and deter future help-seeking

trap.name: Confidentiality always wins
trap.note: A specific, credible threat to a reasonably identifiable person is the established exception to therapeutic confidentiality — the duty to protect overrides it.

options.t: Document the threat and continue outpatient treatment with increased session frequency

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: Documentation alone does not fulfill the duty to protect — when there is a specific, credible threat to an identifiable person, protective action is required.

options.t: Take reasonable protective steps — which may include warning the potential victim, notifying law enforcement, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment
Wait for corroborating evidence before acting — a single session disclosure does not establish genuine intent

trap.name: Wait for action
trap.note: Waiting for corroborating evidence or for the patient to act defeats the entire purpose of the duty to protect — the obligation is triggered by a specific, credible threat, not by subsequent harm.

items.why: Confidentiality always wins, Document and continue, and Wait for action are three forms of inaction in the face of the duty to protect. A specific, credible threat to a named, identifiable person — with described means and timeline — triggers a duty to take reasonable protective steps. The options are broad: warning the victim, notifying police, hospitalizing, or intensifying treatment. The duty does not require certainty that harm will occur.
items.pearl: A specific, credible threat to a reasonably identifiable victim overrides confidentiality — the duty to protect obligates action, not only documentation.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — When a patient makes a serious threat of violence against a reasonably identifiable victim, the clinician has a duty to take reasonable protective steps — which may include warning the potential victim, notifying police, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment.

tier2.q: Why does this duty override therapeutic confidentiality?

options.t: Any mention of violence mandates disclosure under mental health law — the therapist has no discretion
The therapist-patient privilege does not apply in outpatient settings, only in inpatient contexts
A specific, credible threat to a named, identifiable person is the recognized exception — the duty to protect an endangered third party overrides confidentiality in that circumstance
Mentioning intent to harm automatically ends the therapeutic relationship and terminates all confidentiality obligations

tier2.why: The exception is specific and limited: it requires a serious threat to a reasonably identifiable person — not any mention of violence, not a setting restriction, and not automatic termination. Outside this exception, confidentiality stands. Disclosing broadly in response to general hostility or vague threats would itself be an ethical violation. The therapist-patient relationship continues; the duty is to protect, not to terminate.

items.stem: A family meeting is held on hospital day 3 for a 29-year-old man admitted for a first manic episode. His mother interrupts repeatedly: 'He does this every time he stops his medication — he's selfish and he makes us all suffer.' She is tearful and wringing her hands. The attending invites the student to observe what is happening. What is the student's best understanding of this dynamic?

options.t: The mother's criticism is accurate and should be incorporated into the discharge plan as a documented adherence barrier

trap.name: Criticism as fact
trap.note: Accepting high expressed emotion as objective reporting misses the fear and grief driving it — and forecloses the most clinically valuable phase of the meeting.

options.t: The meeting should be suspended — the mother's distress is dysregulating the patient and the therapeutic goals cannot be met

trap.name: Terminate for emotion
trap.note: Cutting off the emotional climate phase forfeits the part of the family meeting where outcomes change most — this phase should be protected, not terminated.

options.t: The mother should be gently corrected about the medication-stopping narrative to address the factual inaccuracy

trap.name: Correct the narrative
trap.note: Redirecting to facts before the emotional climate is acknowledged closes off the therapeutic opportunity — expressed emotion must be heard before it can shift.

options.t: The mother is showing expressed emotion — criticism that likely masks fear and grief — and the student's task is to validate the feeling behind it before moving to problem-solving

items.why: Criticism as fact accepts EE as objective reporting; Terminate for emotion cuts off the highest-yield phase of the meeting; Correct the narrative redirects to facts before the emotional climate has been heard. Expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement — is the measurable family dynamic that predicts relapse. De-shaming and validating the underlying fear or grief, without correcting in the moment, is what the playbook calls the phase that most changes outcomes.
items.pearl: Expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement — often masks fear; validate it without correcting it in the moment, because this phase is where outcomes change.
items.evidence: family_playbook.md 'Hear the family and read the emotional climate' — Listen for expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, and emotional over-involvement — without correcting it in the moment. De-shame: frame symptoms and behavior as illness and regulation, not character or fault. This is the phase that most changes outcomes; protect the time for it.

items.stem: An 82-year-old man on postoperative day 2 after hip arthroplasty is confused and agitated. The Confusion Assessment Method is positive for delirium. He has no history of dementia. Which is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.t: Start scheduled haloperidol — antipsychotics prevent delirium progression in post-surgical patients.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Scheduled antipsychotics are not indicated for delirium prevention and carry a black-box mortality warning in older patients.

options.t: Implement non-pharmacologic delirium measures — reorientation, sleep-wake protection, early mobilization, sensory restoration — investigate the underlying cause, and deprescribe deliriogenic medications.
Start a benzodiazepine PRN — GABAergic agents calm delirium-related agitation while the cause is sought.

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except when the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal, where they are the treatment.

options.t: Order a STAT non-contrast CT head — new confusion in a post-surgical patient indicates intracranial pathology until proven otherwise.

trap.name: CT before non-pharm
trap.note: Imaging may be warranted if there are focal neurological signs, but the immediate priority is non-pharmacologic management and cause investigation, not reflexive CT.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic is the most dangerous trap — scheduled antipsychotics are not for delirium prevention and carry a mortality warning in older patients with dementia-related psychosis. The reflexive benzodiazepine deepens delirium unless the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal. Non-pharmacologic measures — reorientation, sleep-wake cycle protection, early mobilization, sensory aids, deprescribing — are first-line while the cause is found.
items.pearl: Non-pharmacologic measures (ABCDEF bundle, sensory aids, mobility) are first-line for delirium — antipsychotics are for dangerous agitation only, never for prevention.
items.evidence: delirium.md 'Management' — Non-pharmacologic measures come first, not as an afterthought: reorient the patient, protect the sleep–wake cycle, mobilize early, restore sensory aids. Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation only — not for prevention.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease is admitted from her nursing home after 2 days of worsening confusion. A CAM is positive. She is agitated and picking at her IV. The team asks the student to help select an appropriate PRN medication for dangerous agitation. Which of the following is correct?

options.t: A benzodiazepine is the safest first choice — GABAergic agents are better tolerated than antipsychotics in cognitively impaired older patients.

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium and increase fall risk in older patients; they are appropriate only when the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

options.t: Start a scheduled antipsychotic to prevent further deterioration — treating the agitation reduces downstream complications.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Scheduled antipsychotics are not first-line for delirium management and carry a black-box mortality warning in dementia — non-pharmacologic measures come first.

options.t: Combine a benzodiazepine with a low-dose antipsychotic for the best coverage of mixed delirium-related agitation.

trap.name: Polypharmacy first
trap.note: Combination therapy before non-pharmacologic management ignores the standard and adds synergistic CNS depression in a delirious elder.

options.t: If pharmacotherapy is needed after non-pharmacologic measures fail, use the lowest effective antipsychotic dose time-limited with close monitoring; avoid benzodiazepines unless the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

items.why: The reflexive benzodiazepine and Agitation = antipsychotic are both active. Benzodiazepines are appropriate only for alcohol and sedative withdrawal — in other delirium they worsen confusion and increase aspiration and fall risk. If pharmacotherapy is needed for dangerous agitation after non-pharmacologic measures, a low-dose antipsychotic time-limited is the choice. Polypharmacy before non-pharmacologic management is never the correct framework.
items.pearl: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium — reserve them for alcohol and sedative withdrawal only; antipsychotics at the lowest effective dose, time-limited, for dangerous agitation.
items.evidence: delirium.md 'Management' — Avoid benzodiazepines, with the single exception of alcohol or sedative withdrawal, where they are the treatment. Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation only — lowest effective dose, time-limited.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of vivid recurrent visual hallucinations (small animals in the room), episodes of staring with fluctuating cognition, mild rigidity and slowness, and his wife's report that he 'acts out his dreams' and has struck her while asleep. Which dementia subtype does this constellation most strongly suggest?

options.t: Lewy body dementia — the combination of fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder is the characteristic core-feature tetrad.
Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia — visual hallucinations and behavioral change point to frontotemporal degeneration.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Visual hallucinations with parkinsonism and REM behavior disorder are the LBD tetrad — FTD presents with disinhibition and personality change, not this specific constellation.

options.t: Alzheimer disease — amnestic dementia with behavioral symptoms in a 74-year-old is most commonly Alzheimer.

trap.name: Most common = correct
trap.note: Alzheimer is the most prevalent dementia, but the specific tetrad of visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM behavior disorder exceeds any typical Alzheimer presentation.

options.t: Vascular dementia — stepwise decline with parkinsonism and motor slowing points to cerebrovascular disease.

trap.name: Parkinsonian features = vascular
trap.note: Vascular dementia shows stepwise decline with focal neurological signs; the full LBD tetrad including visual hallucinations and dream-enactment behavior is not a vascular pattern.

items.why: Most common = correct drives most errors here: Alzheimer is most prevalent, but the full LBD tetrad — fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder — is present. FTD shows disinhibition and personality change without this constellation. Vascular dementia follows a stepwise course with focal signs, not this tetrad. Recognizing LBD matters urgently because of its neuroleptic sensitivity.
items.pearl: LBD tetrad: fluctuating cognition + recurrent visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM sleep behavior disorder — recognize it before anyone prescribes an antipsychotic.
items.evidence: t_neurocog.md — Lewy body dementia — fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity.

items.stem: A patient with known Lewy body dementia is admitted with agitation and paranoid delusions. A nurse asks whether the team should start haloperidol. The most appropriate response is which of the following?

options.t: Start haloperidol — first-generation antipsychotics are better tolerated in elderly patients than second-generation agents.

trap.name: Newer = better inverted
trap.note: Typicals have greater D2 blockade and the highest risk of precipitating neuroleptic sensitivity in LBD — they are the agents to most avoid.

options.t: Start olanzapine — second-generation antipsychotics do not carry neuroleptic sensitivity risk in LBD.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: SGAs still block dopamine receptors and can trigger neuroleptic sensitivity in LBD; quetiapine and pimavanserin are preferred lower-risk choices.

options.t: Hold the antipsychotic, flag the LBD diagnosis to the team, pursue non-pharmacologic management first, and reserve quetiapine or pimavanserin if pharmacotherapy is truly unavoidable.
Start risperidone — its lower EPS profile compared to haloperidol makes it the safest antipsychotic for LBD.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Risperidone has high D2 occupancy and is not a preferred agent in LBD; quetiapine and pimavanserin are lower-risk when an antipsychotic is truly unavoidable.

items.why: Newer = better in three forms. In LBD, neuroleptic sensitivity can be triggered by any dopamine-blocking agent — the risk is highest with typicals and substantial with high-D2-occupancy SGAs like risperidone and olanzapine. The correct first step is flagging the diagnosis, non-pharmacologic management, and choosing quetiapine or pimavanserin if medication is truly unavoidable.
items.pearl: Avoid antipsychotics in LBD — especially typicals; if pharmacotherapy is unavoidable, quetiapine or pimavanserin are lower-risk choices.
items.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Acute inpatient management' — In Lewy body dementia, avoid antipsychotics (especially typicals) because of life-threatening neuroleptic sensitivity — if one is unavoidable, quetiapine or pimavanserin are lower-risk choices.

tier2.q: Why is neuroleptic sensitivity so severe in Lewy body dementia?

options.t: Alpha-synuclein deposits reduce plasma protein binding of antipsychotics, causing unpredictably high free drug levels.
In LBD, dopaminergic neurons are already severely depleted — antipsychotics block the remaining dopamine receptors, precipitating profound rigidity, autonomic instability, and potentially death.
LBD patients cannot metabolize antipsychotics at standard adult doses due to age-related hepatic decline.
Visual hallucinations in LBD are cholinergic, not dopaminergic — blocking dopamine has no symptom effect and creates only adverse effects.

tier2.why: It is a receptor-depletion problem, not a pharmacokinetic one. LBD selectively destroys dopaminergic neurons in the nigrostriatal pathway, leaving remaining receptors critical for motor function. Blocking them produces an extreme parkinson-like crisis — severe rigidity, autonomic dysregulation, worsening consciousness — that can be fatal. This is why the mechanism matters: it is pharmacodynamic sensitivity, not a dosing issue.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man is referred for evaluation of progressive cognitive decline, urinary incontinence that preceded the cognitive changes by several months, and a gait his wife describes as 'shuffling and magnetic — like his feet are stuck to the floor.' MRI is pending. Which diagnosis should be considered first because of its potential reversibility?

options.t: Alzheimer disease — amnestic-predominant decline with gait changes in a 69-year-old is most likely AD.

trap.name: Most common = correct
trap.note: Alzheimer does not explain the magnetic gait and early urinary incontinence that preceded the cognitive change — the specific triad here points to NPH.

options.t: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus — the triad of magnetic gait apraxia, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence is potentially reversible with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
Vascular dementia — gait dysfunction and cognitive decline indicate stepwise cerebrovascular disease.

trap.name: Parkinsonian features = vascular
trap.note: A magnetic, small-step gait with early incontinence preceding cognition is the NPH triad; vascular dementia follows a stepwise course with focal neurological signs.

options.t: Parkinson disease dementia — gait dysfunction and cognitive decline indicate a Lewy body spectrum disorder.

trap.name: Gait = Parkinson
trap.note: The NPH gait is magnetic and apraxic without tremor or classic rigidity; early urinary incontinence preceding cognition is unusual for PD dementia and is the NPH discriminating feature.

items.why: Most common = correct drives most errors. The specific triad — wet (urinary incontinence), wacky (cognitive decline), and wobbly (magnetic gait) — is classic NPH, and its potential reversibility with shunting makes it a must-diagnose. The magnetic gait is low-clearance, wide-based, and apraxic — different from Parkinsonian tremor-and-rigidity gait. Early incontinence preceding cognition is unusual for Alzheimer or vascular dementia at this stage.
items.pearl: NPH triad = wet, wacky, wobbly (urinary incontinence, cognition, magnetic gait) — potentially reversible with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
items.evidence: t_neurocog.md — normal-pressure hydrocephalus (the triad — wet, wacky, wobbly: urinary incontinence, cognitive decline, magnetic gait).

items.stem: Psychiatry is consulted on an 82-year-old man in the surgical ICU on postoperative day 3. He is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeping between nursing checks — his nurse reports he was interactive at yesterday's evening assessment. His CAM is positive. The covering team wonders why this presentation is more concerning than a 'hyperactive' delirious patient. Which statement best explains the clinical risk?

options.t: Hyperactive delirium carries worse outcomes — the agitation, pulling at lines, and fall risk create more immediate danger than a quiet, withdrawn presentation.

trap.name: Hyperactive = higher risk
trap.note: Hyperactive delirium is more visible and more likely to trigger intervention — hypoactive delirium carries worse overall outcomes because it is commonly missed, mislabeled as depression, and associated with higher mortality.

options.t: The two subtypes have equivalent outcomes — motor presentation does not predict prognosis; treatment targets the underlying cause regardless of subtype.

trap.name: Subtypes equivalent
trap.note: Motor subtype does affect outcomes — hypoactive delirium carries worse prognosis in part because under-recognition delays treatment of the underlying cause.

options.t: Hypoactive delirium responds better to antipsychotics — the reduced agitation creates a therapeutic window for pharmacologic intervention that hyperactive delirium does not allow.

trap.name: Hypoactive = better pharmacologic target
trap.note: Antipsychotics are not for delirium prevention or routine management in either subtype — they are reserved for dangerous agitation; hypoactive delirium is not a 'pharmacologic window,' it is a missed diagnosis with worse mortality.

options.t: Hypoactive delirium carries worse outcomes precisely because it goes unrecognized — the quiet, non-interactive patient does not trigger intervention; it is commonly mislabeled as depression and associated with higher mortality.

items.why: Hyperactive = higher risk, Subtypes equivalent, and Hypoactive = better pharmacologic target all invert the clinical reality. The source states: 'The hypoactive form is the one that gets missed, and it carries worse outcomes precisely because no one is alarmed by a quiet patient.' Recognition requires deliberate screening — the CAM is the tool.
items.pearl: Hypoactive delirium = the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, easily mislabeled as depression.
items.evidence: delirium.md — The hypoactive form is the one that gets missed, and it carries worse outcomes precisely because no one is alarmed by a quiet patient. Hypoactive delirium is the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, and easily mislabeled as depression.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted after 4 months of progressive cognitive decline and withdrawal. Neuropsychological testing suggests a moderate amnestic syndrome. She has no known prior psychiatric or neurological history. Which is the most appropriate first-line laboratory workup before assigning a neurodegenerative diagnosis?

options.t: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and consider RPR/HIV — reversible causes must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis is established.
Anti-NMDA receptor antibody panel — autoimmune encephalitis mimics dementia and should be ruled out first in all new presentations.

trap.name: Jump to autoimmune
trap.note: Anti-NMDA antibodies are appropriate in subacute encephalitis with psychiatric features, seizures, or movement disorder — a progressive 4-month amnestic syndrome warrants the standard reversible-cause panel first.

options.t: Brain MRI with gadolinium — structural imaging is the single most important diagnostic step for a new dementia presentation.

trap.name: Imaging before labs
trap.note: MRI is important in atypical, rapid, focal, or early-onset presentations — but the first workup step is the reversible-cause laboratory screen, which is faster, cheaper, and catches treatable conditions.

options.t: APOE genotyping — an APOE ε4 allele would confirm Alzheimer disease and guide management.

trap.name: Genetic confirmation
trap.note: APOE status informs population-level risk but does not diagnose AD and is not part of the standard workup — reversible causes must be excluded first.

items.why: Jump to autoimmune and Imaging before labs both skip the foundational step. The reversible-cause panel — B12/folate, TSH, CMP, and when indicated RPR/HIV — must precede neurodegenerative labeling because these conditions are treatable and clinically indistinguishable at presentation. APOE genotyping is not a diagnostic standard. MRI is appropriate, especially for atypical or rapid presentations, but not before basic labs.
items.pearl: Order the reversible-cause panel (B12/folate, TSH, CMP, ± RPR/HIV) on every new cognitive presentation before assigning a neurodegenerative diagnosis.
items.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Initial workup' — Labs to catch reversible causes: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and — when indicated — HIV and RPR/treponemal testing. Medication reconciliation to strip anticholinergic and sedative burden.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment is admitted for worsening confusion and agitation over the past week. She recently started diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia and oxybutynin for urge incontinence. The student reviews her medication list. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Add risperidone for the agitation — it is the most evidence-based pharmacotherapy for behavioral symptoms in cognitive impairment.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Adding a dopamine blocker before addressing the obvious medication-related drivers is pharmacologically backwards and potentially harmful.

options.t: Order a 24-hour EEG — medication-induced encephalopathy can produce seizure patterns that explain cognitive worsening.

trap.name: Jump to testing
trap.note: Costly procedural workup before deprescribing the medications most likely causing the problem is a diagnostic error of omission.

options.t: Flag diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as high-risk anticholinergic agents for the team, escalate for deprescribing, and recommend non-pharmacologic sleep and bladder strategies.
Reassure the family that mild cognitive impairment commonly worsens under medical stress and will recover once she is discharged.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Dismissing a potentially reversible pharmacologic cause without addressing identifiable high-risk medications is a clinical error of omission.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic and Face-value reassurance both bypass the diagnosis. Anticholinergic burden is a recognized, reversible driver of cognitive worsening in older adults — diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are among the Beers Criteria's most flagged agents. Jump to testing substitutes cost for the straightforward clinical action. The geriatric psychiatry principle: the drug list is often the diagnosis; deprescribing is active treatment.
items.pearl: In older adults with cognitive change, the medication list is often the diagnosis — assess anticholinergic burden and deprescribe before adding anything.
items.evidence: t_geri.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Apply the Beers Criteria and assess cumulative anticholinergic burden, then actively deprescribe deliriogenic and high-risk agents. 'High-yield pearls' — The drug list is often the diagnosis — deprescribing is active treatment.

tier2.q: Why do anticholinergic medications disproportionately impair cognition in older adults?

options.t: Older adults have reduced hepatic metabolism, causing higher serum drug levels than predicted for a given dose.
Older adults have reduced cholinergic reserve due to aging and often concurrent dementia — blocking acetylcholine impairs attention and memory in a system already depleted.
Anticholinergic agents cause orthostatic hypotension, reducing cerebral perfusion and producing cognitive symptoms.
The mechanism is peripheral: urinary retention and constipation trigger systemic inflammation that secondarily impairs cognition.

tier2.why: It is a pharmacodynamic-reserve problem, not primarily pharmacokinetic. Acetylcholine is essential for attention and memory; older adults — especially those with early Alzheimer or MCI — have fewer cholinergic neurons. Blocking the remaining ones with an anticholinergic produces an outsized, often rapid cognitive effect that clinically mimics dementia progression. This is why cholinesterase inhibitors (which increase acetylcholine) treat AD, and anticholinergics are its pharmacologic enemy.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who reports an 18-month history of increasingly disinhibited behavior — making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, hoarding food, and neglecting hygiene. He has no memory complaints, names and recognizes objects normally, and denies mood symptoms. Neuropsychological testing shows prominent executive dysfunction with intact episodic memory. Most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Bipolar disorder — new-onset mania presents with disinhibition, impulsivity, and executive dysfunction in midlife.

trap.name: Bipolar by default
trap.note: Mania is episodic and includes mood elevation and increased energy — a progressive 18-month course of isolated behavioral change without mood symptoms indicates a neurodegenerative process, not a mood disorder.

options.t: Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia — early disinhibition, socially inappropriate behavior, and executive dysfunction with relative sparing of episodic memory in a younger adult is the classic bvFTD presentation.
Early-onset Alzheimer disease — insidious behavioral change in a 58-year-old is most commonly early-onset AD.

trap.name: Most common = correct
trap.note: Alzheimer typically begins with episodic memory loss — prominent early behavioral disinhibition with intact episodic memory is the FTD signature, not Alzheimer.

options.t: Personality disorder — disinhibition, impulsivity, and boundary violations reflect a longstanding personality pattern rather than a new neurological process.

trap.name: Personality disorder by default
trap.note: A progressive 18-month course representing a clear change from baseline is a neurodegenerative process — personality disorders are stable and longstanding, not new-onset in the sixth decade.

items.why: Bipolar by default, Most common = correct, and Personality disorder by default are three forms of the same error: assigning a functional psychiatric diagnosis before considering neurodegeneration. FTD is the dementia of younger adults, presenting with behavior and personality change or progressive language, while sparing episodic memory early — the exact opposite of Alzheimer.
items.pearl: Frontotemporal dementia: younger onset, behavioral disinhibition or progressive language first, episodic memory spared early — the signature that separates it from Alzheimer.
items.evidence: t_neurocog.md — Frontotemporal — younger onset with early personality/behavior change or progressive aphasia; memory relatively spared early.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her family. She has developed, over the past month, a fixed belief that her neighbors are poisoning her food and has stopped eating. She is alert, coherent, and oriented. There is no mood disturbance. Which is the most important next step?

options.t: Diagnose late-onset schizophrenia — paranoid delusions in late life unexplained by a mood disorder represent a primary psychotic illness.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: First-episode psychosis in a 74-year-old has an extensive organic differential — labeling it late-onset schizophrenia without a medical workup is premature diagnostic closure.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic immediately — the refusal to eat constitutes an acute safety emergency requiring empirical treatment.

trap.name: Treat before diagnosis
trap.note: The safety concern is real but empirical antipsychotic treatment without an organic workup can mask a reversible medical or neurological cause.

options.t: Reassure the family that paranoid ideation is a normal variant of cognitive aging.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Paranoid ideation is not a normal aging variant — in an older adult with no prior psychiatric history, it is a medical red flag requiring evaluation.

options.t: Conduct a medical workup to exclude organic causes of new-onset psychosis — including delirium, medication effect, CNS lesion, metabolic derangement, and autoimmune encephalitis — before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis.

items.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, Treat before diagnosis, and Face-value reassurance all skip the foundational step. New-onset psychosis in an older adult without a prior psychiatric history is a medical emergency until proven otherwise. The differential includes delirium, CNS lesion, metabolic cause, autoimmune encephalitis, and medication-induced psychosis — all requiring workup before a primary psychotic diagnosis is made.
items.pearl: New psychosis in an older adult is a medical emergency until proven otherwise — work up before labeling or treating.
items.evidence: t_geri.md 'High-yield pearls' — New psychosis in an older adult is delirium or a medical cause until proven otherwise.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with bipolar disorder screens positive for catatonia on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale — he is mute, maintains awkward arm postures for extended periods, and stares past the examiner. The team has appropriately held the antipsychotic. What is the indicated next step?

options.t: Administer a lorazepam challenge (IV or IM) — meaningful improvement in catatonic signs after benzodiazepines supports the diagnosis and begins treatment; benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia.
Initiate a clozapine trial — persistent psychiatric symptoms after stopping the antipsychotic indicate a need for a clozapine evaluation.

trap.name: Clozapine for catatonia
trap.note: Clozapine is not the next step after a positive catatonia screen — first-line treatment is benzodiazepines (lorazepam challenge); ECT is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.

options.t: Restart the antipsychotic at a lower dose — catatonic symptoms worsen without dopamine blockade and the patient needs partial antipsychotic coverage.

trap.name: Restart antipsychotic
trap.note: Antipsychotics must be avoided until catatonia is treated — they can precipitate or worsen NMS and malignant catatonia; the first step is a lorazepam challenge, not partial antipsychotic re-exposure.

options.t: Apply soft restraints and obtain an urgent head CT to rule out structural causes before proceeding with any treatment.

trap.name: Restraint before treatment
trap.note: Catatonia is a treatable psychiatric syndrome — the next step after a positive screen is the lorazepam challenge; neuroimaging may help exclude organic causes but should not delay the diagnostic-therapeutic lorazepam trial.

items.why: Clozapine for catatonia, Restart antipsychotic, and Restraint before treatment all defer or undermine first-line treatment. The catatonia source states: 'A test dose of lorazepam is both a diagnostic maneuver and the start of treatment — a meaningful, often rapid improvement supports the diagnosis and predicts response.' Benzodiazepines are first-line; ECT is for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.
items.pearl: After positive catatonia screen + holding the antipsychotic → lorazepam challenge next: both diagnostic and therapeutic.
items.evidence: catatonia.md 'The lorazepam challenge' — A test dose of lorazepam (IV or IM) is both a diagnostic maneuver and the start of treatment; meaningful improvement after the challenge supports the diagnosis and predicts benzodiazepine response. Benzodiazepines are first-line; ECT is for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been mute and posturing for 2 days. Today she is found febrile to 39.6°C, diaphoretic, hypotensive, with lead-pipe rigidity and a markedly elevated CK. Her antipsychotic was increased yesterday. Best next step?

options.t: Administer additional lorazepam challenge doses and observe on the psychiatric unit — the rigidity suggests catatonic stupor responding to benzodiazepines.

trap.name: Underestimate the emergency
trap.note: Autonomic instability + hyperthermia + rigidity + elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation is a medical emergency requiring transfer, not continued psychiatric unit observation.

options.t: Increase the antipsychotic — this is a catatonic variant of treatment-resistant psychosis requiring more aggressive dopamine blockade.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: In a febrile patient with elevated CK and rigidity after an antipsychotic was escalated, this is NMS/malignant catatonia — increasing the dopamine blocker accelerates the emergency.

options.t: Stop all antipsychotics immediately, transfer to a medical unit for hemodynamic monitoring and supportive care, and obtain urgent psychiatric and neurology consultation — ECT should be considered for malignant or refractory catatonia.
Treat empirically for sepsis — fever, hypotension, and elevated CK indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics.

trap.name: Sepsis first
trap.note: Sepsis is on the differential but the timing (antipsychotic escalated yesterday), catatonic signs on exam, and the specific combination of lead-pipe rigidity + fever + elevated CK after a dopamine blocker constitute NMS/malignant catatonia until proven otherwise.

items.why: Underestimate the emergency and Agitation = antipsychotic are the two clinical catastrophes. This is NMS/malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, lead-pipe rigidity, elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation. The correct sequence is stop all antipsychotics, transfer to a medical unit, and emergently consider ECT for malignant or refractory catatonia — not more benzodiazepines on the psychiatric unit and certainly not more antipsychotic.
items.pearl: Malignant catatonia overlaps with NMS: fever + rigidity + elevated CK + autonomic instability after antipsychotic exposure — stop antipsychotics, transfer to medical, and consider ECT urgently.
items.evidence: catatonia.md — The emergency you must never miss is malignant catatonia: autonomic instability, hyperthermia, and rigidity that clinically overlaps with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). ECT is the treatment for severe, malignant, or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating.

tier2.q: Why does ECT have a role in malignant catatonia when benzodiazepines have not been effective?

options.t: ECT provides dopamine agonism that directly counteracts antipsychotic receptor blockade.
ECT is used because it avoids all pharmacologic agents, preventing further receptor blockade.

ECT directly treats the catatonic syndrome regardless of etiology — it is the definitive treatment for malignant or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and its effectiveness does not depend on removing the antipsychotic.
ECT is a last resort used only after a second antipsychotic trial has failed in treatment-resistant psychosis.

tier2.why: ECT acts directly on the motor and autonomic systems driving catatonia — its mechanism bypasses the pharmacologic state that triggered the syndrome. The BAP 2023 catatonia guideline endorses ECT for severe, refractory, or malignant catatonia as a treatment that should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating. The example here illustrates this: benzodiazepines are insufficient for malignant presentations; ECT can be lifesaving even when the antipsychotic cannot be fully cleared.

items.stem: An 82-year-old man with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease is currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. His neurologist asks the student to identify what pharmacotherapy optimization is supported by evidence for this stage of disease.

options.t: Increase donepezil to the maximum tolerated dose — dose escalation of cholinesterase inhibitors alone is the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe disease.

trap.name: Dose escalation alone
trap.note: Dose escalation of a cholinesterase inhibitor alone is not the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe AD — memantine should be added.

options.t: Add memantine — combination of a cholinesterase inhibitor and memantine (NMDA antagonist) is the evidence-based pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.
Switch to a rivastigmine patch — transdermal delivery is more effective than oral donepezil in advanced disease.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Formulation does not determine efficacy — donepezil is appropriate; the treatment gap is the absence of memantine, not the delivery route.

options.t: Start a monoclonal anti-amyloid antibody — these agents are now standard of care for all stages of Alzheimer.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Anti-amyloid antibodies modestly slow early Alzheimer progression and require amyloid confirmation and specialized monitoring; they are not standard of care for all stages and are not started on an inpatient psychiatry unit.

items.why: Dose escalation alone and Newer = better in two forms. For mild-to-moderate AD, cholinesterase inhibitors alone are the standard. For moderate-to-severe AD, adding memantine is the evidence-based optimization. Anti-amyloid antibodies are specialist-initiated, amyloid-confirmed, and restricted to early disease.
items.pearl: Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild-to-moderate AD; add memantine for moderate-to-severe disease.
items.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Cognitive symptoms: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild–moderate Alzheimer/Lewy body disease; add memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate–severe disease.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman with recurrent major depression (last treated 5 years ago) is referred for cognitive evaluation after 3 months of 'memory problems.' On formal cognitive testing she scores in the impaired range on delayed recall but consistently answers 'I don't know' rather than confabulating; she is slow to initiate answers and appears effortfully disengaged. She remains alert and attentive, and scores 22 on the PHQ-9. Most appropriate next step?

options.t: Diagnose major neurocognitive disorder — the cognitive test scores confirm a dementia syndrome independent of mood.

trap.name: Scores = diagnosis
trap.note: Cognitive test performance in the context of active major depression does not establish dementia — scores may normalize with successful mood treatment in pseudodementia.

options.t: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor — the episodic memory impairment indicates Alzheimer-spectrum disease requiring pharmacotherapy.

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated until reversible causes, including depression, are excluded — treating the score without treating the depression is the error.

options.t: Order an amyloid PET scan — direct amyloid visualization definitively distinguishes depression-associated cognitive impairment from Alzheimer disease.

trap.name: Jump to advanced imaging
trap.note: Amyloid PET is a research and specialist tool, not a first-line workup step — the well-established clinical approach is to treat the depression and reassess cognition.

options.t: Prioritize treatment of the depressive episode and reassess cognitive function after remission — the pattern of 'I don't know' responses, effortful disengagement, and a PHQ-9 of 22 is consistent with pseudodementia that may resolve with antidepressant treatment.

items.why: Scores = diagnosis, Treat the number not the patient, and Jump to advanced imaging all bypass the pseudodementia maneuver. 'I don't know' responses with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — rather than confabulation and unawareness — is the clinical signature of depression-associated cognitive impairment (Caine 1981). The correct next step is antidepressant treatment and follow-up cognitive assessment.
items.pearl: Pseudodementia: 'I don't know' with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — treat the depression first and reassess cognition; scores may fully normalize.
items.evidence: t_geri.md — Depression can masquerade as cognitive impairment — the pseudodementia presentation (Caine 1981), where patients say 'I don't know' rather than confabulate, show effortful disengagement, and improve cognitively when mood is treated.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted following a suicide attempt by acetaminophen overdose. When the student asks about means restriction, he asks only: 'Do you have access to anything dangerous at home?' The patient answers 'no.' The attending asks what a complete means safety assessment requires. Which response is best?

options.t: Ask the patient if he feels safe returning home — a verbal assurance of safety constitutes adequate means restriction documentation.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: A general feeling-of-safety answer is not a means safety assessment — specific items must be asked about explicitly and the plan for restriction must be named.

options.t: Ask specifically about firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps and ligatures, and who will remove or secure each item — then ask how it will be confirmed before discharge.
Have the patient and family sign a no-harm contract — a signed document constitutes the means safety plan.

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: No-harm contracts are not evidence-based as a risk-reduction measure and do not substitute for specific, actionable means restriction counseling.

options.t: Document 'means safety discussed' in the note — documenting the discussion fulfills the clinical obligation.

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: 'Means safety discussed' without specifying the items addressed and the restriction plan is weak documentation that does not fulfill the clinical obligation.

items.why: Face-value reassurance and Document and continue are both documentation traps. Means safety requires asking by item — firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps, ligatures, and the patient-specific methods the presentation revealed — and confirming who will secure them and how the team will know it happened. A general safety question or a no-harm contract does not accomplish this.
items.pearl: Means safety = ask by item (firearms, medications, sharps), name who will secure them, and confirm how the team will know.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Means Safety' — Ask specifically. Do not say only 'we discussed safety.' Include: Firearms. Stockpiled medication. Sharps or ligatures when relevant. Who will remove/secure means. How it will be confirmed.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia and two prior suicide attempts is admitted for worsening command hallucinations telling him to jump. He is calm on exam; he reports the voices are 'quieter today' and denies current intent. Which statement best reflects how to frame his suicide risk?

options.t: His current denial of suicidal intent indicates low acute risk — patient self-report is the most reliable indicator of imminent safety.

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: Denial of intent in the context of active command hallucinations and prior attempts is not sufficient to conclude low acute risk — command hallucinations are an explicit acute risk factor.

options.t: His prior attempts are the most important factor and define his overall risk level — chronic factors drive the primary assessment.

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: Chronic factors establish the floor but acute factors — active command hallucinations — are the focus for this admission; relying on chronic factors alone misses the immediate targets.

options.t: His schizophrenia diagnosis independently elevates his risk to high — a psychiatric diagnosis drives the risk classification.

trap.name: Diagnosis = high risk
trap.note: A psychiatric diagnosis is a chronic risk factor, not a standalone determination of the acute risk level — the formulation must address both tiers separately.

options.t: Separate chronic risk (prior attempts, schizophrenia — the floor) from acute risk (active command hallucinations — the current target); the formulation must address both tiers and identify the modifiable acute drivers.

items.why: Denies SI = low risk in two forms and Diagnosis = high risk all produce single-tier formulations that miss the key structure. Risk formulation separates the chronic floor (prior attempts, schizophrenia) from the acute drivers (command hallucinations, current voices) that are the admission's targets. Command hallucinations are explicitly listed as an acute risk factor; denial of intent does not neutralize them.
items.pearl: Separate chronic and acute risk — prior attempts and a psychiatric diagnosis set the floor; command hallucinations and current intent are the acute targets.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Separate Chronic And Acute Risk' — Acute risk: current intent or plan; psychosis or command hallucinations. Chronic risk: prior attempts; chronic psychiatric illness.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman is admitted after a near-lethal suicide attempt. She has three young children and is an ICU nurse. A student notes 'strong family ties and professional identity' as protective factors and proposes these substantially mitigate her acute risk. The attending asks the student to refine this reasoning. Which statement is most accurate?

options.t: The number of protective factors is inversely proportional to acute risk — more factors reliably indicate lower risk.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: The number of protective factors does not reliably predict acute risk — their credibility and availability during the risk window are what matter, not the count.

options.t: Protective factors matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window — a family connection that is geographically unavailable during a crisis does not reduce risk at that moment.
Professional status significantly reduces suicide risk — healthcare workers have lower rates of completed suicide than the general population.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Healthcare workers do not have lower rates of completed suicide — professional identity may create barriers to seeking help rather than functioning as a protective factor.

options.t: Protective factors and acute risk factors can be numerically compared — strong protective factors offset recent preparatory behavior in the calculation.

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: Protective factors and acute risk factors are not numerically additive — protective factors must be evaluated for real-time credibility, and preparatory behavior is a hard escalation indicator.

items.why: Face-value reassurance appears throughout. Protective factors are not protective if they are geographically distant, unavailable, or theoretically present but non-operative during the crisis. Healthcare worker status does not protect against suicide. The page states explicitly: 'Protective factors are not magic. They matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window.'
items.pearl: Protective factors matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window — not as a list, but as real-time assets.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md — Protective factors are not magic. They matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window.

items.stem: A student is asked to draft the safety note for a patient admitted with active suicidal ideation, a stated plan, and unsecured firearm access. Which of the following best illustrates strong safety documentation?

options.t: "Patient endorses suicidal ideation — reviewed risks and benefits of hospitalization, patient agrees to continued treatment."

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: Consent documentation does not substitute for a safety formulation — reviewing risks and benefits of hospitalization does not record chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factor limits, or modifiable targets.

options.t: "Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns."

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: This is the prototypical weak documentation: it records a denial without any formulation, omits the known risk factors, and provides no reasoning for the safety decision.

options.t: "Acute suicide risk elevated due to active plan, persistent insomnia, escalating alcohol use, and firearm access not yet confirmed secured; chronic risk elevated by prior attempt and family history; modifiable targets include means restriction and substance stabilization; continued inpatient care indicated."
"Patient stated: 'I want to die and I have a gun at home.' Verbatim suicidal statement documented per policy."

trap.name: Quotes = documentation
trap.note: Verbatim quotes capture content but do not constitute a risk formulation — the clinician's reasoning about severity, modifying factors, and the safety plan is absent; a defensible note requires formulation, not just transcription.

items.why: Document and continue, Denies SI = low risk, and Quotes = documentation all replace formulation with something easier to write. Strong safety documentation names chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factors with limits, modifiable targets, and the current plan. 'Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns.' is the example the page uses for the weakest possible documentation.
items.pearl: Strong safety documentation = chronic factors + acute drivers + protective factors with limits + modifiable targets + current plan — not 'denies SI/HI.'
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Documentation Sentence' — Strong: [detailed formulation with acute risk factors, chronic risk, means safety status, and plan]. Weak: 'Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns.'

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the inpatient unit after a self-reported suicide attempt. On arrival she is visibly intoxicated with alcohol. The student is attempting to complete an initial risk assessment. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?

options.t: Escalate to the attending immediately — intoxication is an explicit escalation trigger; a reliable risk assessment cannot be completed while she is intoxicated, and medical monitoring is required.
Complete the risk assessment now — gathering history while the patient can still speak is more important than waiting for sobriety.

trap.name: Assess before escalate
trap.note: A meaningful risk assessment cannot be conducted while the patient is intoxicated — the acute safety priority is medical monitoring and attending notification, not history-taking.

options.t: Document 'unable to assess due to intoxication' and defer further evaluation to the morning team.

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: Deferring without escalating creates an unmonitored safety gap — intoxication is an escalation trigger requiring immediate attending notification, not a deferred entry.

options.t: Reassure the patient that alcohol often exaggerates suicidal statements and that a full assessment in the morning will clarify her actual risk level.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Alcohol is an acute risk factor that amplifies risk, not a minimizer — intoxication during a period of expressed suicidal intent requires immediate escalation, not reassurance.

items.why: Assess before escalate and Face-value reassurance both produce the same error: treating an escalation trigger as a reason to delay action. Intoxication is explicitly listed on the card as 'what to escalate immediately.' Document and continue creates an unmonitored gap. The correct approach is immediate attending notification, with the formal risk assessment deferred to sobriety.
items.pearl: Intoxication during active suicidal ideation is an escalation trigger — notify the attending now; complete the formal risk assessment after sobriety.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'What To Escalate Immediately' — Intoxication or withdrawal.

items.stem: A medical student is alone with a patient who says: 'I feel so much better — can you put in a good word with the team about going home today?' The student has not been briefed on this patient's risk. Which response is most appropriate?

options.t: Affirm to the patient that she appears improved and will relay this to the team, then complete a brief suicide screen to provide the team with an update.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Affirming improvement to the patient and conducting an independent assessment crosses the student role boundary — the student cannot produce or communicate a dispositive safety determination.

options.t: Explain that discharge is the team's decision, then complete and document a formal suicide risk assessment in the medical record based on this conversation.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Independently completing and documenting a formal risk assessment in the chart is well outside the student role — the student's job is to gather and relay the patient's report to the team, not to produce a signed clinical assessment.

options.t: Reassure the patient that the team is working toward discharge and provide the hospital's crisis line number.

trap.name: Reassure and defer
trap.note: Providing a crisis line to an admitted patient implies discharge is coming; the student is implying endorsement of a decision the team hasn't made, without any supervisory loop.

options.t: Tell the patient that discharge is the team's decision and that you will let the attending know she wants to discuss it — then inform the team promptly.

items.why: Student clears patient in two forms — direct affirmation and independent documentation — both cross the role boundary. The student's role is to ask, observe, and report to the team — not to clear a patient for discharge or to produce an independent safety assessment. Reassure and defer leaves the student in a limbo of implied endorsement without any supervisory loop.
items.pearl: Students can ask, observe, and report to the team — they cannot independently clear a patient for discharge or conduct a solo risk assessment.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Student Role' — You cannot: Clear a patient for discharge independently.

items.stem: A patient placed in physical restraints 4 hours ago following an agitation episode is now calm, cooperative, and asking to be released. His nurse pages the on-call student. Which of the following best reflects the correct management principle?

options.t: Continue the restraints through the end of the shift to ensure safety is maintained across the nursing team handoff.

trap.name: Restraint as stability
trap.note: Restraints are not a shift-duration safety measure — they must be discontinued the moment the patient is safe, regardless of shift timing.

options.t: Notify the attending immediately — the patient's calm state and request to be released require prompt reassessment; restraints must be discontinued as soon as the patient is safe, not held to shift end.
Ask the patient to demonstrate he can remain calm for 30 minutes, then release him and document the trial.

trap.name: Restraint as stability
trap.note: Imposing a time-contingent test before release inverts the standard — the principle is discontinue as soon as safe, not apply additional criteria.

options.t: Since the original physician order is still active, no action is needed until the order expires.

trap.name: Order = permission to continue
