trap.note: Mixed features by definition include both depressive and activating symptoms simultaneously — framing this as 'mania predominating' misses the dangerous combination.

options.t: The activating symptoms suggest his antidepressant dose is too high and producing anxiety — reduce the dose.

trap.name: Side effect attribution
trap.note: There is no antidepressant on this admission — the activating symptoms are intrinsic mixed features, a high-risk presentation that must be recognized, not attributed to medication.

options.t: Mixed features — concurrent depressive and activating symptoms — carry elevated suicide risk and are easy to miss; this combination warrants heightened safety vigilance.
Mixed features can only occur in bipolar disorder — this patient's mixed presentation requires a bipolar I or II diagnosis before initiating treatment.

trap.name: Bipolar required for mixed
trap.note: DSM-5 allows the 'with mixed features' specifier for both bipolar and unipolar depression — the clinical urgency (elevated suicide risk) applies regardless of the final diagnosis.

items.why: One syndrome at a time, Side effect attribution, and Bipolar required for mixed all delay recognition of the dangerous phenotype. Mixed features — concurrent depression and activation — are explicitly called out on the mood page as easy to miss and carrying elevated suicide risk. This patient's passive SI plus mixed features is the classic high-risk presentation.
items.pearl: Mixed features (depression + racing thoughts/agitation/decreased sleep) carry elevated suicide risk and are easy to miss — heighten safety vigilance.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Mixed features (depressed mood with concurrent activation/agitation) are easy to miss and carry elevated suicide risk.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history presents with 2 weeks of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and grandiosity. Her family calls it her 'first manic episode.' She is on prednisone 40 mg daily for a recent flare of rheumatoid arthritis. Which step is most important before proceeding with a bipolar diagnosis?

options.t: Document the manic episode and start a mood stabilizer — late-onset bipolar is increasingly recognized in older adults.

trap.name: Late-onset bipolar by default
trap.note: New psychiatric presentations in older or medically complex patients require a medical mimic workup; steroid-induced mania is a well-recognized cause that must be excluded.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic for the florid manic symptoms — mood stabilizers are too slow for acute management.

trap.name: Treat before diagnose
trap.note: Treating before ruling out a corticosteroid-induced cause misses the treatable etiology; the mood symptoms may resolve with steroid taper or dose reduction.

options.t: Order a head MRI — new psychiatric symptoms in older adults indicate intracranial pathology until proven otherwise.

trap.name: Imaging before differential
trap.note: Neuroimaging may ultimately be warranted, but the most proximate etiology here is the corticosteroid exposure — medical mimic workup precedes imaging decisions.

options.t: Rule out medical mimics before anchoring on a primary mood diagnosis — corticosteroids are a recognized cause of manic symptoms; evaluate the steroid exposure as a contributing or precipitating cause.

items.why: Late-onset bipolar by default, Treat before diagnose, and Imaging before differential all skip the foundational step. The mood page lists corticosteroids in the medical mimic differential and explicitly states: 'Rule out medical mimics before anchoring on a primary mood disorder.' A 71-year-old on prednisone with a first-lifetime episode is steroid-induced mania until proven otherwise.
items.pearl: New mood episodes in older or medically complex patients require a medical mimic workup — corticosteroids, thyroid disease, intoxication, CNS pathology.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Rule out medical mimics before anchoring on a primary mood disorder: thyroid dysfunction, corticosteroids and other medications, intoxication or withdrawal, and CNS processes.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and two prior suicide attempts is starting maintenance therapy. The team is choosing between lithium and lamotrigine. Which argument most strongly favors lithium?

options.t: Lithium has both the strongest anti-suicidal evidence and the strongest maintenance evidence in the mood stabilizer class — in a patient with prior attempts, both properties directly apply.
Lamotrigine has equivalent anti-suicidal evidence to lithium — the choice should be based on tolerability alone.

trap.name: Anti-suicidal = interchangeable
trap.note: The page specifically cites lithium's anti-suicidal effect as distinct from other mood stabilizers and worth emphasizing in risk calculations — it is not interchangeable with lamotrigine.

options.t: Lithium's anti-suicidal effect is limited to acute suicidality and does not apply to maintenance treatment.

trap.name: Narrow = second-line
trap.note: Lithium's anti-suicidal evidence encompasses both acute and long-term prevention; the page's framing applies specifically to maintenance decisions when risk history matters.

options.t: The narrow therapeutic window makes lithium too risky for long-term maintenance — the monitoring burden outweighs its benefits.

trap.name: Monitoring = disqualifying
trap.note: The narrow window requires monitoring, not avoidance; the page treats monitoring as an integral part of lithium use, not as a reason to choose a different agent in a high-risk patient.

items.why: Anti-suicidal = interchangeable, Narrow = second-line, and Monitoring = disqualifying all undervalue lithium in the highest-risk patient. The page specifically names lithium's anti-suicidal effect (Cipriani 2013) and BALANCE maintenance evidence as reasons to 'use it, and monitor it' — the monitoring is the price of the unique therapeutic profile, not a drawback.
items.pearl: Lithium: strongest anti-suicidal evidence (Cipriani 2013) + strongest maintenance evidence (BALANCE trial) — use it in high-risk patients, and monitor it.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Lithium deserves specific emphasis — it carries a distinct anti-suicidal effect (Cipriani 2013) and is a first-line maintenance mood stabilizer with the strongest long-term evidence (BALANCE trial).

tier2.q: What was the primary finding of the BALANCE trial regarding lithium and valproate for bipolar maintenance?

options.t: Valproate was superior to lithium for preventing depressive relapses in bipolar I disorder.
Lithium and valproate had equivalent relapse prevention — the monitoring burden explains why guidelines favor lithium despite equivalent efficacy.
Lithium was superior to valproate for preventing relapses in bipolar I disorder, supporting lithium as the preferred long-term maintenance mood stabilizer.
BALANCE found that combination lithium + valproate was the only regimen that reduced relapse to below 50% at 2 years.

tier2.why: The BALANCE trial (Geddes 2010) randomized patients with bipolar I disorder to lithium, valproate, or combination. Lithium was superior to valproate for relapse prevention, with the combination not clearly superior to lithium alone. This trial provided the most direct head-to-head evidence supporting lithium as the preferred maintenance agent — which explains the page's specific statement that lithium carries 'the strongest long-term evidence (BALANCE trial)' among maintenance mood stabilizers.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman with treatment-resistant MDD is hospitalized. She has failed two adequate antidepressant trials, has active suicidal ideation, refuses all oral intake, and expresses the nihilistic delusion that her intestines have rotted. The team debates a third antidepressant versus ECT. Which framing is most accurate?

options.t: A third antidepressant combined with an antipsychotic should be tried first — pharmacotherapy is the standard of care before proceeding to procedural interventions.

trap.name: Pharmacotherapy first at any severity
trap.note: ECT is specifically first-line for psychotic, life-threatening, and treatment-resistant depression — deferring it in this clinical picture is not the standard.

options.t: ECT is not a last resort — it is first-line for severe, psychotic, catatonic, or life-threatening mood states and in pregnancy.
rTMS is preferred because it avoids anesthesia and has equivalent efficacy to ECT for psychotic depression.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: rTMS is less potent than ECT; it is not established as equivalent for psychotic or severe treatment-resistant depression — ECT is the standard for this clinical picture.

options.t: Palliative consultation is appropriate — treatment resistance and refusal of oral intake indicate a terminal trajectory.

trap.name: Hopeless by default
trap.note: Treatment-resistant depression with refusal of oral intake is an ECT indication, not a terminal diagnosis — ECT can produce rapid reversal of this clinical picture.

items.why: This patient's presentation meets multiple ECT indications simultaneously. Pharmacotherapy first at any severity, Newer = better, and Hopeless by default all delay a definitive, evidence-based treatment. The mood page states explicitly: 'ECT is not a last resort — it is first-line for psychotic, catatonic, or life-threatening mood states and in pregnancy.' Active suicidality, refusal of food/fluids, psychotic features, and treatment resistance are all named ECT indications.
items.pearl: ECT is not a last resort — it is first-line for psychotic, catatonic, or life-threatening depression; do not defer it when these criteria are met.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — ECT is not a last resort — it is first-line for psychotic, catatonic, or life-threatening mood states and in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with MDD was started on sertraline 50 mg outpatient 4 weeks ago. His PHQ-9 improved from 22 to 18. His outpatient clinician says, 'No response — time to add lithium augmentation.' A student asks what should be verified before changing the plan. Which element of measurement-based, sequential treatment (in the spirit of STAR*D) is most relevant here?

options.t: Whether the patient had adequate sleep — insomnia alone can prevent antidepressant response.

trap.name: Sleep over dose/duration
trap.note: Sleep matters, but the first verification step in sequential treatment is whether the agent was dosed adequately and given sufficient time — a partial response at 4 weeks may represent ongoing response, not treatment failure.

options.t: The patient's family history — poor family response to SSRIs predicts individual non-response.

trap.name: Pharmacogenomics before dose
trap.note: Family history may inform eventual decisions, but the standard verification before augmentation is whether the current agent was given an adequate dose for an adequate duration.

options.t: Whether the dose was adequate and the duration sufficient before declaring non-response — a PHQ-9 drop from 22 to 18 at 4 weeks may represent ongoing response, not treatment failure.
Whether the patient prefers augmentation — patient preference drives the treatment decision in measurement-based care.

trap.name: Preference over protocol
trap.note: Patient preference matters but does not override verifying adequate dose and duration — augmenting an underdosed or short-trial agent adds medication burden without establishing whether the current agent failed.

items.why: A dose increase may be preferable to augmentation when partial response is still emerging. Sleep over dose/duration, Pharmacogenomics before dose, and Preference over protocol all bypass the foundational step. STAR*D's model: pick an agent, dose it adequately, and track response systematically before switching or augmenting. A partial response at 4 weeks on a 50 mg sertraline dose has not yet established non-response.
items.pearl: Sequential treatment (STAR*D): verify adequate dose and adequate duration before switching or augmenting — a partial response is not non-response.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Practice measurement-based, sequential treatment in the spirit of STAR*D: pick an agent, dose it adequately, track response with a scale, and switch or augment by protocol rather than by impression.

items.stem: A patient with bipolar I disorder, admitted during a depressive episode, tells the student: 'I don't see why the staff keeps bothering me about sleep — it doesn't affect my moods.' Which response best reflects the clinical evidence?

options.t: Sleep disruption affects only energy and concentration, not mood stability — the patient's assessment is essentially correct.

trap.name: Sleep = energy only
trap.note: Sleep loss both worsens depression and precipitates mania in bipolar disorder — protecting sleep and circadian rhythm is active treatment, not just a comfort measure.

options.t: Sleep problems are a symptom of bipolar disorder, not a cause — treating the mood disorder will resolve the sleep disruption.

trap.name: Symptom not driver
trap.note: Sleep loss is bidirectional — it is both a symptom and a precipitant of mood episodes; protecting sleep actively accelerates recovery and prevents cycling.

options.t: Sleep medications are the priority — behavioral sleep protection is ineffective without pharmacotherapy.

trap.name: Pharmacotherapy over milieu
trap.note: Behavioral and environmental sleep protection is recommended as active treatment — medication may play a role, but the principle is that sleep protection is itself a therapeutic intervention.

options.t: Sleep loss both worsens depression and precipitates mania in bipolar disorder — protecting sleep and circadian rhythm is active treatment, not optional self-care.

items.why: Sleep = energy only, Symptom not driver, and Pharmacotherapy over milieu all diminish the therapeutic importance of sleep. The mood page is explicit: 'protect sleep and circadian rhythm actively, since sleep loss both worsens depression and precipitates mania.' Sleep protection is a treatment modality, not a lifestyle recommendation.
items.pearl: Sleep is treatment in bipolar disorder — sleep loss worsens depression AND precipitates mania; protecting circadian rhythm is an active clinical intervention.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Protect sleep and circadian rhythm actively, since sleep loss both worsens depression and precipitates mania (Harvey; IPSRT/Frank).

items.stem: A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is admitted for his first acute manic episode. He has no prior mood stabilizer exposure. Which is the most appropriate pharmacological framework for acute mania management?

options.t: First-line options for acute mania — lithium, valproate, or a second-generation antipsychotic — combined with milieu measures to reduce stimulation and restore sleep.
Start an antidepressant first — addressing the depression component of mixed mania speeds recovery.

trap.name: Antidepressant for mania
trap.note: Antidepressants are not indicated for acute mania — they can worsen cycling and are contraindicated as monotherapy for mixed or manic states.

options.t: Benzodiazepine monotherapy is appropriate for a first manic episode — avoid mood stabilizers until the diagnosis is confirmed over multiple episodes.

trap.name: Defer mood stabilizer
trap.note: Mood stabilizers are appropriate to start at first-episode mania; waiting for multiple episodes is not the standard and leaves the patient untreated.

options.t: Clozapine should be considered first because of its superior efficacy in refractory mania.

trap.name: Skip the ladder
trap.note: Clozapine is for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and refractory psychosis; it is not first-line for a first manic episode without prior treatment failure.

items.why: Avoid valproate in anyone of childbearing potential regardless of current pregnancy status. Antidepressant for mania, Defer mood stabilizer, and Skip the ladder all misstate the first-line framework. Acute mania is managed with lithium, valproate, or an SGA, combined with milieu interventions — reduce stimulation and restore sleep, since sleep loss itself perpetuates mania.
items.pearl: Acute mania: lithium, valproate, or SGA + reduce stimulation + restore sleep; antidepressants are contraindicated.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — For acute mania, reduce stimulation, restore sleep, and start or optimize a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is stable on lithium 900 mg daily, level 0.8 mEq/L. He recently started ibuprofen for knee pain and reports new-onset hand tremor and mild mental fogginess for the past week. Most appropriate next step?

options.t: Reassure the patient — tremor is an expected mild lithium side effect that does not indicate toxicity.

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: A new tremor with mental fogginess after starting an NSAID in a lithium-treated patient represents a probable drug interaction raising lithium level — check the level, do not dismiss.

options.t: Check a lithium level immediately — NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin activity, decreasing lithium clearance; new neurological symptoms in this context require urgent assessment for toxicity.
Stop lithium immediately and restart once the pain resolves — the ibuprofen interaction makes continued lithium unsafe.

trap.name: Overreact to interaction
trap.note: Abrupt lithium discontinuation risks rebound mania — the correct step is to check the level and substitute an NSAID-free analgesic; stopping lithium is not the first move.

options.t: Ibuprofen has no interaction with lithium — evaluate for a new neurological diagnosis.

trap.name: No drug interaction
trap.note: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin activity, decrease renal lithium excretion, and raise serum lithium levels — this is a well-documented, clinically significant interaction.

items.why: Treat the number not the patient, Overreact to interaction, and No drug interaction represent a spectrum of errors around a common drug interaction. The correct action is checking the level urgently — not dismissing the symptoms, not stopping lithium abruptly. The clinical situation maps directly to the page's warning about NSAIDs pushing lithium toward toxicity.
items.pearl: New neurological symptoms (tremor, fogginess) in a lithium-treated patient after starting an NSAID → check level urgently; NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push lithium levels toward toxicity.

tier2.q: Which drug classes are known to reduce lithium clearance and push levels toward toxicity?

options.t: Opioids, SSRIs, and calcium channel blockers — they alter renal tubular function via serotonergic and adrenergic mechanisms.

NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and thiazide diuretics — all reduce renal lithium clearance through distinct mechanisms (prostaglandin inhibition, RAAS suppression, sodium depletion with compensatory lithium reabsorption); dehydration has the same effect.
Antipsychotics and anticonvulsants — they compete with lithium for renal tubular transporters.
Beta-blockers — they reduce cardiac output and thereby reduce renal perfusion and lithium clearance.

tier2.why: The three drug classes and dehydration each reduce lithium clearance through different mechanisms but the clinical result is the same — higher serum lithium levels. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing renal blood flow and lithium excretion. ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce angiotensin-driven sodium retention, causing compensatory lithium reabsorption. Thiazides cause sodium depletion, triggering the same compensation. Dehydration for any reason concentrates lithium by reducing urinary output. Any of these alone can push a therapeutic level into toxicity.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted with severe depression. She is convinced her children have died in a car accident — despite video calls with her healthy children — and that her body is 'empty inside.' She is oriented, alert, and attentive. No confusion on exam. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?

options.t: Schizophrenia — fixed, persistent false beliefs constitute a primary psychotic disorder.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Schizophrenia requires a primary psychotic disorder not confined to mood episodes; in a severely depressed patient with mood-congruent nihilistic delusions, a primary mood disorder with psychotic features is the correct diagnosis.

options.t: Delirium with nihilistic ideation — new psychosis in an elderly patient is delirium until proven otherwise.

trap.name: All psychosis in elderly = delirium
trap.note: Delirium features fluctuating consciousness, inattention, and disorganized thinking — this patient is alert, oriented, and attentive; the psychosis here is mood-congruent and consistent with psychotic depression.

options.t: Severe major depression with psychotic features — the nihilistic and guilt-laden delusions are mood-congruent and consistent with the depression; orientation and attention are intact.
Schizoaffective disorder — concurrent mood episodes and psychotic features define this diagnosis.

trap.name: Concurrent = schizoaffective
trap.note: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychotic symptoms that persist independent of mood episodes; when psychosis is confined to the mood episode and is mood-congruent, psychotic depression is the diagnosis.

items.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, All psychosis in elderly = delirium, and Concurrent = schizoaffective all misdiagnose the presentation. Psychotic depression produces mood-congruent delusions (nihilistic, guilt-laden) within the context of a severe depressive episode — the alert, attentive patient without fluctuating consciousness rules out delirium.
items.pearl: Mood-congruent psychotic features (nihilistic/guilt-laden delusions) in severe depression = psychotic depression, not schizophrenia — psychosis confined to the mood episode is the discriminator.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Severe unipolar depression can include mood-congruent psychosis (nihilistic or guilt-laden delusions).

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with 'recurrent unipolar depression' has been on sertraline 100 mg for 8 months. His current episode resolved well, but over the past 2 weeks he has developed markedly decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and impulsive spending. He is not using substances. Which is the most accurate interpretation?

options.t: The patient is experiencing sertraline discontinuation syndrome — the mania-like symptoms are medication side effects that will resolve spontaneously.

trap.name: Side effect attribution
trap.note: Discontinuation syndrome occurs after stopping or rapidly tapering a drug, not during continued use at a stable dose — this presentation is treatment-emergent mood switching.

options.t: He has developed a superimposed stimulant use disorder — the pattern is classic methamphetamine intoxication.

trap.name: Substance first
trap.note: The stem specifies no substance use — attributing a new mood syndrome to undisclosed stimulant use without evidence bypasses the clinical task of recognizing antidepressant destabilization.

options.t: This represents sertraline's therapeutic effect — the energy and motivation improvement of depression recovery can resemble hypomania.

trap.name: Recovery looks like hypomania
trap.note: Depression recovery includes restored energy and motivation, but decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and impulsive spending are not components of normal recovery — they represent mood switching.

options.t: Antidepressant monotherapy has precipitated a manic switch in a patient likely misdiagnosed as unipolar — the diagnosis should be reconsidered as bipolar disorder and the antidepressant should not be continued as monotherapy.

items.why: Side effect attribution, Substance first, and Recovery looks like hypomania all avoid the correct diagnosis. The mood page explicitly states: 'a bipolar depression misread as unipolar can be pushed into mania or rapid cycling by an antidepressant.' This is the clinical manifestation of that process — treatment-emergent mania revealing unrecognized bipolar disorder.
items.pearl: Manic symptoms emerging on antidepressant monotherapy = probable treatment-emergent switch revealing unrecognized bipolar — not side effects, not recovery.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — A bipolar depression misread as unipolar can be pushed into mania or rapid cycling by an antidepressant.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man admitted for severe bipolar depression requests discharge on day 6. His mood has partially improved (PHQ-9 from 24 to 17), but he is still sleeping only 4 hours per night, his safety plan is not yet completed, and he does not have an outpatient appointment scheduled. The attending asks the student to frame the clinical decision. Which is most accurate?

options.t: Discharge readiness is functional and safety-based, not calendar-based — incomplete sleep restoration, an incomplete safety plan, and no follow-up appointment are clinical criteria not yet met; continued inpatient care is indicated.
The partial PHQ-9 improvement indicates adequate response — at day 6 the acute risk has passed and discharge is appropriate.

trap.name: Score = discharge permission
trap.note: A PHQ-9 drop does not constitute discharge readiness in the absence of functional criteria; sleep, safety plan completion, and follow-up are the clinical discharge gates.

options.t: The patient has the right to leave against medical advice — sign him out and provide a safety net number.

trap.name: Autonomy over safety
trap.note: AMA discharge is the patient's right when capacity is intact, but the clinical question asks the student to frame discharge readiness — not to override capacity; the correct frame is that the clinical criteria are not yet met.

options.t: Six days is within the standard inpatient admission length — continue treatment by the calendar.

trap.name: Calendar over function
trap.note: Calendar-based discharge decisions are explicitly what the page advises against; the standard is functional and safety criteria, not length of stay.

items.why: Score = discharge permission, Autonomy over safety, and Calendar over function all substitute a proxy for clinical readiness. The mood page is explicit: 'Discharge readiness is functional and safety-based, not calendar-based: improving mood and resolving acute risk, adequate sleep and intake, an established and tolerated medication, and a concrete follow-up.' None of these criteria are met.
items.pearl: Discharge readiness in mood disorders is functional and safety-based: sleep restored, safety plan complete, follow-up scheduled — not calendar-driven.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Discharge readiness is functional and safety-based, not calendar-based: improving mood and resolving acute risk, adequate sleep and intake, an established and tolerated medication, and a concrete follow-up.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman in her 14th week of pregnancy presents with severe MDD: active suicidal ideation with a plan, refusal to eat, psychomotor retardation, and a prior excellent response to ECT 4 years ago. The team debates continuing the current antidepressant versus offering ECT. Which statement best reflects the clinical standard?

options.t: ECT is contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of uterine contractions during the induced seizure.

trap.name: Absolute contraindication invented
trap.note: ECT has no absolute contraindications; pregnancy is not a contraindication — it is explicitly listed as an indication when medications are undesirable.

options.t: Continue the antidepressant through pregnancy — the benefits of pharmacotherapy always outweigh teratogenic risks in severe depression.

trap.name: Pharmacotherapy always first
trap.note: The clinical picture (active suicidality with a plan, refusal to eat, prior ECT response) is an ECT indication even without pregnancy; pregnancy specifically makes medications less desirable and ECT more appropriate.

options.t: ECT is a preferred treatment option in this presentation — pregnancy is an explicit ECT indication when medications are undesirable, and this patient also has active suicidality, refusal of oral intake, and a prior good ECT response.
Ketamine infusion should be chosen over ECT — it avoids anesthesia and is equally effective for suicidal ideation in pregnancy.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Ketamine/esketamine has rapid anti-suicidal effects but requires REMS monitoring and is not established as equivalent to ECT for this clinical severity; ECT has the longer safety record in pregnancy.

items.why: Absolute contraindication invented, Pharmacotherapy always first, and Newer = better all distort the evidence. ECT has no absolute contraindications; pregnancy is an ECT indication. This patient has four concurrent indications: active suicidality, refusal of oral intake, pregnancy where medications are less desirable, and prior good ECT response.
items.pearl: ECT in pregnancy: no absolute contraindication, explicitly indicated when medications are undesirable — especially when there is active suicidality, refusal to eat, or prior ECT response.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Reserve ECT for severe, psychotic, catatonic, or treatment-resistant depression, for life-threatening states (refusal of food/fluids, acute high suicide risk), and as a preferred option in pregnancy.

tier2.q: Why is ECT specifically listed as a preferred option in pregnancy, compared to pharmacotherapy?

options.t: ECT carries no teratogenic risk because the electrical current does not cross the placenta.

ECT avoids systemic fetal drug exposure — the induced seizure under anesthesia has a well-established safety record in pregnancy with obstetric monitoring, whereas fetal pharmacological exposure carries teratogenic and developmental risks that vary by agent.
ECT is FDA-approved for use in pregnancy, whereas all antidepressants are FDA category D or X.
ECT is faster than pharmacotherapy — rapid treatment is the only advantage, not the avoidance of drug exposure.

tier2.why: The clinical advantage of ECT in pregnancy is that the therapeutic mechanism (induced seizure) does not require systemic pharmacological exposure that crosses the placenta. Many psychotropics have established or potential teratogenic risks, particularly during organogenesis, and all agents have some potential for fetal or neonatal effects. ECT with appropriate obstetric monitoring avoids this entirely. The long safety record of ECT in pregnancy is one reason it appears on the indications list alongside the more familiar severity-based indications.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and disorganized behavior. The team is ready to diagnose schizophrenia and start an antipsychotic. The student asks whether anything should be done first. Which step is most critical?

options.t: Obtain a collateral history from family — schizophrenia cannot be diagnosed without family confirmation.

trap.name: Collateral = diagnosis
trap.note: Collateral is valuable but does not constitute the critical workup step; the priority is excluding secondary medical causes before labeling a primary psychotic disorder.

options.t: Start the antipsychotic immediately — early treatment of schizophrenia reduces the duration of untreated psychosis and improves long-term outcomes.

trap.name: Treat before diagnose
trap.note: Reducing duration of untreated psychosis is important, but the first step is excluding secondary/medical psychosis — a delirium or autoimmune encephalitis requires a different treatment.

options.t: Start a structured first-episode protocol (RAISE) — coordinated specialty care reduces DUP more effectively than routine treatment.

trap.name: Protocol before differential
trap.note: RAISE and coordinated care are appropriate for confirmed first-episode schizophrenia spectrum disorders; the differential diagnosis step precedes the treatment framework.

options.t: Exclude secondary causes of psychosis — delirium, substance-induced psychosis, mood disorder with psychotic features, and autoimmune encephalitis — before labeling a primary psychotic disorder.

items.why: Collateral = diagnosis, Treat before diagnose, and Protocol before differential all skip the foundational step. The page states: 'Psychosis is a syndrome — exclude delirium, substances, and autoimmune/seizure causes before calling it primary.' In a young adult with new-onset psychosis, the organic yield is highest at the first episode.
items.pearl: Psychosis is a syndrome — exclude delirium, substance-induced, mood disorder with psychotic features, and autoimmune encephalitis before diagnosing primary psychotic disorder.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Always exclude secondary/medical psychosis before settling on a primary disorder. High-yield pearls: Psychosis is a syndrome — exclude delirium, substances, and autoimmune/seizure causes before calling it primary.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man presents with his first psychotic episode — 4 weeks of auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and social withdrawal with no prior psychiatric history. Laboratory workup is sent. The team is discussing imaging. When is neuroimaging warranted in first-episode psychosis?

options.t: First-episode psychosis warrants a thorough medical workup — the organic yield is highest when there is no prior psychiatric history; MRI is indicated with focal findings, atypical or abrupt onset, unusual age, seizures, or autoimmune encephalitis on the differential.
Neuroimaging is not indicated in first-episode psychosis — it is expensive and does not alter the psychiatric management plan.

trap.name: Imaging never changes treatment
trap.note: Neuroimaging can detect treatable structural or autoimmune causes of psychosis — the organic yield in first-episode illness is higher than in established schizophrenia, making the workup question more important, not less.

options.t: CT is preferred over MRI in first-episode psychosis because it is faster and avoids the need for patient cooperation during sedation.

trap.name: CT over MRI
trap.note: MRI is preferred when neuroimaging is indicated in first-episode psychosis — it has greater sensitivity for structural and inflammatory lesions.

options.t: MRI should only be ordered if the psychosis does not respond to antipsychotic treatment after 4 weeks.

trap.name: Treat before image
trap.note: Waiting for treatment failure before investigating structural causes delays potentially urgent interventions — for first-episode psychosis, the workup includes neuroimaging based on clinical features, not treatment response.

items.why: Imaging never changes treatment, CT over MRI, and Treat before image all defer a workup that is most valuable precisely at first-episode presentation. The page states first-episode psychosis 'warrants a medical workup because a treatable organic cause is more likely when there is no established psychiatric history' and specifically recommends MRI in the named scenarios.
items.pearl: First-episode psychosis earns a full medical workup including MRI when there are focal signs, atypical onset, seizures, or concern for autoimmune encephalitis — organic yield is highest here.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — First-episode psychosis specifically warrants a medical workup because a treatable organic cause is more likely when there is no established psychiatric history; obtain neuroimaging (MRI preferred) when the exam is focal, onset is atypical or abrupt, age is unusual, or there are seizures.

items.stem: A student argues that lurasidone should be prescribed for a first-episode patient because 'it is one of the newest second-generation agents and therefore most effective.' Which framing from CATIE is most relevant here?

options.t: The student is correct — second-generation agents show consistently superior efficacy in first-episode trials compared to older agents.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: CATIE found first- and second-generation antipsychotics had broadly comparable effectiveness; the 'newer is better' framing is specifically what CATIE challenged.

options.t: Choose the antipsychotic by the patient's specific side-effect risk profile — metabolic, motor, QTc, sedation, and prolactin risks — not by recency or generation.
CATIE found perphenazine was superior to all second-generation agents for first-episode psychosis — first-generation agents should be chosen first.

trap.name: Older = better
trap.note: CATIE showed broadly comparable effectiveness — not that FGAs were superior; the lesson is that side-effect profile, not generation, drives the choice.

options.t: CATIE only applies to chronic schizophrenia — for first-episode psychosis, the newest generation agents should be preferred.

trap.name: CATIE exception for first episode
trap.note: The side-effect-driven selection principle from CATIE is routinely applied to first-episode prescribing — metabolic and EPS risk are particularly relevant in young adults starting long-term treatment.

items.why: Newer = better, Older = better, and CATIE exception for first episode all invert or misapply the CATIE lesson. The conclusion of CATIE: effectiveness is broadly comparable across FGAs and SGAs; the clinically actionable difference is in the side-effect profile matched to the patient's individual vulnerability.
items.pearl: CATIE: antipsychotic choice should be driven by the patient's metabolic, EPS, QTc, and sedation risk — not by generation or recency.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Choose the antipsychotic by side-effect profile, not by 'newer is better': CATIE showed first- and second-generation agents had broadly comparable effectiveness, with differences driven by tolerability.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought to the inpatient unit by his parents. He insists there is nothing wrong with him and refuses to engage with the treatment plan. His parents ask: 'Why won't he just accept that he's sick?' Which response best reflects the clinical approach?

options.t: Confronting the patient with the evidence that he is ill — the psychoeducation-first approach — produces the fastest improvement in insight.

trap.name: The righting reflex
trap.note: Arguing about whether someone is ill damages the alliance and does not produce insight in anosognosia — it produces defensiveness and treatment refusal.

options.t: Anosognosia is a neurobiological deficit in self-awareness, not willful denial — use the LEAP approach (Listen, Empathize, Agree, Partner) to build engagement without requiring the patient to accept the diagnosis first.
Lack of insight is a reliable indicator of poor prognosis — formal involuntary treatment is indicated for any patient who refuses to acknowledge their diagnosis.

trap.name: No insight = no hope
trap.note: Anosognosia is common in schizophrenia and does not automatically indicate poor prognosis or require forced treatment; LEAP provides an evidence-based engagement alternative.

options.t: Accept the patient's denial and focus treatment on behavioral symptoms only — attempting to improve insight in schizophrenia is not evidence-based.

trap.name: Insight is not treatable
trap.note: LEAP and other engagement strategies are evidence-based approaches to working with anosognosia; accepting denial without any engagement effort is not the clinical standard.

items.why: The righting reflex and No insight = no hope displace LEAP-based engagement. The page explicitly states: 'many patients have anosognosia, so use Amador's LEAP approach (Listen, Empathize, Agree, Partner) rather than arguing about whether they are ill.' Anosognosia is a neurobiological symptom, not willful denial — debating it produces resistance, not insight.
items.pearl: Anosognosia is not denial — use LEAP (Listen, Empathize, Agree, Partner) to build engagement without requiring the patient to accept the diagnosis first.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Engagement is its own clinical task: many patients have anosognosia, so use Amador's LEAP approach (Listen, Empathize, Agree, Partner) rather than arguing about whether they are ill.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man with schizophrenia has had an inadequate response to olanzapine (adequate dose and duration) and then risperidone (adequate dose and duration). Residual negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia) have persisted on both trials. The team is now choosing a next step. Which is the evidence-based recommendation?

options.t: Try a third antipsychotic from a different chemical class — a third-line non-clozapine agent should be exhausted before clozapine.

trap.name: Skip the ladder
trap.note: Two adequate antipsychotic trial failures define treatment-resistant schizophrenia; adding a third non-clozapine trial delays an evidence-based treatment without a supporting rationale.

options.t: Add an antidepressant — the residual negative symptoms are likely a secondary depression co-occurring with schizophrenia.

trap.name: Negative symptoms = depression
trap.note: Augmenting with an antidepressant before addressing treatment resistance with clozapine is not the evidence-based sequence; negative symptoms in treatment-resistant illness require clozapine consideration first.

options.t: Increase the risperidone dose further — super-therapeutic doses overcome treatment resistance.

trap.name: More = better
trap.note: Supratherapeutic antipsychotic dosing increases side effects without established benefit in treatment resistance; clozapine is the evidence-based next step.

options.t: Initiate clozapine with baseline ANC and recommended hematologic monitoring per the prescribing information — two failed adequate antipsychotic trials define treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

items.why: Skip the ladder, Negative symptoms = depression, and More = better all defer the evidence-based intervention. The page states: 'two failed adequate antipsychotic trials means consider clozapine, with recommended ANC monitoring per the prescribing information.' This threshold is defined and evidence-based.
items.pearl: Two adequate antipsychotic trial failures = treatment-resistant schizophrenia = clozapine with ANC monitoring; a third non-clozapine trial has no supporting evidence.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Two failed adequate antipsychotic trials means consider clozapine, with recommended ANC (hematologic) monitoring per the prescribing information.

tier2.q: Beyond agranulocytosis, which additional serious adverse effects of clozapine require active monitoring?

options.t: Retinal toxicity and tardive dyskinesia — these are the long-term side effects that require monitoring beyond the first year.
Nephrotoxicity and pulmonary fibrosis — clozapine accumulates in renal and pulmonary tissue with prolonged use.

Myocarditis (especially in the first weeks), severe constipation and ileus (potentially life-threatening), seizures, and orthostatic hypotension — these require active clinical monitoring beyond the ANC.
Hepatic failure and peripheral neuropathy — the CYP1A2 metabolism of clozapine produces hepatotoxic intermediates with chronic use.

tier2.why: The ANC is the best-known monitoring requirement because it drove the REMS program, but the page explicitly names four other serious risks: myocarditis (early, potentially fatal — watch for chest pain, dyspnea, and troponin elevation in the first weeks), severe constipation progressing to ileus (can be fatal and is underrecognized), seizures (dose-dependent, lowered threshold), and orthostasis. 'Beyond the ANC: clozapine can cause myocarditis (especially in the first weeks), severe constipation/ileus, seizures, and orthostasis — monitor for these, not just the count.'

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with schizophrenia started haloperidol 5 days ago. She is now febrile to 39.9°C, diaphoretic, and rigid. Nursing staff describe her muscle tone as 'like a pipe.' Her CK is 5,400. What is the most important immediate action?

options.t: Stop the antipsychotic immediately, transfer to a medical unit for supportive care, and monitor vital signs and CK serially — this is neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Increase the antipsychotic dose — the psychotic agitation underlying the NMS-like symptoms requires more aggressive dopamine blockade.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Increasing dopamine blockade in NMS will worsen the syndrome — the antipsychotic must be stopped immediately.

options.t: Start empiric antibiotics — fever and rigidity after medication initiation represent a superimposed infection in an immunocompromised patient.

trap.name: Fever = infection
trap.note: Sepsis is in the differential, but fever + lead-pipe rigidity + elevated CK + antipsychotic initiation is NMS until proven otherwise; stopping the antipsychotic cannot wait for culture results.

options.t: Administer a benzodiazepine for the agitation and recheck vitals in 4 hours before escalating.

trap.name: Treat and wait
trap.note: Benzodiazepines may play a role in NMS management but do not replace stopping the causative agent immediately; a wait-and-see approach is dangerous in an evolving NMS emergency.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Fever = infection, and Treat and wait all delay the single most important intervention: stopping the antipsychotic. NMS is the can't-miss antipsychotic emergency — fever + lead-pipe rigidity + elevated CK after dopamine blocker initiation requires immediate drug cessation and medical-level care.
items.pearl: NMS: fever + lead-pipe rigidity + elevated CK after antipsychotic → stop the antipsychotic immediately and transfer to medical care.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, elevated CK) is the can't-miss antipsychotic emergency — stop the antipsychotic and treat supportively.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman develops subacute psychosis, behavioral changes, and seizures over 4 weeks. She also has involuntary mouth movements and facial grimacing, and her family reports fluctuating states of agitation and relative unresponsiveness. Which diagnosis should be actively considered in this presentation?

options.t: Cannabis-induced psychosis — young adults with psychosis and behavioral changes most commonly have substance-induced illness.

trap.name: Substance first
trap.note: Cannabis can cause psychosis, but the specific combination of subacute psychosis + seizures + dyskinesias + autonomic fluctuation is the profile for anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, which requires specific workup and treatment.

options.t: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis — the combination of subacute psychosis with seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and fluctuating consciousness characterizes this autoimmune syndrome and requires urgent CSF and antibody testing.
Schizophrenia — the presence of psychosis, behavioral change, and movement abnormalities in a young woman is classic for schizophrenia spectrum illness.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Schizophrenia does not produce seizures or orofacial dyskinesias as primary features — the subacute course with these specific features points to autoimmune encephalitis, which is treatable.

options.t: Bipolar disorder with psychotic features — the fluctuating states and behavioral change represent rapid cycling.

trap.name: Bipolar by default
trap.note: Orofacial dyskinesias and seizures are not features of bipolar disorder — the specific combination here is the anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis profile requiring urgent autoimmune workup.

items.why: Substance first, Psychosis = schizophrenia, and Bipolar by default all produce premature diagnostic closure on a treatable condition. The page specifically names anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis as a can't-miss mimic: 'subacute psychosis with seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability' — the triad here maps directly to that presentation.
items.pearl: Subacute psychosis + seizures + orofacial dyskinesias + fluctuating consciousness = anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis until proven — urgent CSF and antibody testing.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Do not miss autoimmune/limbic encephalitis (e.g., anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis — subacute psychosis with seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability).

items.stem: A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with first-episode schizophrenia. His family asks, 'What kind of treatment should we expect — just medication?' Which response best reflects the evidence-based approach for first-episode psychosis?

options.t: Yes — antipsychotic medication alone is the evidence-based standard for first-episode psychosis; psychosocial interventions are added only after medication stabilization.

trap.name: Medication alone for first episode
trap.note: RAISE demonstrated that medication alone is not the evidence-based approach — coordinated specialty care with active family involvement and early psychosocial intervention from the start improves outcomes.

options.t: Clozapine should be initiated immediately for first-episode schizophrenia — early aggressive treatment reduces DUP most effectively.

trap.name: Skip the ladder
trap.note: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness after two failed adequate trials; it is not appropriate as a first-line agent for a first episode.

options.t: Coordinated specialty care, including antipsychotic medication, active family involvement, early psychosocial intervention, and integrated care — as supported by the RAISE project — is the evidence-based approach for first-episode psychosis.
The focus for first-episode psychosis should be on medication titration alone; family involvement risks creating dependency and should be avoided in young adults.

trap.name: Family involvement = dependency
trap.note: Family involvement is an active component of the evidence-based RAISE model for first-episode psychosis — it is not a risk factor for poor outcomes.

items.why: Medication alone for first episode, Skip the ladder, and Family involvement = dependency all fail to apply the RAISE evidence. The page explicitly states: 'For first-episode patients, RAISE supports coordinated specialty care with active family involvement and early psychosocial intervention, not medication alone.'
items.pearl: First-episode psychosis: coordinated specialty care (RAISE model) — medication + family involvement + psychosocial intervention from the start, not medication alone.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — For first-episode patients, RAISE supports coordinated specialty care with active family involvement and early psychosocial intervention, not medication alone.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man with no prior psychiatric history is noted to be 'psychotic' — he is making nonsensical statements, appears to be responding to internal stimuli, and is alternating between agitation and somnolence. He was admitted 2 days ago for a hip fracture repair. Which diagnosis should be considered first?

options.t: Late-onset schizophrenia — psychosis with no prior history in an older adult indicates a late-onset primary psychotic disorder.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: New psychiatric presentations in medically ill older patients are delirium until proven otherwise — alternating agitation and somnolence after surgery is the classic delirium picture.

options.t: Bipolar disorder with late-onset psychotic mania — the agitation and apparent hallucinations indicate a mood disorder with psychotic features.

trap.name: Bipolar by default
trap.note: Fluctuating consciousness and somnolence alternating with agitation are delirium features, not bipolar features — the post-surgical context and the fluctuating level of consciousness are the discriminating cues.

options.t: Brief psychotic disorder — the onset after a medical stressor meets the criteria for brief psychotic disorder.

trap.name: Stress-reactive psychosis
trap.note: Brief psychotic disorder cannot be diagnosed when the disturbance is better explained by delirium or a general medical condition — the fluctuating consciousness, post-surgical context, and alternating agitation and somnolence all point to delirium as the primary diagnosis.

options.t: Delirium — acute onset after surgery with fluctuating consciousness, inattention, disorganized thinking, and alternating agitation and somnolence is delirium until proven otherwise.

items.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, Bipolar by default, and Stress-reactive psychosis all assign a primary psychiatric diagnosis to what is clinically delirium. The page states: 'Think delirium first in any acute, fluctuating presentation with inattention or clouded consciousness.' The alternating agitation and somnolence, post-surgical timing, and older age converge on the delirium diagnosis.
items.pearl: Delirium first in any acute, fluctuating presentation with clouded consciousness — new 'psychosis' after surgery in an older patient is delirium until proven otherwise.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Think delirium first in any acute, fluctuating presentation with inattention or clouded consciousness.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia on clozapine for 6 months presents with 3 days of fever, severe constipation, and abdominal distension. His ANC is within the monitored range. Which clozapine adverse effect must be immediately considered?

options.t: Severe constipation progressing to ileus — an overlooked but potentially fatal clozapine complication; obstipation and abdominal distension require urgent evaluation.
Agranulocytosis — fever in a clozapine-treated patient always indicates a dropping ANC regardless of the current count.

trap.name: All fever = agranulocytosis
trap.note: A normal ANC largely rules out agranulocytosis as the cause of this fever; the page explicitly lists severe constipation and ileus as serious non-ANC risks of clozapine — abdominal distension points to this diagnosis.

options.t: Myocarditis — clozapine-associated myocarditis presents with fever and should be evaluated by cardiac workup first.

trap.name: Fever = myocarditis
trap.note: Myocarditis is a serious early clozapine risk (first weeks), but in a 6-month established patient with constipation and abdominal distension, ileus is the more proximate diagnosis; myocarditis would present with cardiac symptoms, not abdominal ones.

options.t: Clozapine toxicity — fever and abdominal symptoms indicate supratherapeutic levels requiring a dose reduction.

trap.name: Toxicity explains everything
trap.note: Clozapine toxicity produces sedation, hypersalivation, and neurological effects; the specific presentation of fever with severe constipation and abdominal distension is the ileus/obstipation complication, not generic toxicity.

items.why: All fever = agranulocytosis, Fever = myocarditis, and Toxicity explains everything all focus on the better-known risks while missing the one the presentation actually points to. The page explicitly states: 'severe constipation/ileus' as a serious clozapine risk that must be monitored 'beyond the ANC.' Ileus from clozapine is underrecognized and can be fatal.
items.pearl: Clozapine beyond the ANC: severe constipation → ileus is a potentially fatal complication; fever + abdominal distension in a clozapine-treated patient requires urgent GI evaluation.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Beyond the ANC: clozapine can cause myocarditis (especially in the first weeks), severe constipation/ileus, seizures, and orthostasis — monitor for these, not just the count.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions coinciding with a severe depressive episode. Between prior mood episodes she has no psychotic symptoms. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this pattern?

options.t: Schizophrenia — persistent auditory hallucinations lasting 2 weeks meet duration criteria for schizophrenia.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Schizophrenia requires psychotic symptoms independent of mood episodes; when psychosis is confined to a mood episode, a mood disorder with psychotic features is the diagnosis.

options.t: Mood disorder with psychotic features — psychosis confined to the mood episode and absent between episodes, distinguishing this from schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia.
Schizoaffective disorder — concurrent psychosis and a mood episode always indicate schizoaffective disorder.

trap.name: Concurrent = schizoaffective
trap.note: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychotic symptoms that persist for at least 2 weeks independent of mood episodes — psychosis confined to mood episodes is a mood disorder with psychotic features.

options.t: Brief psychotic disorder — the acute onset within a depressive episode qualifies for a brief psychotic disorder diagnosis.

trap.name: Brief = distinct diagnosis
trap.note: Brief psychotic disorder is used for sudden-onset psychosis without a mood disorder cause — psychosis within a clearly defined mood episode is better classified as mood disorder with psychotic features.

items.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, Concurrent = schizoaffective, and Brief = distinct diagnosis all misidentify the key discriminating feature: does the psychosis persist independent of mood episodes? When psychosis is confined to mood episodes, the diagnosis is mood disorder with psychotic features, not schizophrenia or schizoaffective.
items.pearl: Psychosis confined to mood episodes = mood disorder with psychotic features; schizoaffective disorder requires ≥2 weeks of psychosis independent of any mood episode.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Distinguish a mood disorder with psychotic features (psychosis confined to mood episodes) from a primary psychotic disorder.

tier2.q: What is the minimum distinguishing criterion between schizoaffective disorder and a mood disorder with psychotic features?

options.t: The number of mood episodes — schizoaffective disorder requires at least three mood episodes with psychosis.

Psychotic symptoms that persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode — this independent psychosis distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from a mood disorder with psychotic features.
The severity of hallucinations — complex auditory hallucinations with formed voices indicate schizoaffective disorder; simple noises indicate a mood disorder.
The presence of negative symptoms — negative symptoms are only found in schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia, not in mood disorders with psychotic features.

tier2.why: The DSM-5 criterion that distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from mood disorder with psychotic features is straightforward but clinically important: schizoaffective disorder requires a period of at least 2 weeks where delusions or hallucinations are present without any major mood episode (depressive, manic, or mixed). If psychosis is always and only present during mood episodes, the diagnosis is a mood disorder — not schizoaffective. This distinction matters because the treatment focus differs significantly.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia has had a modest response to risperidone 4 mg/day for 6 weeks. His attending considers this a non-response and wants to proceed to clozapine. The student questions whether the treatment resistance threshold has been met. What must be true before clozapine is indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia?

options.t: One failed antipsychotic trial at any dose is sufficient to establish treatment resistance and justify clozapine.

trap.name: One trial sufficient
trap.note: The evidence-based threshold is two adequate antipsychotic trials — adequate meaning therapeutic dose for adequate duration — before clozapine is indicated; one trial does not meet the standard.

options.t: Failure of any antipsychotic regardless of dose or duration qualifies — the current trial started 6 weeks ago and is adequate.

trap.name: Duration sufficient alone
trap.note: This option uses only ONE failed antipsychotic trial to justify clozapine — the evidence-based threshold requires TWO failed adequate trials (adequate dose AND adequate duration); one well-conducted trial is not sufficient to declare treatment resistance.

options.t: Two adequate antipsychotic trials — at therapeutic doses, for adequate durations — must be documented before treatment-resistant schizophrenia is established and clozapine is considered.
Trial of ECT followed by failure of one antipsychotic qualifies — somatic therapy plus pharmacotherapy failure establishes the threshold.

trap.name: ECT in the ladder
trap.note: The clozapine threshold is defined by two failed antipsychotic trials — ECT is not part of the treatment-resistance definition for schizophrenia in standard guidelines.

items.why: One trial sufficient, Duration sufficient alone, and ECT in the ladder all misstate the threshold. The page defines treatment resistance as 'inadequate response to two adequate antipsychotic trials' — both trials must be at therapeutic doses for adequate durations. One partially-dosed trial does not qualify.
items.pearl: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia = inadequate response to two adequate antipsychotic trials (therapeutic dose, adequate duration) — both criteria must be met before clozapine.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — For treatment-resistant schizophrenia (inadequate response to two adequate antipsychotic trials), clozapine is the evidence-based agent.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man with first-episode psychosis was started on haloperidol 3 days ago. He has been pacing the unit continuously, reports an inner urge to move, and the team has correctly identified this as akathisia. The attending decides that haloperidol should be continued for now at the same dose. Which pharmacological intervention has the strongest evidence as first-line treatment for akathisia in this setting?

options.t: Benztropine — anticholinergic agents are first-line for all antipsychotic-induced movement disorders, including akathisia.

trap.name: Anticholinergic first-line for akathisia
trap.note: Benztropine and other anticholinergic agents are first-line for antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, but they have weaker evidence for pure akathisia compared to propranolol. Anticholinergics are the correct add-on when parkinsonism co-exists with akathisia, not as the default first-line for akathisia alone.

options.t: Propranolol 20–40 mg BID — a non-selective beta-blocker with the strongest evidence base for akathisia from multiple small RCTs and Cochrane review.
Immediate switch to clozapine — clozapine's low D2 affinity eliminates akathisia risk and is the definitive treatment when any antipsychotic causes akathisia.

trap.name: Clozapine as immediate first-line
trap.note: Clozapine's low D2 affinity does make it a preferred option in patients with severe EPS, but it is not the first intervention for new akathisia — it requires ANC monitoring enrollment, carries significant metabolic and cardiac risks, and is reserved for treatment-resistant or EPS-prone patients. The first pharmacological trial for akathisia is propranolol, not clozapine.

options.t: Standing diazepam — benzodiazepines are the first-line pharmacological agent for dopamine-blocker-induced restlessness.

trap.name: Benzodiazepine first-line for akathisia
trap.note: Benzodiazepines (typically clonazepam) provide adjunctive relief and are useful when propranolol is insufficient or contraindicated, but they are third-line specifically for akathisia. Starting with standing diazepam also introduces dependence risk, falls, and sedation; propranolol is both more specific and better-evidenced (Lima et al., Cochrane 2004).

items.why: Anticholinergic first-line, Clozapine immediately, and Benzodiazepine first-line all misorient the management hierarchy. Propranolol (B) has the strongest evidence for akathisia: it is effective in multiple small RCTs reviewed in the Cochrane systematic analysis (Lima et al. 2004). The management sequence is: (1) reduce antipsychotic dose or switch if possible — the mechanism fix; (2) propranolol when dose reduction isn't immediately available; (3) benztropine if parkinsonism co-exists; (4) benzodiazepine adjunct if symptoms remain severe. Avoid escalating the antipsychotic — the cardinal error.
items.pearl: Akathisia pharmacotherapy: propranolol 20–40 mg BID is first-line (strongest evidence); add benztropine if parkinsonism co-exists; benzodiazepine is third-line adjunct.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md 'When akathisia is identified' — Propranolol 20–40 mg BID is the pharmacological first-line for akathisia with the strongest evidence from multiple small RCTs and Cochrane review (Lima et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004). Management hierarchy: reduce dose or switch → propranolol → benztropine if parkinsonism co-exists → benzodiazepine adjunct.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted to the inpatient psychiatry unit. He is anxious, diaphoretic, and tremulous. His heart rate is 102. He says he has always been 'an anxious person.' The team prepares to increase his home sertraline. Which step is most important before attributing this presentation to his anxiety disorder?

options.t: Obtain a psychiatric consultation — his elevated heart rate may indicate a panic attack requiring specialist evaluation.

trap.name: Specialist before differential
trap.note: Obtaining consultation does not replace completing the medical differential; the vital signs and diaphoresis suggest a medical or withdrawal etiology that precedes the psychiatric assessment.

options.t: Screen for medical and withdrawal causes first — diaphoresis, tachycardia, and tremor require workup for hyperthyroidism, withdrawal states, arrhythmia, and hypoglycemia before attributing symptoms to primary anxiety.
Increase the sertraline — the anxiety disorder history provides the most parsimonious explanation.

trap.name: Anchoring to prior diagnosis
trap.note: A prior anxiety diagnosis does not preclude new medical or withdrawal causes; acting on a prior label without investigating new-admission vital sign abnormalities is anchoring bias.

options.t: Obtain an ECG and troponin immediately — the anxiety symptoms likely represent cardiac ischemia.

trap.name: Single diagnosis before differential
trap.note: Cardiac workup may be part of the evaluation, but the correct move is to work the full differential, not jump to one specific etiology before establishing what the presentation represents.

items.why: Specialist before differential, Anchoring to prior diagnosis, and Single diagnosis before differential all bypass the foundational step. The page's first pearl: 'Anxiety is a symptom before it is a diagnosis — clear the medical and withdrawal mimics first.' In a newly admitted patient with diaphoresis, tremor, and tachycardia, alcohol or sedative withdrawal must top the differential.
items.pearl: Anxiety is a symptom before it is a diagnosis — clear medical and withdrawal mimics (thyroid, withdrawal, arrhythmia, hypoglycemia) before treating the disorder.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Anxiety is a final common pathway, so screen the body first: cardiopulmonary causes, thyroid disease, hypoglycemia, caffeine and stimulant intoxication, and alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with panic disorder and alcohol use disorder in early recovery is admitted for assessment. She is anxious and requesting 'something to help right away.' The student considers adding a standing lorazepam dose for anxiety management. Which response reflects the inpatient standard?

options.t: Start lorazepam 0.5 mg twice daily and titrate to response — benzodiazepines are first-line for inpatient anxiety.

trap.name: Benzos for anxiety disorder
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are not first-line maintenance treatment for anxiety disorders, especially on an inpatient unit with comorbid SUD — they drive dependence, worsen delirium risk, and are specifically contraindicated in this context.

options.t: Give a single dose of lorazepam now and plan to stop it in 24 hours — brief PRN use avoids dependence.

trap.name: One dose is safe
trap.note: Even single doses establish a pattern in SUD recovery, and the plan to stop in 24 hours frequently escalates; the standard is to avoid benzodiazepines as an anxiety strategy and use alternative approaches.

options.t: Avoid standing benzodiazepines on the inpatient unit — they drive dependence, falls, and delirium, and are especially hazardous with comorbid SUD; use skills-based approaches and SSRI/SNRI planning instead.
Benzodiazepines are acceptable for a few days in any patient — dependence only develops with chronic outpatient use.

trap.name: Inpatient benzos are safe short-term
trap.note: Dependence and withdrawal risk are not confined to outpatient chronic use; on the inpatient unit, standing benzodiazepines also impair cognition, raise fall risk, and — in this patient — risk activating craving and relapse behavior.

items.why: Benzos for anxiety disorder, One dose is safe, and Inpatient benzos safe short-term all contradict the page's explicit guidance. The page states: 'Avoid standing benzodiazepines on the unit — they drive dependence, falls, and delirium, and are especially hazardous with comorbid SUD or in older adults.' This patient has both risk factors.
items.pearl: Standing benzodiazepines are a liability on the inpatient unit — dependence, falls, delirium; especially avoid with SUD or in older adults; use SSRIs + behavioral skills instead.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Avoid standing benzodiazepines on the unit — they drive dependence, falls, and delirium, and are especially hazardous with comorbid SUD or in older adults.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man with OCD spends 4–6 hours daily performing handwashing and checking rituals that he recognizes as excessive. He asks what the most effective treatment for his OCD is. Which response is most accurate?

options.t: Cognitive restructuring — identifying and challenging the distorted beliefs underlying the OCD cognitions is the first-line behavioral approach.

trap.name: Cognitive restructuring over ERP
trap.note: Standard CBT for OCD focuses on behavioral exposure rather than cognitive restructuring alone; the evidence-based behavioral treatment is specifically ERP, not generic cognitive work.

options.t: Prolonged exposure — reliving the feared OCD content in an imaginal narrative is the evidence-based treatment for OCD.

trap.name: ERP confused with PE
trap.note: Prolonged exposure (PE) is the behavioral treatment for PTSD, not OCD; ERP — gradually exposing to feared triggers while preventing the compulsive response — is the evidence-based approach for OCD.

options.t: Mindfulness-based stress reduction — cultivating non-judgmental awareness of obsessional thoughts reduces their power over the patient's behavior.

trap.name: Mindfulness over ERP
trap.note: Mindfulness may be a helpful adjunct, but ERP has the strongest evidence for OCD; mindfulness alone does not address the exposure-response chain that maintains OCD.

options.t: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) — gradually exposing the patient to feared triggers while preventing the compulsive ritual, breaking the anxiety-reduction cycle that maintains OCD.

items.why: Cognitive restructuring over ERP, ERP confused with PE, and Mindfulness over ERP all substitute adjacent techniques for the specific evidence-based intervention. The page states: 'Definitive treatment is behavioral — ERP for OCD.' The mechanism of ERP (exposure + ritual prevention breaks the anxiety-reduction cycle) is what distinguishes it from general cognitive or mindfulness work.
items.pearl: First-line behavioral treatment for OCD is ERP (exposure and response prevention) — not PE (which is PTSD), not generic CBT, not mindfulness alone.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Pair pharmacology with disorder-specific behavioral work: exposure and response prevention (ERP) for OCD.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted from the emergency department with a possible psychotic disorder. He is noted to perform elaborate ritualized behaviors before eating — arranging his tray precisely, touching items in a fixed sequence, and repeating phrases — and he becomes extremely distressed if interrupted. He describes intrusive thoughts about contamination. He acknowledges the behaviors are excessive and senseless but cannot stop performing them. Which is the most accurate interpretation of this presentation?

options.t: OCD can masquerade as psychosis when rituals are elaborate — the structured, ego-dystonic nature of the rituals and the contamination preoccupation are consistent with OCD, not a primary psychotic disorder.
This confirms a psychotic disorder with magical thinking — ritualized behavior during a psychotic episode indicates command hallucinations driving the rituals.

trap.name: Rituals = psychosis
trap.note: OCD rituals are ego-dystonic and performed to reduce anxiety from recognized obsessions — the patient recognizes them as excessive; psychotic rituals driven by hallucinations have a different phenomenological quality.

options.t: This is catatonia — the stereotyped movements and distress on interruption indicate a catatonic episode requiring lorazepam challenge.

trap.name: Stereotypy = catatonia
trap.note: Catatonia involves waxy flexibility, stupor, mutism, posturing, and negativism — not purposeful anxiety-driven rituals with intact communication; OCD rituals are purposeful and relief-driven.

options.t: This represents an autism spectrum disorder with restricted/repetitive behaviors — pursue developmental history and ASD workup.

trap.name: Repetitive behavior = ASD
trap.note: ASD restricted behaviors are ego-syntonic routines that provide comfort; OCD rituals are ego-dystonic — recognized as excessive and performed to reduce anxiety. Both can occur, but the contamination-driven, distress-on-interruption pattern points to OCD.

items.why: Rituals = psychosis, Stereotypy = catatonia, and Repetitive behavior = ASD all replace OCD with other diagnoses based on surface features. The page notes: 'OCD can masquerade as psychosis when rituals are elaborate.' The discriminating features are ego-dystonicity (patient recognizes the ritual as excessive) and the contamination obsession → relief-seeking ritual chain.
items.pearl: Elaborate ego-dystonic rituals + contamination obsessions on a psychiatric unit = OCD masquerading as psychosis — clarify ego-dystonicity before committing to a psychosis diagnosis.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — OCD can masquerade as psychosis when rituals are elaborate, or as treatment refusal when contamination fears collide with the milieu.

items.stem: A student is reviewing a patient with OCD and notes serial Y-BOCS scores in the chart: 32 on admission, 24 at one week, and 20 at two weeks. The attending asks the student to interpret what the Y-BOCS measures and what these scores indicate. Which response is most accurate?

options.t: The Y-BOCS is a patient self-report symptom checklist for OCD — scores above 20 indicate clinical disorder; a drop from 32 to 20 reflects the patient's subjective sense of improvement.

trap.name: Y-BOCS = self-report
trap.note: The Y-BOCS is a clinician-rated measure, not a patient self-report — it assesses both a symptom checklist phase and 10 severity items scored by the clinician; self-report vs clinician-rated tools have different psychometric properties and different uses.

options.t: The Y-BOCS (Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale) is the gold-standard clinician-rated measure of OCD severity and treatment response — it includes obsession and compulsion domains scored separately, and the drop from 32 to 20 indicates a meaningful response to treatment.
The Y-BOCS is a broadband anxiety screen — it measures generalized anxiety severity across all anxiety disorders and is used to track treatment response in any anxiety condition.

trap.name: Broadband anxiety screen
trap.note: The Y-BOCS is OCD-specific — it does not measure generalized anxiety, panic, or social anxiety; using it as a general anxiety measure would conflate very different constructs.

options.t: The Y-BOCS is a behavioral observation tool completed by nursing staff during the hospital stay, documenting observable compulsive behaviors rather than the patient's internal experience.

trap.name: Behavioral observation only
trap.note: The Y-BOCS assesses both behavioral and cognitive dimensions, including obsessional distress and the patient's ability to resist intrusive thoughts — it is clinician-administered, not a nursing observation form.

items.why: Y-BOCS = self-report, Broadband anxiety screen, and Behavioral observation only all mischaracterize the instrument. The page specifically names the Y-BOCS as 'the gold-standard clinician-rated measure of OCD severity and treatment response.' Serial tracking — obsessions and compulsions scored separately — is the measure's primary clinical value.
items.pearl: Y-BOCS = gold-standard clinician-rated OCD scale; obsessions and compulsions scored separately; use it to track treatment response, not just screen at baseline.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — The scale to know for OCD is the Y-BOCS (Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale) — the gold-standard clinician-rated measure of OCD severity and treatment response.

tier2.q: What is the structure of the Y-BOCS that makes it sensitive to treatment response over time?

options.t: A single total score calculated from patient self-report items rated on a 0–4 scale — simple total tracking over serial administrations.

A symptom checklist phase (cataloguing which obsessions and compulsions are present) followed by 10 severity items (5 for obsessions, 5 for compulsions) rated by the clinician — the two subscores can detect differential improvement in obsessions vs compulsions.
A frequency-only scale that counts the hours per day spent on rituals — higher ritual time equals higher severity regardless of patient distress.
A functional impairment scale that rates the impact of OCD on work, relationships, and ADLs — not symptom severity per se.

tier2.why: The Y-BOCS structure is what makes it the gold standard. The symptom checklist phase establishes which obsessions and compulsions are present (a dimensional catalogue of content types), but the severity rating is driven by the 10 severity items — 5 for obsessions and 5 for compulsions — rated by the clinician across dimensions like time occupied, distress, resistance, and control. Because obsessions and compulsions are scored separately (0–20 each, 0–40 total), the Y-BOCS can detect when medication reduces compulsions while obsessions persist, or vice versa, which informs the decision to intensify ERP vs pharmacotherapy.
