items.stem: A 32-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has refused treatment for 2 years. His wife is desperate to help and asks the team what she can do. The team is considering a traditional confrontational intervention approach. Which family therapy modality is specifically evidence-based for this scenario?

options.t: CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training) — the family member changes her own behavior in specific ways that reduce the reinforcement of drinking and increase the appeal of treatment-seeking, without confrontation or blame.
Structural family therapy (Minuchin) — the focus is on realigning the roles and boundaries in the marriage to reduce the enabling dynamic.

trap.name: Structural for substance refusal
trap.note: Structural therapy addresses role and boundary dysfunction but does not provide the specific behavioral strategies for family members managing a treatment-refusing person with SUD; CRAFT is specifically designed for this scenario.

options.t: A family confrontation (traditional intervention) — bringing family and friends together to confront the patient with consequences is the most evidence-based approach.

trap.name: Confrontational intervention
trap.note: Traditional confrontational interventions have mixed evidence and can damage the therapeutic alliance; CRAFT specifically trains families to use non-blame behavioral strategies and has a larger evidence base for engagement.

options.t: Emotionally focused therapy (EFT) — addressing the attachment disruption in the marriage will resolve the motivational impasse for the patient.

trap.name: EFT for treatment refusal
trap.note: EFT is couples-attachment focused and is the modality for a distressed couple's negative cycle — it is not specifically designed for a family member trying to invite a treatment-refusing person into care.

items.why: Structural for substance refusal, Confrontational intervention, and EFT for treatment refusal all apply less-specific frameworks. CRAFT is the specific modality: 'the family changes its own behavior to invite treatment — no blame.' It trains the wife to use behavioral strategies (reinforcing non-drinking behavior, withdrawing reinforcement of drinking, using teachable moments) that increase the patient's engagement with treatment.
items.pearl: CRAFT: the family changes its OWN behavior to invite treatment — no blame, no confrontation; evidence-based for families of treatment-refusing people with SUD.
items.evidence: family_modalities.md — CRAFT (Community Reinforcement & Family Training): the family changes its own behavior to invite treatment — no blame.

items.stem: A quality-improvement team wants to identify the single inpatient psychological intervention with the strongest readmission-prevention evidence. Which intervention has the hardest numbers?

options.t: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) — approximately 50% fewer suicidal behaviors.

trap.name: Safety planning hardest numbers
trap.note: Safety planning has strong evidence (50% reduction in suicidal behaviors), but the question asks about readmission prevention specifically — psychoeducation has the hardest readmission-specific numbers.

options.t: Psychoeducation — the hardest inpatient numbers for readmission prevention: readmission NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) and relapse NNT 9; and it costs nothing except time.
Behavioral activation — the most evidence-based inpatient psychological intervention for any condition.

trap.name: BA = strongest overall
trap.note: BA has the strongest evidence for acute depression (SMD −0.78) and is the best-fit inpatient technique, but readmission NNT 5 for psychoeducation specifically addresses the readmission-prevention question.

options.t: Problem-solving therapy (PST) — NNT 12 for repeat self-harm re-presentation.

trap.name: PST hardest numbers
trap.note: PST has an NNT of 12 for self-harm re-presentation — meaningful evidence, but psychoeducation's readmission NNT of 5 is the strongest number on the brief psychotherapy page.

items.why: Safety planning hardest numbers, BA = strongest overall, and PST hardest numbers each reference real evidence for different outcomes. For readmission prevention specifically, psychoeducation's NNT 5 is the standout: 'Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient numbers (readmission NNT 5) — and it's free.' This is the quality-improvement answer.
items.pearl: Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient readmission numbers: NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) — the highest-evidence, lowest-cost psychological intervention for preventing readmission.
items.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient numbers (readmission NNT 5) — and it's free.

items.stem: A 17-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa has been starved for 4 months and is starting nutritional rehabilitation. On day 3 of refeeding, her phosphate drops to 2.1 mg/dL. She is also mildly confused and has new-onset leg weakness. What is the most important diagnosis to recognize?

options.t: Refeeding syndrome — the metabolic shift from catabolic to anabolic metabolism drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells; hypophosphatemia is the hallmark and can cause cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and delirium.
Electrolyte depletion from malnutrition alone — she was already malnourished on admission, so the low phosphate reflects pre-existing deficiency rather than a refeeding process.

trap.name: Pre-existing deficiency only
trap.note: While pre-existing malnutrition contributes to baseline deficiencies, the precipitous drop in phosphate after initiating refeeding is the refeeding syndrome pattern — the metabolic shift of refeeding, not chronic depletion, is the mechanism.

options.t: Conversion disorder — the confusion and leg weakness represent a functional neurological symptom disorder superimposed on the eating disorder.

trap.name: Functional explanation for metabolic emergency
trap.note: Confusion and leg weakness in the context of a falling phosphate during refeeding is refeeding syndrome until proven otherwise — it is a medical emergency, not a functional disorder.

options.t: Thiamine deficiency — the neurological symptoms indicate Wernicke encephalopathy from B1 deficiency.

trap.name: Thiamine over phosphate
trap.note: Thiamine deficiency is a real risk in eating disorders and requires prophylactic replacement before carbohydrate loading, but a falling phosphate on day 3 of refeeding with weakness and confusion is the classic refeeding syndrome presentation — phosphate is the hallmark electrolyte.

items.why: Pre-existing deficiency only, Functional explanation for metabolic emergency, and Thiamine over phosphate all miss the refeeding-specific mechanism. The page calls refeeding syndrome 'the complication that kills' — hypophosphatemia is the hallmark. Note that D (thiamine) is also clinically relevant and the page specifically says 'give thiamine before or with carbohydrate' — but the presenting electrolyte abnormality and timing point to refeeding syndrome as the primary diagnosis.
items.pearl: Refeeding syndrome: watch phosphate — the hallmark is hypophosphatemia after starting nutrition in the severely malnourished; start low, go slow; supplement phosphate; give thiamine before carbs.
items.evidence: t_eating.md — Refeeding syndrome — the complication that kills: hypophosphatemia is the hallmark; the danger is cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and delirium. Supplement phosphate and give thiamine before or with carbohydrate.

tier2.q: Why does hypophosphatemia develop after initiating refeeding in a severely malnourished patient, rather than during the starvation period itself?

options.t: Carbohydrate refeeding increases renal phosphate excretion — the kidneys preferentially excrete phosphate when insulin levels rise.

Refeeding shifts metabolism from catabolic to anabolic — glucose and insulin drive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells for new cellular synthesis; since total body stores are depleted from malnutrition, the extracellular pool drops precipitously.
Starvation preserves phosphate by reducing cellular metabolic demand — refeeding simply re-activates the pre-existing phosphate deficiency that was masked.
Thiamine deficiency prevents phosphate absorption from the gut — refeeding exposes this deficiency because oral phosphate intake increases.

tier2.why: During starvation, catabolism releases phosphate from cells into the extracellular space, partially maintaining serum levels despite total body depletion. When refeeding begins, glucose triggers insulin release, which drives phosphate (along with potassium and magnesium) into cells for anabolic processes (glycolysis, ATP synthesis, protein synthesis). This intracellular shift drops extracellular phosphate rapidly — in an already-depleted patient, the serum level can fall to dangerous levels within 24–72 hours of starting nutrition. This is why refeeding syndrome occurs early in the refeeding course and why the most malnourished patients are at highest risk.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred for 'weight-related anxiety.' She is at normal weight and denies dieting. However, she endorses recurrent binge episodes followed by self-induced vomiting several times weekly, and she reports that her self-worth is almost entirely based on her weight and shape. On exam, you note calluses on her right hand knuckles. Which diagnosis should be suspected?

options.t: Anorexia nervosa, binge-purging subtype — the purging behavior and weight preoccupation are classic for anorexia.

trap.name: Normal weight rules out AN misread as AN
trap.note: Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low weight — this patient is at normal weight; her presentation is much more consistent with bulimia nervosa.

options.t: Binge-eating disorder — binge episodes with distress are the defining feature; no compensatory behavior is required.

trap.name: Binge = BED
trap.note: Binge-eating disorder specifically involves binges WITHOUT regular compensatory behavior; this patient has self-induced vomiting as a compensatory behavior, which distinguishes bulimia nervosa from BED.

options.t: Bulimia nervosa — normal weight does not rule out bulimia; the binge-purge cycle, weight/shape self-evaluation, and Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) are the diagnostic markers.
Purging disorder — recurrent purging in the absence of objectively large binge episodes, with weight/shape concern, is classified as purging disorder.

trap.name: Purging without binges = purging disorder
trap.note: Purging disorder requires the absence of recurrent objective binge episodes — this patient has both binge episodes AND purging, which meets bulimia nervosa criteria; purging disorder is diagnosed only when purging occurs without the binge component.

items.why: Normal weight rules out AN, Binge = BED, and Normal weight = malingering all miss the defining features. The page: 'Bulimia nervosa — weight is often normal or high — a normal weight does not rule it out. Look for Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid enlargement, and dental enamel erosion.' All three examination findings distinguish BN from BED: the presence of compensatory behaviors (purging) is the key.
items.pearl: Normal weight DOES NOT rule out bulimia nervosa — look for binge-purge cycle + Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) + parotid swelling + dental erosion.
items.evidence: t_eating.md — Bulimia nervosa — weight is often normal or high — a normal weight does not rule it out. Look for Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid enlargement, and dental enamel erosion.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman who delivered 6 days ago is brought by her husband with confusion, talking to people who aren't there, and expressing beliefs that her baby 'was sent to test her faith.' She had been laughing and crying alternately. She was seen yesterday and appeared fine for two hours. What is the most critical diagnosis to consider?

options.t: Baby blues — mild postpartum mood changes are expected in the first 2 weeks and are self-limited.

trap.name: Baby blues by default
trap.note: Baby blues involves mild mood lability without functional impairment and certainly without psychotic features or confusion; the presentation here — new perceptual disturbance, delusions, and confusion — is not baby blues.

options.t: Postpartum depression — the mood lability and behavioral change represent a perinatal major depressive episode.

trap.name: Postpartum depression default
trap.note: Postpartum depression does not include psychotic features, delusions, or confusion in its non-psychotic form; the abrupt-onset psychosis with waxing-and-waning course within days of delivery is postpartum psychosis — a different and urgent entity.

options.t: Postpartum psychosis — this is a psychiatric emergency; abrupt onset within days of delivery, waxing-and-waning course, psychotic features centered on the infant, and the lucid interval does not provide reassurance.
Medical emergency — new psychosis postpartum indicates eclampsia or infection until proven otherwise.

trap.name: Medical cause only
trap.note: Medical causes must be excluded (thyroid, infection, eclampsia) but the waxing-and-waning course with psychotic features centered on the infant in the first week postpartum is the postpartum psychosis picture — the clinical priority is both psychiatric emergency evaluation AND medical workup simultaneously.

items.why: Baby blues by default, Postpartum depression default, and Medical cause only all fail to identify postpartum psychosis as the emergency. The page: 'Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently.' The lucid interval yesterday is explicitly stated to not provide reassurance: 'A lucid interval does not rule out psychosis — the waxing/waning course is part of the illness.'
items.pearl: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency — abrupt onset, waxing/waning course, infant-focused delusions within days of delivery; a lucid interval does NOT rule it out.
items.evidence: t_perinatal.md — POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS IS A PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently. A lucid interval does not rule out psychosis — the waxing/waning course is part of the illness, not reassurance.

tier2.q: What psychiatric history most strongly predicts postpartum psychosis, and why does this influence the medication decision at discharge?

options.t: A history of major depressive disorder — postpartum psychosis is an extension of unipolar depression and responds best to antidepressants.
A history of bipolar disorder — postpartum psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar spectrum illness; stopping maintenance mood stabilizer nearly triples the risk of postpartum relapse.
A history of schizophrenia — postpartum psychosis is simply a schizophrenic relapse triggered by the hormonal changes of delivery.
No prior psychiatric history predicts postpartum psychosis — it is idiopathic and equally likely in any postpartum patient.

tier2.why: Postpartum psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar disorder — patients with bipolar disorder have a risk approximately 100-fold higher than the general population. This matters for discharge because 'stopping maintenance medication nearly triples postpartum relapse (pooled ~35% overall; ~66% off medication vs ~23% on prophylaxis).' The medication-stop decision in a postpartum patient with bipolar disorder is itself a high-risk intervention — 'stop everything' is not a safe default.

link.label: Open the Somatic Symptom Disorders page

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred for psychiatric consultation for 'medically unexplained' chest pain and fatigue. Her symptoms are real and distressing, her workup is negative, and she spends hours daily researching health threats and 4–5 hours daily focused on her symptoms. Which DSM-5-TR principle is most relevant to the diagnosis?

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder requires that the symptoms have no identifiable organic cause — the diagnosis is made only after medical explanation is definitively excluded.

trap.name: SSD = medically unexplained
trap.note: This is the pre-DSM-5 framing — DSM-5-TR shifted the definition of SSD away from 'medically unexplained' to focus on the excessive psychological response; the symptom may or may not be medically explained.

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder requires at least 3 distinct somatic complaints across different organ systems.

trap.name: Multiple organ systems required
trap.note: The DSM-5-TR criterion is ≥1 distressing somatic symptom plus excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors — not a minimum number of symptoms or organ systems; one symptom with excessive response qualifies.

options.t: These complaints are best diagnosed as illness anxiety disorder because the patient's main symptom is health preoccupation rather than multiple somatic symptoms.

trap.name: Preoccupation = IAD not SSD
trap.note: Illness anxiety disorder (IAD) features preoccupation with having a disease with minimal somatic symptoms — this patient has distressing somatic symptoms (chest pain, fatigue) plus the excessive cognitive response; this fits SSD, not IAD.

options.t: DSM-5-TR defines somatic symptom disorder by the excessive thoughts, feelings, and behaviors around symptoms — not by whether those symptoms are medically explained; a patient with a confirmed medical diagnosis can still meet SSD criteria if her response to symptoms is disproportionate.

items.why: SSD = medically unexplained, Multiple organ systems required, and Preoccupation = IAD all misstate the DSM-5-TR diagnosis. The page's first pearl: 'SSD is defined by the excessive response to symptoms, not by whether they're medically explained (a key DSM-5-TR shift from medically unexplained).' This is a tested concept: the diagnosis no longer hinges on medical explanation.
items.pearl: SSD (DSM-5-TR): defined by excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors about symptoms — NOT by whether the symptoms are medically unexplained; a confirmed medical illness can coexist with SSD.
items.evidence: t_somatic.md — SSD is defined by the excessive response to symptoms, not by whether they're medically explained (a key DSM-5-TR shift from 'medically unexplained').

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted with a 3-day history of right-sided paralysis and inability to walk. Neurological workup is negative. When the examiner tests voluntary right hip extension, extension is absent; however, strong right hip extension is felt involuntarily when the patient flexes the left hip against resistance (positive Hoover sign). Which statement about the diagnosis is most accurate?

options.t: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion) is diagnosed here by a positive examination finding — the Hoover sign; this is a rule-in diagnosis, not solely a diagnosis of exclusion.
The diagnosis requires a psychiatric interview confirming psychosocial stress as the precipitant before a neurological cause can be excluded.

trap.name: Psychiatric cause required
trap.note: DSM-5 removed the requirement for an identified psychological precipitant from the conversion disorder criteria; the diagnosis is made by positive examination signs (rule-in), not by excluding all neurology and confirming a psychological cause.

options.t: The diagnosis requires a complete neurological workup including MRI, EMG, and nerve conduction studies before conversion can be considered.

trap.name: Full workup before conversion
trap.note: Positive examination signs like the Hoover sign are themselves diagnostic and are not simply 'tests not yet done'; waiting for a complete negative workup before considering conversion delays a treatable diagnosis.

options.t: The positive examination finding is unreliable — the Hoover sign has poor sensitivity and should not anchor a diagnosis.

trap.name: Hoover sign unreliable
trap.note: The Hoover sign has good specificity for functional weakness — it is a clinically validated examination finding that supports a rule-in diagnosis, not an unreliable anecdotal maneuver.

items.why: Psychiatric cause required, Full workup before conversion, and Hoover sign unreliable all delay diagnosis or require unnecessary conditions. The page is explicit: 'Conversion/functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis — Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, non-epileptic seizures. Name conversion by its positive signs — don't make it a diagnosis of exclusion alone.'
items.pearl: Functional neurological disorder (conversion) is diagnosed by POSITIVE examination signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness) — not solely by exclusion; DSM-5 removed the psychological precipitant requirement.
items.evidence: t_somatic.md — Conversion/functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis — Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, non-epileptic seizures. Name conversion by its positive signs — don't make it a diagnosis of exclusion alone.

tier2.q: Why did DSM-5 remove the requirement for an identified psychological stressor from the diagnosis of functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion)?

options.t: To make the diagnosis easier to code — the removal was an administrative convenience rather than a clinical improvement.

Because a psychological precipitant is not reliably identifiable in all cases, and requiring it was clinician-attributed (confabulated) rather than patient-reported; the diagnosis now rests on the neurological examination finding, which is objective.
Because DSM-5 de-medicalized all psychiatric diagnoses — the psychological stressor requirement was removed from all diagnoses in the somatic section.
To increase the sensitivity of the diagnosis — more patients qualify without requiring documentation of a precipitant.

tier2.why: The pre-DSM-5 requirement for an identified psychological stressor was criticized because (1) clinicians often attributed stress confabulatorily rather than patients actually reporting a clear precipitant, (2) it was unreliable across clinicians, and (3) it implied that the absence of an identified stressor could falsely reassure about the diagnosis. DSM-5 shifted the criteria to rest on the positive neurological examination finding — an objective, replicable observation — which better separates functional from structural neurological disease and removes the subjective psychological stressor requirement.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman has been hospitalized multiple times for recurrent infections. Staff have noted that her central line infections always follow nursing shifts during which she is left alone with the IV port. A camera reveals that she is injecting herself with contaminated fluid. She appears distressed when confronted and says, 'I just need doctors to take care of me.' There is no evidence of secondary gain (no pending disability, no legal issue). Which diagnosis is most consistent?

options.t: Malingering — the deliberate production of symptoms for secondary gain is the defining feature.

trap.name: Deliberate = malingering
trap.note: Deliberate production of symptoms is present in BOTH factitious disorder and malingering; the critical distinction is motivation — malingering requires an external incentive (financial, legal, drug-seeking), which is absent here.

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder — the recurrent hospitalizations and the distress of the patient indicate a pattern of disproportionate health concern.

trap.name: Recurrent admissions = SSD
trap.note: SSD is characterized by excessive worry about symptoms — not by deliberate production of illness; the conscious self-injection places this in a different diagnostic category entirely.

options.t: Conversion disorder — the pattern of self-limited infections with resolution suggests a functional mechanism.

trap.name: Episodic = functional
trap.note: Conversion disorder is unconscious and produces neurological symptoms; deliberate self-injection with contaminated fluid is a conscious act in a medically serious, not functional, illness category.

options.t: Factitious disorder imposed on self — conscious falsification or induction of illness motivated by assuming the sick role, without external incentive; 'I need doctors to take care of me' is the factitious driver.

items.why: Deliberate = malingering, Recurrent admissions = SSD, and Episodic = functional all apply the wrong framework. The page's diagnostic table: 'Factitious disorder — conscious falsification or induction of illness (self or another) motivated by assuming the sick role, without external reward.' The two-axis rule: 'Separate on two axes: conscious? and external incentive? Factitious = internal motive (sick role); malingering = external incentive (and is not a disorder).'
items.pearl: Factitious = conscious, internal motive (sick role); malingering = conscious, external incentive (money/drugs/legal); neither has unconscious somatic symptoms.
items.evidence: t_somatic.md — Factitious = internal motive (sick role); malingering = external incentive (and is not a disorder). Separate on the two axes: conscious? and external incentive?

tier2.q: A caregiver is suspected of intentionally inducing illness in her 6-year-old child to maintain hospital access and medical attention. Which specific diagnosis and clinical obligation apply?

options.t: Malingering by proxy — the external incentive (social support, housing) makes this malingering rather than factitious disorder; no mandatory reporting obligation applies.
Factitious disorder imposed on another (medical child abuse) — this is a form of child abuse and a mandatory reporting obligation; protecting the child takes priority over confronting the caregiver.
Munchausen syndrome by proxy — this is a historical term; no specific mandatory reporting obligation exists because psychiatric diagnosis does not create reporting duties.
Somatic symptom disorder imposed by parent — the parent's excessive health preoccupation shapes the child's medical utilization; no reporting duty applies.

tier2.why: The current DSM-5-TR term is 'factitious disorder imposed on another' (formerly Munchausen by proxy). The page explicitly states it is a form of abuse: 'Factitious disorder imposed on another (medical child abuse) is reportable.' The clinical obligation is to protect the dependent (the child) and file a mandatory report — this takes precedence over psychiatric consultation, confrontation, or treatment of the caregiver. The page cross-references the ethics and law teaching: 'Imposed on another (formerly Munchausen by proxy) is a form of abuse — report it.'

items.stem: A 55-year-old Puerto Rican woman is brought to the emergency department by her family. She is hyperventilating, trembling, shouting uncontrollably, and has fallen to the floor. Her family says this has happened before after a stressful family argument. Her vitals are normal and she recovers fully within 30 minutes. Which culturally informed interpretation is most accurate?

options.t: This is a panic disorder episode — the hyperventilation and trembling meet the physiological criteria for a panic attack.

trap.name: Symptoms match panic
trap.note: While the symptoms overlap with panic, applying a Western diagnostic label before exploring cultural context risks misdiagnosis; the episodic, stress-triggered, interpersonally mediated presentation with full recovery is classic for ataque de nervios, a culturally recognized pattern.

options.t: This is a functional neurological disorder — the shouting and falling indicate a non-epileptic seizure.

trap.name: Motor symptoms = functional seizure
trap.note: Functional neurological disorder requires positive examination signs and an individual assessment; without those, attributing a culturally patterned episode to conversion is premature and bypasses cultural context.

options.t: This may be ataque de nervios — a Latino cultural concept of distress characterized by trembling, shouting, hyperventilation, and sometimes falling, typically precipitated by family stress; cultural inquiry is essential before applying a Western diagnostic label.
This is malingering — the rapid recovery and interpersonal context suggest the episode served a social function.

trap.name: Socially embedded = malingering
trap.note: Cultural idioms of distress may serve interpersonal functions within their cultural context without constituting malingering — applying malingering to a culturally recognized pattern without adequate assessment is both inaccurate and harmful.

items.why: Symptoms match panic, Motor symptoms = functional seizure, and Socially embedded = malingering all bypass cultural inquiry. The page: 'Cultural concepts of distress (e.g., ataque de nervios) can mimic panic or psychosis — ask before you label.' Using Kleinman's explanatory-model questions would surface the patient's interpretation and cultural meaning before assigning a diagnosis.
items.pearl: Ataque de nervios: culturally patterned distress in Latino communities — trembling, shouting, hyperventilation, falling, stress-triggered — can be misread as panic, seizure, or psychosis without cultural inquiry.
items.evidence: cultural_psychiatry.md — Cultural concepts of distress (e.g., ataque de nervios, susto) can be mistaken for panic, psychosis, or malingering. Ask before you label.

tier2.q: What is the purpose of Kleinman's explanatory-model questions in cross-cultural clinical encounters?

options.t: To confirm that the patient's illness understanding matches the biomedical diagnosis — explaining any discrepancy corrects cultural misunderstanding.

To elicit the patient's own framework for what the illness means, what caused it, what they fear, and what treatment they expect — surfacing beliefs and expectations that shape adherence and therapeutic relationship.
To determine whether the patient requires a medical interpreter — the questions reveal whether language is the primary communication barrier.
To screen for psychosis — patients who attribute illness to supernatural causes are flagged for psychiatric assessment.

tier2.why: Kleinman's explanatory-model questions ('What do you call this problem? What do you think caused it? How does it affect you? What are you most afraid of? What treatment do you expect?') are not about correcting the patient's beliefs or screening for pathology. They are about surfacing the patient's illness framework so the clinician understands what the illness means to the patient — beliefs about cause, significance, and expected treatment that directly influence adherence, trust, and therapeutic planning. Cultural concepts of distress may emerge through these questions that would otherwise be mislabeled as panic or psychosis.

items.stem: A 34-year-old Black man presents with paranoid ideation, disorganized thinking, and social withdrawal that began 3 months ago. A student suggests schizophrenia. The attending asks the student to consider a documented cultural bias. Which statement reflects the clinical evidence?

options.t: Black patients present with more severe schizophrenia symptoms on average, which explains the higher diagnostic rate.

trap.name: Severity explains disparity
trap.note: The higher rate of schizophrenia diagnoses in Black patients is not explained by symptom severity — it reflects a documented diagnostic bias; the same presentations in Black patients are more often labeled schizophrenia and less often labeled mood disorder.

options.t: The diagnostic difference reflects differential rates of schizophrenia across demographic groups — epidemiological data confirm higher prevalence in this population.

trap.name: Epidemiology explains disparity
trap.note: The prevalence difference in diagnosis rates does not reflect true prevalence differences — it reflects clinician diagnostic bias; the page specifically states these disparities are driven by clinician bias, not different rates of underlying illness.

options.t: Cultural mistrust in the clinical encounter leads Black patients to endorse more psychotic symptoms on screening, creating a false-positive signal.

trap.name: Patient behavior explains disparity
trap.note: The documented disparity is driven by clinician diagnostic behavior (over-applying schizophrenia, under-applying mood disorders), not by patient reporting patterns.

options.t: Black patients are disproportionately over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders relative to comparable presentations — a documented clinician bias that is not explained by symptom profile or true prevalence differences.

items.why: Severity explains disparity, Epidemiology explains disparity, and Patient behavior explains disparity all misattribute the cause. The page is explicit: 'Black (and some other minority) patients are disproportionately over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders relative to comparable presentations — a documented bias to guard against.' This is a patient-safety issue that requires active self-monitoring.
items.pearl: Documented bias: Black patients are over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders — not due to prevalence differences, but clinician diagnostic bias; guard against it.
items.evidence: cultural_psychiatry.md — Black (and some other minority) patients are disproportionately over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders relative to comparable presentations — a documented bias to guard against.

items.stem: A 30-year-old mother, 3 weeks postpartum, scores a 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). She is distressed and anxious. The student says, 'She screened positive for postpartum depression — start sertraline.' The attending asks what the student may have missed. Which is most accurate?

options.t: The EPDS is not validated for postpartum use — use the PHQ-9 instead.

trap.name: EPDS not validated postpartum
trap.note: The EPDS is specifically designed and validated for postpartum screening; this is factually incorrect.

options.t: A score of 14 on the EPDS requires hospitalization — outpatient sertraline is below the level of care indicated.

trap.name: EPDS score mandates hospitalization
trap.note: EPDS scores guide clinical decisions but do not directly mandate a specific level of care; the clinical picture (function, safety, psychotic features) determines disposition.

options.t: The EPDS screens for depression and anxiety but does NOT detect psychotic or manic symptoms — explicitly ask about hallucinations, delusions, and manic symptoms before assuming postpartum depression rather than psychosis or bipolar relapse.
Sertraline is contraindicated in the first 4 weeks postpartum — the student should recommend a different SSRI.

trap.name: Sertraline contraindicated postpartum
trap.note: Sertraline and escitalopram are specifically mentioned in the page as usual first-line SSRIs for perinatal depression; there is no 4-week postpartum contraindication.

items.why: EPDS not validated, EPDS score mandates hospitalization, and Sertraline contraindicated all misstate the evidence. The page's explicit pearl: 'The EPDS screens depression, not psychosis — ask about delusions and perceptual disturbance directly.' The student's error is treating a positive depression screen as a complete psychiatric assessment — the EPDS misses psychosis and mania by design.
items.pearl: EPDS screens for depression and anxiety — it does NOT detect psychosis or mania; always ask explicitly about delusions, hallucinations, and manic symptoms in every postpartum patient.
items.evidence: t_perinatal.md — The EPDS screens depression, not psychosis — ask about delusions and perceptual disturbance directly.

tier2.q: A postpartum patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of accidentally dropping her baby, which she finds horrifying. She does not act on these thoughts and goes out of her way to avoid holding the baby near stairs. What is the correct interpretation, and how does it differ from a concerning psychotic feature?

options.t: This is a command hallucination instructing her to harm the baby — she requires emergency admission and a safety plan for infant protection.

This is postpartum OCD — the intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic (horrifying to her), and she avoids situations that could lead to the feared outcome; this differs from psychotic phenomena — voices experienced as external or beliefs about the infant held with delusional conviction, which are an emergency regardless of how distressed the mother is by them — and the correct response is clinical support and reassurance, not emergency separation from the baby.
This is a normal postpartum anxiety response — new mothers universally have intrusive thoughts about infant safety, which resolves without treatment.
This is a delusion of persecution — the belief that she might harm her child is a paranoid misinterpretation that requires antipsychotic treatment.

tier2.why: Postpartum OCD intrusive thoughts are a critically important differential. The page states: 'Postpartum OCD intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic and not command hallucinations — distinguish them to avoid both over- and under-reaction.' Key discrimination: (1) Ego-dystonic: the patient is horrified by the thoughts and does not want to act on them. (2) She avoids, not approaches, situations that could lead to the feared outcome. (3) Psychotic phenomena are experienced as external perceptions (voices) or held with delusional conviction; the mother's distress does not rule them out, and risk tracks conviction and appraisal of the experience, not ego-syntonicity. Mislabeling postpartum OCD as command hallucinations leads to emergency separation and antipsychotic treatment of a patient who needs reassurance and OCD-specific treatment.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted after an assault. He has a documented history of truancy, fire-setting, and cruelty to animals beginning at age 12. Which finding is required to diagnose antisocial personality disorder?

options.t: Evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15
A current age of at least 16 years

trap.name: Wrong age threshold
trap.note: ASPD requires the patient be at least 18; conduct disorder is the childhood-onset antecedent.

options.t: The presence of psychotic symptoms during the aggressive episodes

trap.name: Psychosis conflation
trap.note: ASPD is a personality disorder, not a psychotic illness — psychosis is not a criterion.

options.t: A single act of serious violence in adulthood

trap.name: One-act fallacy
trap.note: ASPD requires a pervasive pattern of disregard for others' rights, not one act.

items.why: ASPD requires the person be ≥18 AND show evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15 — the childhood antecedent is mandatory.
items.pearl: Antisocial personality disorder: age ≥18 plus evidence of conduct disorder before age 15.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: antisocial PD requires age at least 18 plus conduct disorder onset before age 15.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man believes coworkers are subtly undermining him and reads hidden hostile meaning into ordinary remarks, present for decades. He has never had hallucinations, sustained delusions, or functional collapse. Most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Delusional disorder, persecutory type

trap.name: Delusion overreach
trap.note: Delusional disorder requires a fixed sustained delusion; pervasive lifelong distrust without one is the personality pattern.

options.t: Paranoid personality disorder
Schizophrenia, paranoid presentation

trap.name: Psychosis conflation
trap.note: Schizophrenia requires frank psychosis and functional decline, absent here.

options.t: Schizotypal personality disorder

trap.name: Cluster A mix-up
trap.note: Schizotypal features odd beliefs/magical thinking, not pure pervasive distrust.

items.why: Pervasive, longstanding distrust and suspiciousness without frank delusions or psychosis is paranoid personality disorder (Cluster A).
items.pearl: Pervasive lifelong distrust without frank psychosis = paranoid personality disorder.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: paranoid PD vs psychotic disorders.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has few relationships, magical thinking, ideas of reference, and odd speech; her social anxiety does not lessen as she gets to know people and stems from paranoid discomfort rather than fear of embarrassment. Which best fits?

options.t: Schizoid personality disorder

trap.name: No-desire mix-up
trap.note: Schizoid patients are indifferent to relationships and lack odd beliefs/magical thinking.

options.t: Avoidant personality disorder

trap.name: Fear-of-rejection mix-up
trap.note: Avoidant anxiety is driven by fear of rejection and eases with acceptance; here it is paranoid and persistent.

options.t: Schizotypal personality disorder
Social anxiety disorder

trap.name: State-vs-trait error
trap.note: Social anxiety disorder lacks the odd beliefs, ideas of reference, and eccentric cognition.

items.why: Odd beliefs, magical thinking, ideas of reference, and eccentric cognition with persistent paranoid social anxiety define schizotypal PD (Cluster A).
items.pearl: Odd beliefs + magical thinking + persistent paranoid social discomfort = schizotypal.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: schizotypal vs schizoid vs avoidant.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder and recurrent self-harm asks what treatment is most likely to help long-term. Most appropriate first-line recommendation?

options.t: Long-term benzodiazepines for affective instability

trap.name: Benzo trap
trap.note: Benzodiazepines worsen disinhibition and carry dependence risk; not a BPD treatment.

options.t: An antipsychotic as definitive monotherapy

trap.name: Med-as-cure trap
trap.note: No medication is first-line or curative for BPD; pharmacotherapy is adjunctive.

options.t: Brief supportive counseling as the whole treatment plan

trap.name: Therapeutic nihilism
trap.note: BPD responds well to structured psychotherapy.

options.t: A structured evidence-based psychotherapy such as dialectical behavior therapy

items.why: Structured psychotherapy (DBT and related) is first-line for BPD; medications are adjunctive and symptom-targeted, and benzodiazepines are avoided.
items.pearl: BPD: psychotherapy (DBT) first-line; meds adjunctive; avoid benzodiazepines.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Acute inpatient management and disposition; psychotherapy.md — DBT for BPD/self-harm.

items.stem: A 50-year-old accountant is preoccupied with rules, lists, and perfectionism so that tasks are never finished; he sees nothing wrong with this and is proud of his standards. He has no true obsessions or compulsions. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder

trap.name: OCD conflation
trap.note: OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions and anxiety-reducing rituals — absent here.

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Worry mislabel
trap.note: GAD is pervasive worry, not perfectionistic character.

options.t: Narcissistic personality disorder

trap.name: Cluster B mix-up
trap.note: Perfectionism/control is not grandiosity or need for admiration.

items.why: OCPD is an ego-syntonic Cluster C pattern of perfectionism, orderliness, and control without true obsessions or compulsions (which define OCD).
items.pearl: OCPD = ego-syntonic perfectionism/control, no true obsessions/compulsions; OCD is ego-dystonic with rituals.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: OCPD vs OCD.

items.stem: On rounds you are asked to group the personality disorders. Which pairing of cluster and descriptor is correct?

options.t: Cluster A = anxious; Cluster B = odd; Cluster C = dramatic

trap.name: Shuffled clusters
trap.note: Misassigned — A is odd, B dramatic, C anxious.

options.t: Cluster A = odd/eccentric; Cluster B = dramatic/erratic; Cluster C = anxious/fearful
Cluster A = dramatic; Cluster B = anxious; Cluster C = odd

trap.name: Shuffled clusters
trap.note: Reversed — A is odd/eccentric.

options.t: There is no descriptive grouping of the personality disorders

trap.name: Denies the schema
trap.note: DSM groups the ten PDs into clusters A/B/C.

items.why: DSM clusters: A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) odd/eccentric; B (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic) dramatic/erratic; C (avoidant, dependent, OCPD) anxious/fearful.
items.pearl: Cluster A = odd, B = dramatic, C = anxious.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: Cluster A/B/C descriptors.

items.stem: A patient is irritable and demanding during an acute manic episode; the team wonders about a personality disorder. What best distinguishes a personality disorder from this presentation?

options.t: Difficult behavior during one acute inpatient episode

trap.name: Difficulty-equals-PD trap
trap.note: Unit behavior during acute illness is not a personality disorder; first rule out the treatable state.

options.t: Reliable diagnosis during an acute mood or psychotic episode

trap.name: Timing error
trap.note: Traits should be assessed after the acute state resolves and with collateral across settings.

options.t: Enduring cross-context traits beginning by adolescence or early adulthood
A single dramatic behavior that captures the patient's character

trap.name: One-behavior fallacy
trap.note: Personality disorders require an enduring, pervasive pattern, not one memorable behavior.

items.why: Difficulty-equals-PD trap, Timing error, and One-behavior fallacy all diagnose too quickly. Personality disorder requires an enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern beginning by adolescence or early adulthood and present across contexts — not behavior limited to an acute manic, psychotic, intoxicated, or withdrawal state.
items.pearl: Diagnose personality from an enduring cross-context pattern, not from acute-episode behavior.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: general PD criteria and diagnostic overshadowing.

items.stem: A 9-year-old is referred for inattention and hyperactivity. Which is required to diagnose ADHD?

options.t: Symptoms limited to the classroom

trap.name: Single-setting error
trap.note: ADHD requires impairment in at least two settings; one setting suggests a situational cause.

options.t: New onset after age 12 with normal early childhood

trap.name: Late-onset error
trap.note: Several symptoms must be present before age 12.

options.t: A confirmatory brain MRI or EEG

trap.name: Test-confirmation trap
trap.note: ADHD is a clinical diagnosis; no scan confirms it.

options.t: Symptoms before age 12 with impairment in at least two settings

items.why: ADHD requires several symptoms before age 12, ≥6 months, with impairment in ≥2 settings; it is a clinical diagnosis.
items.pearl: ADHD: symptoms before age 12, ≥2 settings, clinical diagnosis.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: ADHD criteria.

items.stem: A 10-year-old has ADHD with significant impairment despite behavioral supports. First-line pharmacologic treatment?

options.t: A stimulant
An antipsychotic

trap.name: Off-target trap
trap.note: Not first-line for ADHD; metabolic and movement risks.

options.t: A benzodiazepine

trap.name: Sedative trap
trap.note: No role in ADHD; can worsen disinhibition.

options.t: An SSRI

trap.name: Wrong-class trap
trap.note: SSRIs treat depression/anxiety, not core ADHD.

items.why: Stimulants are first-line and most effective for core ADHD symptoms when not contraindicated; non-stimulants such as atomoxetine, viloxazine, and alpha-2 agonists are alternatives when risk-benefit concerns point away from stimulants.
items.pearl: ADHD: stimulants first-line; non-stimulants are alternatives when risk or tolerability changes the plan.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: ADHD medication.

items.stem: An 8-year-old is argumentative, loses his temper, and defies adults, but has never been physically aggressive, destroyed property, stolen, or seriously violated others' rights. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Conduct disorder

trap.name: CD overreach
trap.note: Conduct disorder requires aggression, destruction, deceit/theft, or serious rule violations — none present.

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder
Antisocial personality disorder

trap.name: Adult-dx error
trap.note: ASPD cannot be diagnosed before age 18.

options.t: Intermittent explosive disorder

trap.name: IED mismatch
trap.note: IED is recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts, not the pervasive defiant pattern.

items.why: ODD is angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, and vindictiveness WITHOUT the aggression, destruction, deceit, or serious rule-violations of conduct disorder.
items.pearl: ODD = defiant/argumentative without violating others' rights; conduct disorder adds aggression/destruction/deceit.
items.evidence: t_impulse.md — ODD vs conduct disorder; antisocial PD developmental spine.

items.stem: A 4-year-old has marked deficits in social communication and reciprocity plus restricted, repetitive behaviors and insistence on sameness, present since early development. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Social (pragmatic) communication disorder

trap.name: Missing-the-RRBs trap
trap.note: That disorder lacks restricted/repetitive behaviors, which are present here.

options.t: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

trap.name: Wrong-domain trap
trap.note: ADHD is inattention/hyperactivity, not the ASD pattern.

options.t: Autism spectrum disorder
Childhood-onset schizophrenia

trap.name: Psychosis mislabel
trap.note: ASD lacks hallucinations/delusions.

items.why: ASD requires BOTH social-communication deficits AND restricted, repetitive behaviors with early onset; the restricted/repetitive domain separates it from social communication disorder.
items.pearl: Autism = social-communication deficits PLUS restricted/repetitive behaviors, early onset.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: autism spectrum disorder.

items.stem: A 12-year-old has had multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, waxing and waning for 18 months, onset at age 9. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Persistent (chronic) motor OR vocal tic disorder

trap.name: Single-modality error
trap.note: Chronic tic disorder is motor OR vocal; Tourette requires both.

options.t: Provisional tic disorder

trap.name: Duration error
trap.note: Provisional = tics <1 year; these have lasted 18 months.

options.t: Functional movement disorder

trap.name: Wrong-category trap
trap.note: The chronic multi-tic pattern fits Tourette.

options.t: Tourette disorder with motor and vocal tics

items.why: Tourette requires BOTH multiple motor tics AND ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year, onset before age 18.
items.pearl: Tourette: multiple motor tics AND ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year, onset before 18.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: tic disorders.

items.stem: A 7-year-old has primary nocturnal enuresis with normal daytime continence and a normal exam. Most appropriate first-line management?

options.t: Behavioral measures plus an enuresis alarm
Open-ended desmopressin as first-line therapy

trap.name: Med-first trap
trap.note: Desmopressin helps short-term control but relapse is common; the alarm has better long-term cure.

options.t: Imipramine as first-line therapy

trap.name: Outdated/risk trap
trap.note: TCAs are later-line because overdose cardiotoxicity matters.

options.t: Fluid restriction and punishment for wet nights

trap.name: Harm trap
trap.note: Punitive approaches are ineffective and harmful.

items.why: For primary nocturnal enuresis with normal daytime continence and a normal exam, reassurance and behavioral measures are first-line; the enuresis alarm has the best long-term cure. Desmopressin is useful for short-term control, and TCAs are later-line because of toxicity.
items.pearl: Enuresis: alarm for long-term cure; desmopressin for short-term control; never punish wet nights.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: nocturnal enuresis.

items.stem: A child is evaluated for intellectual disability. What determines the severity level (mild, moderate, severe, profound)?

options.t: Full-scale IQ score alone

trap.name: IQ-only trap
trap.note: DSM-5-TR grades severity by adaptive functioning, not IQ cutoffs alone.

options.t: Adaptive-functioning impairment
Chronological age at testing

trap.name: Age error
trap.note: Age does not set intellectual-disability severity.

options.t: Presence of a known genetic syndrome

trap.name: Etiology error
trap.note: Etiology may explain the disorder but does not set severity.

items.why: Intellectual disability requires deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning with developmental-period onset; severity is graded by adaptive functioning, not IQ alone.
items.pearl: Intellectual disability severity = adaptive functioning, not IQ alone.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: intellectual disability.

items.stem: A patient with untreated mania insists on leaving; the team considers an involuntary hold. Which criterion must generally be met?

options.t: The team simply believes admission would be beneficial

trap.name: Paternalism trap
trap.note: Perceived benefit alone is not a legal basis for a hold.

options.t: The patient disagrees with the diagnosis

trap.name: Disagreement trap
trap.note: Disagreement is not grounds for commitment.

options.t: Mental illness plus dangerousness or grave disability
Family request for admission

trap.name: Third-party trap
trap.note: A family request alone does not satisfy criteria.

items.why: Involuntary hospitalization generally requires mental illness plus danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability; statutes vary by jurisdiction and local policy.
items.pearl: Involuntary hold = mental illness + (danger to self / others / grave disability).
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Involuntary hospitalization.

items.stem: A resident asks whether a delirious patient is 'competent' to refuse a lumbar puncture. Most accurate framing?

options.t: Capacity and competence are identical bedside labels

trap.name: Conflation trap
trap.note: Capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is a legal status.

options.t: Judicial review for every medical decision

trap.name: Over-legalization
trap.note: Clinicians assess capacity at the bedside; courts determine competence.

options.t: Lost capacity is permanent once documented

trap.name: Permanence error
trap.note: Capacity can fluctuate and is decision-specific.

options.t: Capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is legal

items.why: Capacity is clinical, decision-specific, and can fluctuate; competence is a legal status decided by a court. The four abilities frame the bedside capacity assessment.
items.pearl: Capacity = clinical, decision-specific, fluctuates; competence = legal, court-determined.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Capacity vs competence.

items.stem: An unconscious patient arrives after an overdose, no surrogate reachable, needing immediate life-saving treatment. Which principle applies?

options.t: Emergency exception with implied consent
Wait for a court-appointed guardian before treating

trap.name: Delay-harm trap
trap.note: Waiting in a life-threatening emergency causes avoidable harm.

options.t: Require written consent before any intervention

trap.name: Consent-absolutism
trap.note: Written consent is not required for emergency life-saving care when consent cannot be obtained.

options.t: Treat an unrelated prior refusal as binding

trap.name: Irrelevant-refusal trap
trap.note: An unrelated prior refusal does not govern emergency overdose care.

items.why: The emergency exception allows necessary treatment to prevent death or serious harm when the patient lacks capacity and no surrogate or applicable advance directive is available.
items.pearl: Emergency exception: implied consent covers necessary urgent care when consent cannot be obtained.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Consent and the emergency exception.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

items.stem: A patient with intact capacity and a terminal illness refuses a recommended life-prolonging treatment; the team disagrees. Ethically correct action?

options.t: Override because the treatment would prolong life

trap.name: Beneficence-override trap
trap.note: Beneficence doesn't override an autonomous capacitated refusal.

options.t: Respect the refusal — a patient with capacity may decline even life-sustaining treatment
Obtain a court order to compel treatment

trap.name: Coercion trap
trap.note: Courts don't compel treatment of a capacitated patient who refuses.

options.t: Declare the patient incompetent for refusing

trap.name: Capacity-punishment trap
trap.note: Disagreement isn't incapacity; capacity turns on the four abilities.

items.why: Autonomy governs: a capacitated patient may refuse even life-sustaining treatment, and disagreement with the team does not establish incapacity.
items.pearl: A capacitated patient may refuse even life-sustaining treatment; a 'wrong' choice isn't incapacity.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Autonomy and refusal of treatment.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

items.stem: A patient permanently lacks capacity and has no advance directive, but the surrogate knows the patient's long-standing values and prior wishes about a proposed procedure. Which standard applies first?

options.t: The surrogate's own preference

trap.name: Surrogate-substitution trap
trap.note: The surrogate represents the patient's wishes, not personal preference.

options.t: Best interest despite known patient values

trap.name: Skips-the-hierarchy trap
trap.note: Best interest is the fallback when the patient's wishes and values are unknown.

options.t: Substituted judgment based on known values and prior wishes
Whatever the physician prefers

trap.name: Deference trap
trap.note: The decision belongs to the surrogate applying the patient's values, with clinician guidance.

items.why: When the patient's values or prior wishes are known, the surrogate applies substituted judgment — what the patient would have chosen. Best interest is the fallback when those wishes and values are unknown.
items.pearl: Surrogate hierarchy: known wishes or values → substituted judgment → best interest when values are unknown.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Surrogate decision-making.

items.stem: A patient repeatedly produces factitious illness — contaminating urine samples and injecting herself to cause infection — with no external reward, apparently to occupy the sick role. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Malingering for external incentive

trap.name: External-incentive error
trap.note: Malingering is intentional symptoms for an external incentive; none is present here.

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder

trap.name: Intentionality error
trap.note: Somatic symptom disorder is not intentionally produced.

options.t: Illness anxiety disorder

trap.name: Wrong-mechanism trap
trap.note: Illness anxiety is preoccupation with having illness, not self-induced disease.

options.t: Factitious disorder imposed on self

items.why: Factitious disorder is intentional falsification/induction of illness to assume the sick role WITHOUT external incentive; malingering has an external incentive; SSD/illness anxiety are not intentionally produced.
items.pearl: Factitious = deliberate, sick-role, no external gain; malingering = deliberate, external gain; SSD = not intentional.
items.evidence: t_somatic.md — Factitious disorder vs malingering vs SSD.

items.stem: Fourteen months after her spouse's death, a woman has persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with the deceased, difficulty accepting the death, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, and a feeling that life is meaningless. Symptoms impair function and exceed her cultural norms. Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis best fits?

options.t: Prolonged grief disorder
Normal bereavement

trap.name: Under-call trap
trap.note: Grief this intense and impairing beyond ~12 months, exceeding cultural norms, is prolonged grief disorder.

options.t: Major depressive disorder

trap.name: Overlap trap
trap.note: Grief centers on yearning/preoccupation with the deceased; they can co-occur but are distinguishable.

options.t: Adjustment disorder

trap.name: Duration/threshold trap
trap.note: Adjustment disorder is shorter-term; the persistent ≥12-month grief syndrome is prolonged grief disorder.

items.why: Prolonged grief disorder is grief-specific: at least 12 months after the death of a close person in adults, intense yearning or preoccupation plus additional grief symptoms causes impairment and exceeds cultural norms. MDD can co-occur, but grief centers on yearning and preoccupation with the deceased.
items.pearl: Prolonged grief disorder: persistent yearning/preoccupation plus grief-specific symptoms beyond 12 months in adults, with impairment beyond cultural norms.
items.evidence: t_mood.md — Grief vs depression anchor: prolonged grief disorder vs normal bereavement vs MDD.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with heavy alcohol use is admitted with confusion, gaze-evoked nystagmus with impaired eye movements, and a wide-based unsteady gait. What is the immediate priority?

options.t: Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose
Give IV dextrose immediately to correct presumed hypoglycemia

trap.name: Glucose-first trap
trap.note: Giving glucose before thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy — thiamine goes first.

options.t: Start a benzodiazepine taper and defer thiamine

trap.name: Wrong-priority trap
trap.note: Withdrawal management matters, but the ophthalmoplegia-ataxia-confusion triad demands thiamine now.

options.t: Obtain an MRI before any treatment

trap.name: Delay trap
trap.note: Wernicke is a clinical diagnosis treated empirically and urgently; imaging must not delay thiamine.

items.why: The triad of encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia is Wernicke encephalopathy. Give thiamine before glucose, because a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen it.
items.pearl: Wernicke = confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia; give thiamine BEFORE glucose.
items.evidence: t_sud.md — Alcohol: Wernicke encephalopathy and thiamine.
items.retiredReason: Redundant: Wernicke/thiamine-before-glucose is already triple-covered by attested qb_sud_002, qb_sud_003, qb_sud_007.

items.stem: A patient with alcohol use disorder is medically stable and motivated to cut down, with compensated cirrhosis. Which maintenance pharmacotherapy is a reasonable first-line choice?

options.t: Naltrexone (if no contraindication) or acamprosate — both are first-line for alcohol use disorder
A scheduled long-term benzodiazepine

trap.name: Dependence trap
trap.note: Benzodiazepines treat withdrawal, not maintenance, and carry dependence and overdose risk in this population.

options.t: Disulfiram as the automatic first choice for everyone

trap.name: Adherence trap
trap.note: Disulfiram is aversive and adherence-dependent; it is not first-line and requires abstinence and reliability.

options.t: No pharmacotherapy is effective for alcohol use disorder

trap.name: Nihilism trap
trap.note: Naltrexone and acamprosate have solid evidence for reducing drinking/relapse.

items.why: Naltrexone (reduces heavy drinking; avoid in acute hepatitis/opioid use) and acamprosate (supports abstinence; usable in liver disease, adjust in renal impairment) are first-line for AUD. Disulfiram is second-line and adherence-dependent.
items.pearl: AUD maintenance: naltrexone or acamprosate first-line; disulfiram is adherence-dependent second-line.
items.evidence: t_sud.md — Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy.
items.retiredReason: Redundant: AUD maintenance (naltrexone/acamprosate first-line) duplicates attested qb_sud_009; fold the compensated-cirrhosis nuance into qb_sud_009 if desired.

items.stem: A 22-year-old has had delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech for the past 3 months with functional decline and no mood episode or substance cause. Which diagnosis best fits at this point?

options.t: Schizophrenia

trap.name: Duration trap
trap.note: Schizophrenia requires ≥6 months of continuous signs; at 3 months the correct label is schizophreniform.

options.t: Brief psychotic disorder

trap.name: Duration trap
trap.note: Brief psychotic disorder resolves within 1 month; this has lasted 3 months.

options.t: Delusional disorder

trap.name: Symptom-profile trap
trap.note: Delusional disorder features non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations/disorganization and relatively preserved function.

options.t: Schizophreniform disorder

items.why: Psychotic symptoms lasting 1–6 months with functional decline, no mood/substance cause, is schizophreniform disorder. <1 month = brief psychotic disorder; ≥6 months = schizophrenia.
items.pearl: Psychosis duration: <1 mo = brief psychotic; 1–6 mo = schizophreniform; ≥6 mo = schizophrenia.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Duration and mood anchors: brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, and schizophrenia.

items.stem: A patient has had auditory hallucinations and delusions for two weeks with no significant mood symptoms during that period, but has also had major depressive episodes during most of the illness. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Schizoaffective disorder
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

trap.name: Overlap trap
trap.note: In MDD with psychotic features, psychosis occurs ONLY during mood episodes; here psychosis persisted ≥2 weeks WITHOUT mood symptoms.

options.t: Schizophrenia without prominent mood burden

trap.name: Mood-burden trap
trap.note: Schizophrenia does not feature mood episodes for the majority of the illness, which are present here.

options.t: Bipolar I with psychotic features

trap.name: History trap
trap.note: No manic episode is described; the mood burden is depressive with independent psychosis.

items.why: Schizoaffective disorder requires a period of at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms, plus mood episodes present for the majority of the illness. Psychosis confined to mood episodes is mood disorder with psychotic features; schizophrenia does not have mood episodes occupying most of the illness.
items.pearl: Schizoaffective: ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms + mood episodes for most of the illness.
items.evidence: t_psychosis.md — Duration and mood anchors: schizoaffective disorder vs mood disorder with psychotic features.

items.stem: A young man with schizophrenia is being discharged to his parents. Which family intervention has the best evidence for reducing his relapse risk?

options.t: Keeping illness discussion out of the discharge plan

trap.name: Avoidance trap
trap.note: Silence does not lower expressed emotion or relapse; structured psychoeducation does.

options.t: Family psychoeducation (including multifamily groups)
Limiting family contact as the relapse-prevention plan

trap.name: Isolation trap
trap.note: Cutting off support is not evidence-based; improving the family climate is.

options.t: Individual insight-oriented therapy for the patient alone

trap.name: Wrong-target trap
trap.note: Insight therapy is not the intervention shown to reduce relapse via the family pathway.

items.why: Family psychoeducation and multifamily group approaches reduce relapse in schizophrenia, largely by lowering expressed emotion and improving problem-solving and support.
items.pearl: Family psychoeducation reduces schizophrenia relapse — the evidence-based family intervention.
items.evidence: family_modalities.md — Family psychoeducation and relapse prevention.

items.stem: A patient with alcohol use disorder says, 'I don't really think my drinking is a problem.' Which response best reflects motivational interviewing?

options.t: 'You clearly have a serious problem and need to stop now.'

trap.name: Righting-reflex trap
trap.note: Confronting and directing typically increases resistance; MI evokes the patient's own change talk.

options.t: 'If you don't quit, you'll end up back in the hospital.'

trap.name: Fear-appeal trap
trap.note: Warnings and pressure tend to entrench ambivalence rather than resolve it.

options.t: 'What have you noticed about how drinking fits with the things that matter to you?'
'Fine, it's your choice — let me know if you ever want help.'

trap.name: Disengagement trap
trap.note: Passive withdrawal abandons the alliance; MI stays engaged and curious.

items.why: Motivational interviewing rolls with resistance and evokes the patient's own reasons for change through open, values-linked questions — rather than confronting, warning, or disengaging (the 'righting reflex').
items.pearl: MI evokes change talk with open, values-linked questions; avoid the confronting 'righting reflex.'
items.evidence: motivational_interviewing.md — MI spirit: evoking change talk.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

items.stem: A patient's adult son calls the unit asking for details of his mother's diagnosis and medications. The patient has not authorized this. What is the most appropriate response?

options.t: Share diagnosis and medications because he is family

trap.name: Family-exception myth
trap.note: Family status alone does not authorize protected clinical disclosure.

options.t: Refuse any conversation and hang up

trap.name: Over-restriction trap
trap.note: You can listen and provide general education without disclosing protected specifics.

options.t: Verify identity, then disclose the full record

trap.name: Identity-only trap
trap.note: Identity verification does not substitute for the patient's authorization to disclose.

options.t: No specific disclosure without consent; general support is okay

items.why: Without the patient's consent, do not confirm or share specific diagnosis or medication information. You can still listen, offer general support and education, and coordinate a consented family meeting; safety exceptions are separate.
items.pearl: No consent means no specific disclosure; general support and education are still allowed.
items.evidence: family_modalities.md — Confidentiality and families; ethics_legal.md — disclosure.

items.stem: A patient with panic disorder and frequent panic attacks wants long-term treatment. Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic option?

options.t: SSRI plus CBT maintenance
Long-term benzodiazepine monotherapy

trap.name: Dependence trap
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are short-term bridges at most; they are not first-line maintenance.

options.t: An antipsychotic for maintenance

trap.name: Off-target trap
trap.note: Antipsychotics are not first-line for panic disorder.

options.t: Reassurance without structured treatment

trap.name: Nihilism trap
trap.note: Panic disorder has effective first-line treatment with SSRIs and CBT.

items.why: SSRIs, paired with CBT such as interoceptive exposure, are first-line for panic disorder. Benzodiazepines are short-term bridges at most given dependence risk.
items.pearl: Panic disorder: SSRI plus CBT first-line; benzodiazepines are not maintenance monotherapy.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Exam treatment anchors: panic disorder treatment.

items.stem: A patient with OCD has distressing obsessions and time-consuming compulsions. Which is the evidence-based first-line treatment?

options.t: A benzodiazepine as monotherapy

trap.name: Wrong-mechanism trap
trap.note: Benzodiazepines do not treat the core of OCD; ERP and SSRIs do.

options.t: An SSRI (often at higher doses) plus exposure and response prevention
Supportive therapy alone without exposure work

trap.name: Under-treatment trap
trap.note: Generic support without ERP is not the evidence-based psychotherapy for OCD.

options.t: An antipsychotic as first-line monotherapy

trap.name: Adjunct-vs-first-line trap
trap.note: Antipsychotics are an augmentation strategy in refractory OCD, not first-line monotherapy.

items.why: OCD is treated first-line with an SSRI (frequently at higher doses than for depression) plus exposure and response prevention (ERP). Clomipramine is an effective second-line agent; antipsychotics augment refractory cases.
items.pearl: OCD: SSRI (higher dose) + ERP first-line; clomipramine second-line; antipsychotic augmentation if refractory.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Exam treatment anchors: OCD treatment; psychotherapy.md — ERP.

items.stem: A veteran with PTSD has nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance. Which approach is first-line, and what should generally be avoided?

options.t: Scheduled benzodiazepines as the mainstay

trap.name: Harm trap
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in PTSD because they do not treat core symptoms and carry risk.

options.t: Antipsychotic monotherapy for core symptoms

trap.name: Off-target trap
trap.note: Antipsychotics are not first-line monotherapy for core PTSD.

options.t: Trauma-focused psychotherapy and/or SSRI/SNRI; avoid routine benzodiazepines
Watchful waiting without treatment

trap.name: Nihilism trap
trap.note: Effective trauma-focused therapies and medication options exist.

items.why: First-line PTSD care prioritizes trauma-focused psychotherapy such as CPT or prolonged exposure, with sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine as medication options when medication is chosen. Routine benzodiazepines are generally avoided.
items.pearl: PTSD: trauma-focused therapy first; SSRI/SNRI when medication is chosen; avoid routine benzodiazepines.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Exam treatment anchors: PTSD treatment and benzodiazepine avoidance.

items.stem: A student develops intense anxiety only when performing music in public but is comfortable in other social situations. Which best describes the condition and a reasonable option?

options.t: Social anxiety disorder, Performance type requiring PRN medication
Generalized anxiety disorder requiring daily long-term medication

trap.name: Overgeneralization trap
trap.note: Anxiety limited to performance is not pervasive GAD; the performance-only subtype can be managed PRN.

options.t: Panic disorder requiring PRN medication

trap.name: Wrong-dx trap
trap.note: There are no recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about attacks; this is performance-limited social anxiety.

options.t: A normal reaction requiring no discussion

trap.name: Dismissal trap
trap.note: Impairing performance anxiety is a recognized, treatable condition.

items.why: Anxiety confined to discrete public performances is performance-only social anxiety. When medically appropriate, a PRN beta-blocker can reduce tremor, tachycardia, and sweating for those events; generalized social anxiety is treated with CBT/exposure and SSRI/SNRI when medication is needed.
items.pearl: Performance-only social anxiety: PRN beta-blocker for physical performance symptoms; generalized social anxiety needs CBT/exposure ± SSRI/SNRI.
items.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Exam treatment anchors: performance-only social anxiety.
