items.stem: A patient with depression and passive suicidal ideation is being discharged. Which single intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing suicide death?

options.t: Means restriction — counseling to remove or secure firearms and lethal medications
Having the patient sign a no-suicide contract

trap.name: Contract myth
trap.note: No-suicide contracts are not protective and can create false reassurance; a collaborative safety plan is preferred.

options.t: Scheduling routine follow-up in three months

trap.name: Gap trap
trap.note: A distant single appointment leaves the highest-risk early window uncovered.

options.t: Prescribing a large supply of a sedative for sleep

trap.name: Access trap
trap.note: A large lethal supply increases risk; means restriction is the goal.

items.why: Means restriction — especially securing or removing firearms and limiting access to lethal medication — is the most evidence-based single intervention to reduce suicide death. No-suicide contracts are not protective.
items.pearl: Means restriction (firearms above all) is the highest-yield suicide-prevention step; contracts are not protective.
items.evidence: suicide.md — Means restriction; safety planning.

link.label: Open the Suicide Risk & Safety Planning page

items.stem: During which period is a psychiatric patient's suicide risk generally highest?

options.t: The middle of a long stable outpatient course

trap.name: Low-acuity trap
trap.note: Risk is not highest during stable maintenance; transitions carry the peak.

options.t: The immediate post-discharge period after a psychiatric hospitalization
During the acute inpatient stay

trap.name: Setting trap
trap.note: The inpatient stay is comparatively protected; the transition out is the higher-risk window.

options.t: Suicide risk is constant and does not vary over time

trap.name: Flat-risk trap
trap.note: Risk is dynamic; the peri- and post-discharge transition is a recognized high-risk window.

items.why: The peri-discharge and especially the immediate post-discharge period is among the highest-risk windows. Discharge planning — follow-up, safety planning, means restriction — is a safety intervention, not paperwork.
items.pearl: Highest-risk window is right after discharge — treat the transition as the intervention.
items.evidence: suicide.md — High-risk windows and discharge planning.

items.stem: A patient on an SSRI is started on tramadol and develops agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, and lower-extremity clonus with hyperreflexia. What is the diagnosis, and the key bedside discriminator from NMS?

options.t: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — lead-pipe rigidity

trap.name: Wrong-syndrome trap
trap.note: NMS follows dopamine blockade and shows lead-pipe rigidity with lower reflexes, not clonus and hyperreflexia.

options.t: Anticholinergic toxicity — dry flushed skin

trap.name: Wet-vs-dry trap
trap.note: Anticholinergic toxicity is dry and flushed; serotonin syndrome is diaphoretic with clonus.

options.t: Serotonin syndrome — clonus and hyperreflexia
Malignant hyperthermia — anesthetic trigger

trap.name: Context trap
trap.note: Malignant hyperthermia follows volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, not a serotonergic combination.

items.why: A serotonergic combination (SSRI plus tramadol) with agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, lower-extremity clonus, and hyperreflexia is serotonin syndrome. The bedside discriminator from NMS is the neuromuscular exam: clonus/hyperreflexia in serotonin syndrome vs lead-pipe rigidity with lower reflexes in NMS.
items.pearl: Clonus and hyperreflexia after a serotonergic change = serotonin syndrome; NMS is lead-pipe rigidity after dopamine blockade.
items.evidence: toxidromes.md — Serotonin syndrome vs NMS discriminators.

items.stem: You are assessing a patient's risk of violence on the unit. Which is the single strongest predictor of future violence?

options.t: A specific psychiatric diagnosis alone

trap.name: Diagnosis-label trap
trap.note: Diagnosis alone is a weak predictor; past violent behavior is the strongest single predictor.

options.t: The patient's stated remorse

trap.name: Reassurance trap
trap.note: Stated remorse does not reliably lower short-term risk.

options.t: Male sex by itself

trap.name: Single-demographic trap
trap.note: Demographics contribute modestly; past violence is the dominant predictor.

options.t: A history of past violence

items.why: Past violence is the strongest single predictor of future violence. Distinguish static factors (history — fixed) from dynamic factors (acute psychosis, intoxication, agitation — modifiable and the treatment target).
items.pearl: Past violence is the best predictor; separate static (history) from dynamic (treatable) risk.
items.evidence: violence.md — Static vs dynamic risk; past violence as predictor.

items.stem: A 40-year-old executive expects constant admiration, believes he is uniquely special and entitled to the best of everything, and dismisses colleagues as beneath him; he becomes enraged by mild criticism. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Narcissistic personality disorder
Antisocial personality disorder

trap.name: Rights-violation trap
trap.note: ASPD centers on disregard for and violation of others' rights; NPD centers on grandiosity, entitlement, and need for admiration.

options.t: Histrionic personality disorder

trap.name: Attention-mechanism trap
trap.note: Histrionic patients seek attention through emotionality/seductiveness, not grandiosity and entitlement.

options.t: Bipolar disorder, manic episode

trap.name: State-vs-trait trap
trap.note: Mania is an episodic mood state; this is an enduring characterological pattern.

items.why: Grandiosity, need for admiration, entitlement, and lack of empathy define narcissistic personality disorder — distinct from antisocial (rights violations) and histrionic (attention through emotionality).
items.pearl: NPD = grandiosity + need for admiration + entitlement + lack of empathy.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: narcissistic personality disorder.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman cannot make everyday decisions without excessive reassurance, feels helpless when alone, and urgently seeks a new relationship for care whenever one ends. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Avoidant personality disorder

trap.name: Cluster-C mix-up
trap.note: Avoidant patients want relationships but avoid them from fear of criticism/rejection; dependent patients cling and urgently seek care.

options.t: Dependent personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: BPD conflation
trap.note: BPD features identity disturbance, self-harm, and unstable intense relationships, not the pure submissive/clinging dependence described.

options.t: Histrionic personality disorder

trap.name: Attention-seeking trap
trap.note: Histrionic is attention-seeking emotionality, not the need to be cared for described here.

items.why: A pervasive, excessive need to be taken care of — submissiveness, difficulty making decisions without reassurance, and urgently seeking a replacement relationship for care — defines dependent personality disorder (Cluster C).
items.pearl: Dependent PD = excessive need to be cared for, submissive/clinging, urgently replaces lost relationships.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: dependent personality disorder.

items.stem: A 29-year-old is uncomfortable when not the center of attention, is dramatic and seductive with staff, shows rapidly shifting shallow emotions, and considers acquaintances closer than they are. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: BPD conflation
trap.note: BPD features abandonment fears, identity disturbance, and self-harm; histrionic centers on attention-seeking emotionality and seductiveness.

options.t: Narcissistic personality disorder

trap.name: Grandiosity trap
trap.note: Narcissistic patients seek admiration for specialness; histrionic patients seek attention through emotionality.

options.t: Histrionic personality disorder
Dependent personality disorder

trap.name: Cluster-C mix-up
trap.note: Dependent patients seek care and reassurance, not attention through dramatic emotionality.

items.why: Excessive attention-seeking, dramatic and seductive behavior, shallow shifting emotions, and overestimating intimacy define histrionic personality disorder (Cluster B).
items.pearl: Histrionic PD = attention-seeking, dramatic/seductive, shallow shifting emotions.
items.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: histrionic personality disorder.

items.stem: A 7-year-old refuses school, complains of stomachaches on school mornings that resolve on weekends, and is terrified that something will happen to his mother while apart. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Over-broad trap
trap.note: GAD is pervasive worry across domains; here the fear is specifically about separation from an attachment figure.

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder

trap.name: Defiance mislabel
trap.note: This is fear-driven school refusal, not an angry/defiant pattern.

options.t: Malingering for external gain

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: The somatic complaints are anxiety-driven, not consciously feigned for external gain.

options.t: Separation anxiety disorder

items.why: Developmentally inappropriate, excessive fear of separation from attachment figures — with somatic complaints and school refusal, lasting ≥4 weeks in a child — is separation anxiety disorder.
items.pearl: Separation anxiety disorder: excessive separation fear, somatic complaints, school refusal (≥4 weeks in children).
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: separation anxiety disorder.

items.stem: A 6-year-old repeatedly soils his underwear; exam reveals a large stool mass and history of painful, infrequent bowel movements. Best diagnosis and initial management?

options.t: Retentive encopresis from constipation
Conduct disorder with deliberate defiance

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: Retentive encopresis with overflow is not willful defiance; it stems from constipation.

options.t: Primary psychotic process

trap.name: Overpathologizing
trap.note: Soiling from constipation is not a psychotic symptom.

options.t: Normal age-appropriate behavior

trap.name: Under-call trap
trap.note: Encopresis is diagnosed at chronological age 4 or older and warrants treatment.

items.why: Encopresis at age 4 or older is often retentive with overflow incontinence. Treat the constipation with disimpaction and maintenance, add toileting routine and behavioral support, and avoid punishment.
items.pearl: Encopresis: usually retentive overflow — treat the constipation first, add behavioral measures.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: encopresis.

items.stem: A 6-year-old speaks normally at home but consistently fails to speak at school, where she is otherwise engaged; this has lasted the school year and impairs learning. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Autism spectrum disorder

trap.name: Social-communication trap
trap.note: ASD involves pervasive social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors; selective mutism is situation-specific with normal speech elsewhere.

options.t: Selective mutism
A language (communication) disorder

trap.name: Capacity trap
trap.note: The child can speak normally at home; the failure is situational, pointing to an anxiety disorder, not a language deficit.

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder

trap.name: Defiance mislabel
trap.note: The mutism is anxiety-driven, not willful defiance.

items.why: Selective mutism is a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations (e.g., school) despite speaking normally elsewhere, interfering with functioning — an anxiety-spectrum disorder, not a language or defiance problem.
items.pearl: Selective mutism: won't speak in specific settings but speaks normally elsewhere — an anxiety disorder.
items.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: selective mutism.

items.stem: During an interview, a child discloses details strongly suggesting physical abuse at home. The parent asks you to keep it confidential. What must you do?

options.t: Keep it confidential because the parent requested it

trap.name: Confidentiality-override trap
trap.note: Confidentiality yields to mandatory reporting of suspected child abuse; a parent cannot waive that duty.

options.t: Wait until you have definitive proof before reporting

trap.name: Proof trap
trap.note: Reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof.

options.t: Make a mandated report to child protective services based on reasonable suspicion
Wait for the child to request a report

trap.name: Assent trap
trap.note: The duty to report does not depend on the child's request.

items.why: Suspected child abuse is a mandatory report based on reasonable suspicion — you do not need proof, and confidentiality (including a parent's request) does not override the duty. Elder/dependent-adult abuse carries similar duties.
items.pearl: Suspected child abuse = mandatory report on reasonable suspicion; confidentiality does not override it.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Mandatory reporting.

items.stem: A 15-year-old comes alone requesting evaluation. Which statement about consent for a minor is most accurate?

options.t: Parental consent is required for every non-emergency service

trap.name: Absolutism trap
trap.note: Emancipated-minor, confidential-service, and emergency exceptions vary by jurisdiction.

options.t: A minor has broad adult authority for routine care

trap.name: Over-broad trap
trap.note: Minors do not have blanket adult authority; parental consent is the general rule.

options.t: Emergency care waits while staff reach a parent

trap.name: Emergency trap
trap.note: Emergency care proceeds under implied consent when delay would cause harm.

options.t: Parental consent is usual, with defined exceptions

items.why: Parental consent is the general rule for minors, but important exceptions exist: emancipated or mature minors, certain confidential services depending on jurisdiction, and the emergency exception. Local law matters.
items.pearl: Minors usually need parental consent, with jurisdiction-dependent confidential-service, emancipated-minor, and emergency exceptions.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Consent and minors.

items.stem: A hospitalized patient invites the student doctor to meet socially and offers a substantial personal gift. What is the appropriate response?

options.t: Decline the invitation and substantial gift respectfully
Accept both to preserve rapport

trap.name: Rapport-over-boundaries trap
trap.note: Rapport does not justify boundary violations; the therapeutic frame protects the patient.

options.t: Accept the gift but decline the social meeting

trap.name: Partial-boundary trap
trap.note: A substantial personal gift is itself a boundary crossing to avoid.

options.t: Revisit the invitation after discharge if both agree

trap.name: Timing trap
trap.note: Professional boundary concerns do not disappear at discharge.

items.why: Professional boundaries protect patients: decline social invitations and substantial personal gifts respectfully. Sexual or romantic involvement with a patient is never acceptable, and significant gifts or dual relationships are boundary crossings to avoid.
items.pearl: Decline significant gifts and dual relationships respectfully; sexual or romantic involvement with a patient is never acceptable.
items.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Professional boundaries.

items.stem: A 20-year-old has months of overwhelming daytime sleepiness with sudden, brief episodes of bilateral leg weakness triggered by laughter, plus vivid hallucinations while falling asleep and episodes of waking paralysis. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Obstructive sleep apnea

trap.name: Mechanism trap
trap.note: OSA causes fragmented sleep and sleepiness but not cataplexy, the emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss described.

options.t: Narcolepsy (type 1, with cataplexy)
A primary psychotic disorder

trap.name: Hallucination trap
trap.note: Hypnagogic hallucinations at sleep onset are a narcolepsy feature, not a primary psychosis.

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Wrong-domain trap
trap.note: The tetrad points to narcolepsy, not anxiety.

items.why: The narcolepsy tetrad — excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations — with low CSF orexin/hypocretin defines narcolepsy type 1; MSLT shows short REM latency.
items.pearl: Narcolepsy: sleepiness + cataplexy + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations; low orexin.
items.evidence: t_sleep.md — Narcolepsy.

items.stem: A woman develops sudden left-arm paralysis after an argument; exam shows a positive Hoover sign and findings inconsistent with any neuroanatomic lesion, and workup is normal. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Malingering for external incentive

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: Functional neurologic symptoms are not consciously produced for external gain.

options.t: Factitious disorder imposed on self

trap.name: Sick-role trap
trap.note: Factitious disorder involves deliberate falsification for the sick role; conversion is not intentional.

options.t: Functional neurological symptom disorder
Acute ischemic stroke

trap.name: Exam trap
trap.note: A positive Hoover sign and neuroanatomically incompatible findings with normal workup argue against a structural lesion.

items.why: Neurologic symptoms with internal inconsistency incompatible with recognized disease, such as a positive Hoover sign, define functional neurological symptom disorder when not intentionally produced. It is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive signs, not merely normal tests.
items.pearl: Functional neurological symptom disorder is ruled in by positive inconsistent signs, not by accusation or exclusion alone.
items.evidence: t_somatic.md — Functional neurological symptom (conversion) disorder.

items.stem: A woman with a severe childhood trauma history has recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events and describes two distinct identity states with different names and behaviors that others have witnessed. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: Identity-disturbance trap
trap.note: BPD identity disturbance is an unstable self-image, not distinct alternating identity states with amnesia.

options.t: Malingering for external gain

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: The presentation, corroborated by others and tied to severe trauma, is not simply feigned for gain.

options.t: Schizophrenia with primary psychosis

trap.name: Psychosis conflation
trap.note: 'Split personality' is not schizophrenia; DID involves identity states and amnesia, not primary psychosis.

options.t: Dissociative identity disorder

items.why: Two or more distinct personality states plus recurrent amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting, strongly associated with severe early trauma, defines dissociative identity disorder — commonly confused with (but distinct from) schizophrenia.
items.pearl: DID = ≥2 distinct identity states + amnesia, linked to severe early trauma; not schizophrenia.
items.evidence: t_dissociative.md — Dissociative identity disorder.
